#3524. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3: The Secret Fire Explained

You cannot pass! The dark fire will not avail you, flame of spoilers for "The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 3, "The Secret Fire."

"The Rings of Power" Season 3 does a lot of things right, especially when Sauron is on screen attempting to make a shiny piece of jewelry to master all other pieces of jewelry — all while being haunted by the ghost of Celebrimbor. Indeed, the show shines most when it focuses on the bad guys, like introducing the stunning-looking Nazgnagôl or Adam Young's orc with shifting loyalties and a penchant for poetry.

One thing that is different this season is the lack of mystery identities. We now know very well who Sauron is, we know that The Stranger is actually Gandalf, we finally learn this season who the Dark Wizard is, and we even know why Theo is still in this story. It's as if "The Rings of Power" creators J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay got tired of the waiting around and decided to have god himself come down and explain things directly at the audience.

Well, that is actually exactly what happens in Episode 3, because Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) has an actual burning bush moment and talks to the actual god of J. R. R. Tolkien's Legendarium to learn about the Secret Fire, and his purpose in the story.

In the episode, Tom Bombadil (Rory Kinnear) sends Gandalf on a quest to chase a rabbit. This leads Gandalf to an altar where the rabbit combusts into a flame that speaks to the wizard and explains he is the almighty, whose Secret Fire burns inside every creature on Middle-earth.

Even though "The Rings of Power" is set in a world of magic rings, dragons, dwarves and elves, we have not really seen a lot of thel supernatural — despite it being relatively common in Middle-earth. The world of J. R. R. Tolkien is one of angels and elves that get resurrected, a world that literally goes from flat to round when the creator of all existence gets angry at men and sinks an entire continent to the bottom of the sea.

This is the most overt example of supernatural fantasy we've got in "The Rings of Power" so far, as Gandalf hears a strange voice (Allan Corduner) coming from a manifestation of a flame. The flame gives Gandalf (after calling him by his original Quenya name Olórin) a cosmic vision as the voice reveals itself to be the one who "built the heavens and the stars," that which burns within all living things. As the voice says, "all of Middle-earth is cradled within my flame."

That is the Secret Fire, which is alluded to by Gandalf in the original "Lord of the Rings" trilogy. The Secret Fire, or Flame Imperishable, is Gandalf's higher calling, essentially the power of Tolkien's equivalent of God. Named Erū Ilúvatar, this being is the creator of the whole world, and his Secret Fire is what gives life to the universe. That fire is inside all living beings, and is the thing Morgoth craved most, because he was unable to create life without it, the reason he was driven to the shadow. In Tolkien's world, the Secret Fire is the equivalent of the Holy Spirit in Abrahamic religions, the manifestation of the almighty within all beings.

It is quite funny that "The Rings of Power" has arguably its biggest exposition dump of Season 3 come directly from god, who reveals to Gandalf the entire history of the Istari and reveals the identity of the Dark Wizard. After 2 seasons of audiences trying to work out the identity of the Dark Wizard and his purpose, along drops god from the heavens and just outright explains that he is actually a Blue Wizard and gives audiences the whole backstory in a single scene.

Of course, as shocking as Erū Ilúvatar appearing in "The Rings of Power" is, it makes sense for the show to introduce him now. That's because he has a big role to play in Season 4 and the fall of Númenor. Still, the idea that this show has now officially involved higher beings in the conflict against Sauron is a deep cut concept that separates this from other fantasy shows.

In Tolkien's text, the Valar (essentially the gods of Olympus under Erū Ilúvatar's Zeus) don't get directly involved in the wars of Middle-earth (at least not since Elrond's father convinced the Valar to physically aid in the fight against Morgoth), but their influence and power is felt all throughout the Second Age of Middle-earth and the war against Sauron. "The Rings of Power" leaning more into the supernatural fantasy of Tolkien is one way of making this already quite expansive world even more interesting and complex.

#3523. Boston Blue's [Spoiler] Recalls Past Suicide Attempt in Emotional Reveal

Boston Blue‘s newest episode took an emotional turn when a main character revealed a past suicide attempt.

During the Friday, November 13, episode of the CBS series, Sean Reagan (Mika Amonsen) and Jonah Silver (Marcus Scribner) searched for a fellow officer, whom they believed was a risk to himself. They were able to talk him down after Sean revealed his own mental health challenges. He specifically recalled struggling with suicidal ideation after his mother’s death and how a past attempt had pushed him to address his issues.

Before Boston Blue, Sean’s journey was featured on Blue Bloods, which ran from 2010 to 2024. The spinoff, which premiered in October 2025, kicked off with Danny (Donnie Wahlberg) visiting Boston after Sean ended up in a coma. This version of Sean looked a little different, as Andrew Terraciano previously played the role.

“There’s been some negativity [from viewers], for sure,” Amonsen exclusively told Us in November 2025 about taking over the part. “But when I look under those posts that have the negativity, there’s a lot of fans rallying for Sean and people saying that they really enjoyed this character that I’ve created — or my version of character.”

Amonsen noted that he wanted to make Blue Bloods fans happy with his performance, saying, “They’re really enjoying the show, and they love where it’s going in terms of Sean, and that makes me happy.”

The actor recalled feeling “a ton of pressure” over the situation.

“I felt the pressure to respect an actor before me because I wanted to respect Andrew the best I could. There were even certain visual choices that I made that I wanted to keep in terms of hair styling and certain ways of being [as Sean],” he continued. “I really want to maintain Sean as close as I can in the ways that I do it out of respect for this character that everyone loves — but also the character Andrew built.”

He continued: “When I booked the show, it all happened really quickly. It was within about a week’s time, and I was really thrown into it quickly. I did binge-watch as much as I could, and I found doing the later seasons was more helpful. I wanted to get a sense of who Sean was toward the end of the show. I really wanted to get a sense of his character at that point into adulthood and his relationship with Danny.”

Terraciano, meanwhile, broke his silence to Us about the shakeup.

“I had somebody call me — actually the day that I was graduating — and they had spoken to my mom, and she called me [crying]. They were like, ‘They might be looking for a different Sean,'” Terraciano shared with Us in December about the onscreen change. “Shortly after we got the news, Donnie called me. It was a really beautiful moment of getting to hear from an old friend but also somebody that you respect so much and have learned so much from.”

Terraciano expressed gratitude for his time on Blue Bloods.

“It’s beautiful because you’ll always remember every single line and every day that you had the opportunity to be that character,” he shared. “It doesn’t mean for even a second that somebody else can’t go and do something beautiful with it.”

Terraciano continued: “I got the joy of playing Sean, and I got to send him off into the world. Now somebody else gets that joy. We’re both getting to show what we do and then send Sean off into the world.”

Boston Blue airs on CBS Fridays at 10 p.m. ET.

Jordan Firstman spoke to CinemaBlend about his movie's conclusion.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Major spoilers ahead for Club Kid. Go see this movie before reading!

We're coming towards the end of 2026, and it's been a solid year for movies. I've seen plenty of them, but I've got to say that Jordan Firstman's Club Kid is my favorite film of the year. The new A24 movie tells a modern, queer story not unlike Big Daddy, where a 30-something party promoter in NYC suddenly finds out he's got a 10-year-old son. The pair find a way to bond, in a movie that's chock full of laughs, tears, and authentic LGBTQ+ representation. I had to ask Firstman about the movie's ending, and the decision not to show protagonist Peter and his son Arlo reuniting onscreen.

I loved how Club Kid portrayed queer nightlife, but the real heart of the story is about the father/son relationship between Peter and Arlo. After they develop a true love for each other, Arlo ends up taken away and sent back across the pond to England. It's truly heartbreaking, and after failing to get custody and a year-long time jump, Peter gets his first contact with his son via a phone call. This final scene absolutely destroyed me, and as you can see in the video above, I asked Firstman (who wrote, directed, and starred in the movie) why we hear Arlo but never actually see him during the call. He explained to me:

We're with Peter from moment one of this movie, and I felt that I wanted the audience to feel what Peter felt. And so when you hear his voice for the first time and you haven't seen him in so long, like, you feel what Peter feels. Like, that's why he's crying. It's like, you know, when [Oscar] says, 'Good cry or bad cry?' It's just like a release. It's just emotional. You know what I mean? And sometimes you can't put words to, like, what the emotion is. I have visions of like, when I see my ex for the first time that I haven't seen since we broke up. I'm gonna, like, I don't know. When I think about it, I start crying. I don't know, people probably feel this way with death too.

Honestly, he's not wrong. While it would have been satisfying to see Peter visiting Arlo in the U.K., or even seeing the latter's coverage in their phone call scene, it might have cheapened the emotional impact of Club Kid's ending. Instead, we stay in Peter's POV the entire time, as he's supported by Diego Calva's Oscar. Firstman offers an emotionally devastating performance, with the mixture of joy, loss, and hope all registering on his face at the same time.

It's heartwarming watching Peter and Arlo connect with each other throughout Club Kid's 121-minute runtime, which makes their separation and year-long span of no contact all the more tragic. At that point of the movie the audience (myself included) is invested in their relationship, and likely would have loved to see them back together again. Later in our conversation, Firstman spoke more about his decision not to give us that resolution, telling me:

It's grief, you know what I mean? And, like, so, so I just wanted the audience to be there with Peter and, like, and, you know, there was, there were also fights about that with, like one of my producers really wanted me to shoot coverage of Arlo. And I was like, 'No.' I was like, 'It just defeats the entire point. Like, you have to... You... The audience can't ever see him again if Peter doesn't.'

Firstman has made fans laugh through his performances in English Teacher and I Love LA (the latter of which is streaming with a HBO Max subscription), but his dramatic work in Club Kid's third act is remarkable. The fact that he both directed and wrote the brilliant dramedy is even more impressive. While I would have loved to see the movie's two lead characters get a reunion, I respect his creative decision to curtail this, with the audience never getting a chance to see Arlo again after he's taken away.

Club Kid is in theaters now as part of the 2026 movie release list. While it's in limited release, I highly recommend finding a screener near you. Although I'd advise bringing some tissues along just in case.

#3521. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

#3520. Jensen Huang’s Scandal Explained: Alleged Affairs and Spying Claims

Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang is at the center of a major scandal involving alleged affairs, suspected Chinese espionage and questions about his leadership.

Jensen, 63, cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and helped build the technology giant into a global tech powerhouse.

Nvidia is best known for producing the advanced computer chips that power artificial intelligence systems, making it hugely influential in the AI industry.

Jensen, who has been married to his wife, Lori Huang, since 1985, is facing scrutiny following reports about his personal relationships and a possible connection to a Chinese intelligence operation.

So, what exactly happened? Scroll on for everything to know about the Jensen Huang scandal.

Jensen admitted to cheating on his wife via a message to Nvidia employees sent on November 8.

In the statement, he apologized for being “unfaithful” to Lori and “letting down” his family. (The couple share two children.)

“There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he wrote. “Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.”

Jensen did not share additional details about his alleged affair or release any names of anyone involved.

Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, (no family relation to Jensen Huang) has been linked to Jensen. She is also known as Huang Le.

Speculation around the nature of their relationship has caused huge controversy.

According to reports, Jensen developed a personal relationship with Alice, who worked as an executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed International.

Investigators reportedly raised concerns that she may have been a “honey trap,” potentially using her relationship with Jensen to gain access to sensitive business information.

However, the espionage allegations have not been publicly proven, and there is no established evidence that Jensen knowingly passed sensitive information to China or that Alice was acting as a spy.

China has rejected the espionage allegations, dismissing them as baseless. Alice has not publicly responded to the claims.

Further allegations of more extra-marital affairs involving the tech billionaire have since emerged.

According to The New York Times, Jensen was also linked to Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare.

Reuters subsequently reported on November 12 that Jensen allegedly had an intimate relationship with another woman who worked at Nvidia. Her identity has not been publicly disclosed.

Reuters reported that efforts to reach the woman were unsuccessful, and Nvidia declined to comment.

Us reached out to Powell and Nvidia for further comment.

As Jensen continues to face backlash, he resigned as Nvidia CEO on November 12, after more than three decades leading the company.

“The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” Nvidia said in a news release announcing his resignation.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO while the board attempts to find a permanent replacement.

Nvidia’s board reportedly launched an independent investigation into whether Jensen had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation and whether any confidential company information may have been compromised.

#3519. Marvel Officially Confirms Whether RDJ's Doctor Doom Is A Tony Stark Variant

When Marvel Studios announced Robert Downey Jr. would play Doctor Doom in "Avengers: Doomsday" fans used one word to describe it: desperate. But anticipation for RDJ's return has only grown as "Doomsday" has drawn nearer. Still, significant confusion remains. After all, Downey Jr.'s best-known role is that of Tony Stark/Iron Man in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Now, he's back in that same franchise as a supervillain? It's all a bit confounding, really, and while Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige has just tried to clear it all up, he's also somehow made things even more confusing.

Speaking to Empire, Feige was asked whether RDJ is playing a Tony Stark variant in "Doomsday" or an entirely different character. The Marvel Studios boss seemed to indicate the latter is true. "Is Steve Rogers a Johnny Storm variant?" he said in reference to Chris Evans having played both characters at different points throughout Marvel's cinematic history. "People wondered, 'Is Doom just a variant of another character? Is this just a shortcut to bringing back another character?' The answer is no. He's Victor Von Doom."

Evans played Johnny Storm in a an entirely different cinematic universe, specifically portraying the Fantastic Four member in the 20th Century Fox Marvel movies. He then played Steve Rogers/Captain America in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Downey Jr., however, played Tony Stark in the MCU and is now back as Victor Von Doom in that same universe. Sure, the multiverse has made all of this more nebulous. We saw Evans' Johnny Storm in "Deadpool & Wolverine," which means both he and Evans' Steve Rogers could, conceivably, appear together in the MCU. But it would surely feel like a letdown to bring back the most popular and important actor in MCU history as a villain and let that be that.

Doctor Doom was once Iron Man in the comics, and in 2010's "What If? Iron Man: Demon in an Armor" an amnesiac Tony Stark became the supervillain. But Kevin Feige has seemingly confirmed the Victor Von Doom of "Avengers: Doomsday" is like neither of these examples.

According to the Marvel Studios head, Robert Downey Jr. is playing an entirely separate character to Tony Stark, likely thanks to the multiversal incursions that threaten to collapse the universe in "Doomsday." What we'll essentially see, then, is a character named Victor Von Doom who hails from an entirely different timeline to the main MCU (likely the one that gave us 2025's "Fantastic Four: First Steps"), has no connection to Tony Stark, and just happens to look like the former Iron Man. I feel confident in saying that this only raises more questions. Is there another Tony Stark in Doom's timeline? Is there really no connection at all between RDJ's villain and the Iron Man of the MCU?

Regardless, "Doomsday" directors Joe and Anthony Russo promised Empire that this Doctor Doom will be a truly scary villain, with Joe saying he's "a Gothic character" and "a very powerful character with some very dark magic" who's "not above selling his soul to get what he wants. He's worth being scared of." Interestingly, the co-director added that RDJ's Doom is a "father who's a victim of trauma" and that he has "lost a child." The only parallel there between Downey Jr.'s Tony Stark and his Doom is that the former was once particularly shaken by losing Tom Holland's Spider-Man to Thanos' snap in 'Avengers: Infinity War." Otherwise, he's never lost a child, which is further proof that this is a different character and not a Tony Stark variant.

According to Joe Russo, those who've seen early screenings of "Avengers: Doomsday" have said "it's a very scary movie" due to Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom being "so profoundly damaged." Clearly, the loss of his child is what drives this particular incarnation of Doom — which puts some of the "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer footage in context. In the trailer, we hear Vanessa Kirby's Sue Storm/Invisible Woman saying, "Victor [...] used to be different. He used to be kind, he used to be caring. And then, everything he loved was taken from him." This is obviously in reference to the loss of his child. In that same trailer, Doom accuses all the heroes of having lived "stolen lives," suggesting that something they did in previous MCU installments might have triggered the event that led to his child's death.

Unfortunately, while Downey Jr. did talk to Empire, he didn't shed much light on the Tony Stark variant question. Instead he talked about Michael Douglas at the end of "Falling Down," saying "He goes, 'I'm the bad guy?' I had that realization a couple of days into shooting 'Doomsday,' because all the heroes are over there, and I'm the problem." The actor recalled having "leaned in" to being the villain and having a "glorious time." That's lovely Rob, but are you Iron Man or not? Otherwise, he described Doom as being on a "scorched earth" mission, adding "Whatever you think he may be entertaining, I would ten times it, and you'll probably be closer to the ballpark."

Did Marvel really bring back RDJ without intending to at least hint at Tony Stark's possible return? It seems unbelievable. For now, we'll have to wait until "Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026 to find out.

#3518. See Bruce Springsteen, Martin Scorsese, and Surprise Guest Tom Cruise Honor Steven Spielberg at MoMA

Bruce Springsteen and Steven Spielberg are good friends. They’ve vacationed together a number of times on the director’s yacht, the Seven Seas. They went to Portofino in 2019, Sicily in 2017, and to Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat in 2024—the latter time with Bono and The Edge. But when Springsteen took the stage at MoMA Thursday night to toast Spielberg at the museum’s annual Film Benefit, he had a bone to pick with the director.

“In June of 1975, I went to a small theater directly across from the Atlantic Ocean and I saw Jaws. I was 25 years old,” Springsteen said. “Now, one of the great pleasures on the Jersey Shore in 1975 was night swimming, preferably naked, on one of those 90-degree, 80% humidity August nights, preferably with someone you wanted to have sex with. There was nothing like after the bars closed, you had a few drinks in you—naked night swim.”

“Steven Spielberg fucked that up,” Springsteen continued. “He fucked it up good. Now, many times over the years, I asked myself, Why? Why would a nice man like that—why would he do that?”

Here at MoMA, a guitar slung around his back, Springsteen then attempted a bit of playful psychoanalysis. He recalled his trips on the Spielberg family yacht. Maybe, thought the guy who wrote “Born to Run,” the guy who directed Jaws is scared of swimming.

“I’ve been on that boat many times and I can tell you: Steven Spielberg does not go in that water— ever. Steven’s boat is so fucking big it has water on it. There’s a pool on it. Steven Spielberg does not go in that fucking pool—and I mean ever,” Springsteen said. “I’m not sure I’ve seen him in a bathing suit. So the reason night swimming is fucked—not just on the Jersey Shore, but every fucking place in the world—is because that nice man, Steven Spielberg, is very afraid of the water.”

“The name of that boat is the Seven Seas,” Springsteen finished. “And I guarantee you, Steven Spielberg has not been in any of the water on any of those fucking seven seas.”

Springsteen added, of course, that he loves Spielberg and his wife, the filmmaker and artist Kate Capshaw. And he wanted to sing a song for them. So he broke into “Dancing in the Dark.”Ch

The whole night was like this. I’ve been to the MoMA Film Benefit a number of times, and it’s always a celebrity-stuffed evening at the museum, always sponsored by Chanel, a highlight of the season. But this was on another level. The museum was honoring a director synonymous with the modern era of blockbuster movies: the avatar of American celluloid excellence, the closest thing Hollywood has to a Michael Jordan. What’s more, there’s a true connection between the art institution and the director. His first theatrical feature, The Sugarland Express, had its New York premiere at MoMA, in 1974, as part of a series called New Directors/New Films.

“This is where it all began, here at MoMA,” Spielberg said. “Why did you wait so long to invite me back?”

He went on to praise the institution’s herculean efforts to restore films and add them to the collection. He also thanked Chanel for dressing him in a look way fancier than his usually quite casual (but fawned over) director ’fits, and for supporting the benefit over nearly two decades.

“MoMA’s dedication, since 1935, to curation, preservation, and restoration is what makes this honor so deeply personal for me, for all of us who love film,” Spielberg said.

Earlier in the night, Spielberg caught up with Amy Sherald, showing the artist some pictures on his phone, as Jeff Goldblum, who played Dr. Ian Malcolm in a little movie called Jurassic Park, pulled up to his table. Nearby, Christopher Walken—who had a great turn in Spielberg’s Catch Me If You Can—was wandering toward his seat, looking a bit lost, when another slightly older man came up to say hello. It was Robert De Niro.

The artist Taryn Simon and her husband, Jake Paltrow, were chatting with Christy Turlington Burns at the bar when Stephen Colbert went up to get a drink. Studio Museum director Thelma Golden was chatting with MoMA board president Sarah Arison, and Jennifer Lawrence strolled in with her husband, the art dealer Cooke Maroney. Michael Ovitz, the collector and MoMA board member for nearly four decades, who happens to also have a long history with Spielberg—“Michael Ovitz, my former agent from a long time ago!” Spielberg said onstage—invited the artist Nicolas Party and the novelist Sarah Blakley Cartwright to his table, with Larry Gagosian sitting nearby.

Lorne Michaels was chatting with collector Ray McGuire—though when everyone sat for the opening remarks, the seat across from Michaels remained mysteriously empty. Soon, a montage of iconic Spielberg clips filled the room. As the lights came up, a figure walked across the stage, mouthing the word “wow” over and over. Surprise: It was Tom Cruise. A MoMA rep, sitting near me, confirmed that Spielberg had no idea that the star of Minority Report and War of the Worlds would be attending the event.

“Since I was a young man, you were very generous with me, always on movie sets—and at your home with Kate, the meals that we had together, the hours that you shared talking about your films and what inspired making them,” Cruise said from the stage. “The stories about you as a young boy with that eight-millimeter camera. You were gracious enough to listen to my stories about the jobs that I took, so that I could buy the tickets to go see your movies.”

Cruise later waded into the crowd to hug his director and take that empty seat across from Michaels. MoMA director Christophe Cherix then got up to gush about his favorite Spielberg movies before introducing the next speaker: Martin Scorsese.

“The films he has made have changed the world. So art does matter. It always will,” Scorsese said. “We’re here tonight surrounded by art in the museum, and it’s really the appropriate setting all the more to honor Steven. And so Steve, I don’t want to… Listen, we’ve known each other since 1972, and how do we get to be in our 80s? What happened?”

To introduce Spielberg himself, the museum managed to rope in Steve Martin and Martin Short, who have never been in a Spielberg-directed movie. Actually, they have no obvious connection to the honoree, except for the fact that they’re two of the funniest people alive.

“You know Steven is very proud that he has never used AI in any of his films. By the way, AI is Steven’s nickname for us,” Steve Martin said.

“I’ll never forget the first time I saw Saving Private Ryan,” Martin Short said. “I found the film so mesmerizing that, halfway through, I whispered into my phone, ‘I’m going to have to call you back.’”

Spielberg was dying in his seat, just losing it laughing, and then had to follow up Martin and Short, which he compared to playing after a Taylor Swift concert. “Marty and Steve, I’d happily follow you anywhere, except up here,” the director joked.

Michelle Pfeiffer, Steven Spielberg, and Michelle Williams

He looked even more moved as Springsteen ripped through a no-bullshit, full-throated performance of “Dancing in the Dark,” which is not something you usually get to see at a museum that’s got The Starry Night and Les Demoiselles d’Avignon hanging upstairs. And then it was time to leave the museum, to go back to the reality of a stormy New York where you can’t catch a cab. In the coat check line, Spike Lee turned to Donna Langley, the studio head at Universal, for whom he’s made a number of pictures.

Then Lee bounced outside, giving a fist bump to every single security guard working the door at MoMA, greeting each of them with what’s going to be a lifelong mantra: “Knicks in five.” “Knicks in five.” “Knicks in five.”

Season 35 of Dancing With the Stars is in full swing on the 2026 TV schedule, with the series officially in its semi-finals era once again. The competition is as tense as ever, with surprising eliminations practically every week. And every week, fans give their thoughts on just about everything. This includes the continuing discourse of whether celebrities with dance training should be allowed to compete.

DWTS always has a wide range of celebrities each season, from actors to musicians to athletes to comedians to influencers and yes, even politicians. This means that everyone has different backgrounds, and naturally, there will be some people who have dance training, whether it was a long time ago or very recently. For Season 35 specifically, a lot of people have been calling out Jenna Dewan, whose experience in dance includes being a backup dancer for artists such as Janet Jackson and in the Step Up films. X user swifferwins shared their opinion on the situation, pointing out just how much of an advantage Dewan has over some of her competitors:

ok at the risk of getting hate for opening my mouth - i am not deep into dwts and haven’t ever really minded when someone w dance experience is on dancing with the stars but someone who was danced in movies, award shows, and major artist TOURS being a star is WILD to me

I personally couldn’t care less if a celebrity on Dancing With the Stars has prior dance experience, since ballroom dancing is so different. Dewan has even opened up about having to unlearn some of the stuff she’s picked up over the years because of the stark differences. That being said, she still has the skills, but X user n1taydefender makes a good point:

Ballroom and Latin is different than most modern dance styles, ballroom has so many rules! But I agree to a certain degree, it’s just really hard to find stars with no dance background at all, since most of them have some kind of theatrical training

On average, DWTS’ celebrity roster each season usually consists of around 16, so it might be hard to find that many celebrities, all in different careers, with next to no dancing background. However, it’s understandable that a lot of people wouldn’t like it since DWTS is all about teaching celebrities the art of dance and seeing them improve. Glee alum Harry Shum Jr. has also been getting a lot of heat for his own experiences, as kismetdiviner replied in the thread:

i feel this heavy about both harry & jenna this season. coming from someone with competitive ballroom dance experience, their backgrounds both give them an incredibly unfair advantage. it’s truly insane!! and prior to the show, harry’s danced with julianne, & jenna with derek 🫠

Just because you have dance experience doesn’t mean that you’re a shoo-in to win the whole thing. For instance, Dewan was just eliminated in this week’s episode with her partner, Val Chmerkovskiy. While it came as a shock, fans are certainly making their voices heard, and it could mark a shift in the entire competition. It can still be anyone’s game, and with the semis coming up, you never know just what will happen.

A handful of actors with musical theater experience also include Jordan Fisher and Corbin Bleu, with Milo Manheim, Zendaya, Chandler Kinney, and Roshon Fegan also coming from Disney Channel and showing off their extensive dancing skills. Out of those six, Fisher was the only one to win the Mirrorball. Not to mention the few Dance Moms contestants who have also graced the ballroom floor, like JoJo Siwa and Mackenzie Ziegler, with neither winning.

All this to say that there’s never a guarantee that someone with dance experience is going to take home the Mirrorball. Even if a couple has a perfect score, they could still go home, which is what happened with Dewan and Chmerkovskiy. Now that we’re getting down to the final couples, fans will be working harder than ever to make sure that their favorites make it to the top, with or without dance experience. And people will still be divided, regardless. Tune in on Tuesday at 8 p.m. ET on ABC to see who could be making it to the DWTS finals.

#3516. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

#3515. Avengers: Doomsday's Official Writing Credits Confirm Two Major Marvel Cameos

As the December 18 release of "Avengers: Doomsday" rapidly approaches, fan speculation is running rampant over just about every aspect of the movie. Is Doctor Doom a Tony Stark variant? Which characters will die? And who will make surprise cameos? Anthony Mackie recently spoiled the return of Paul Bettany's Vision, while there's also been talk that the finalized Writers Guild of America writing credits would tip the appearances of two hugely popular characters. This talk is now fact.

Those credits are now official, and, per the WGA website, Stephen McFeely and Michael Waldron will share the coveted "written by" credit (with an "and" instead of an "&," which means they did not write as a team). Meanwhile, quite a few folks received Additional Literary Material credits (which will not be seen on screen). Here's the list: McFeely, Waldron, Eric Pearson, Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Jeff Loveness, Andrew Lanham, Destin Daniel Cretton, Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman.

Yep, the previously uncredited Reynolds and Jackman will join the spandex showdown as Deadpool and Wolverine. Probably. I mean, it'd be funny if the fellas were hired to punch up Kelsey Grammer's dialogue, but, no, this almost certainly means the indestructible duo is back. As for how significant a role they'll play in "Avengers: Doomsday," your guess is as good as mine. So let's get to guessin'!

My greatest fear regarding "Avengers: Doomsday" is that it'll be undone by superhero clutter. If the Russos don't have a compelling story (and we know they began shooting without a finished script), it could be a comic book version of those leaden 1960s all-star romps like "Casino Royale," "Candy" and "The Magic Christian," where each actor's sole function is to pop up on camera so the viewer can say "Hey, there's Orson Welles!"

I've been encouraged by some of what I've heard over the last month – in particular, that James Marsden's Cyclops plays a significant role in the film. If this means we'll get a resumption of hostilities between the humorless Scott Summers and cocky Logan, I'll be so very happy. Add the exponentially more antagonistic Deadpool into the mix, and that just may be enough to drive Summers into the steely arms of Doctor Doom.

I'm most excited to see Deadpool be the straw that stirs the drink. I really don't want a relentlessly dour "Avengers: Doomsday," which is the vibe I'm getting from the pea green aesthetic of the trailers (and its fast food tie-ins). Are they going to get MCU fans to buy back in with a surfeit of character deaths? Gunn's "Superman" caught on because it foregrounded hope in a thoughtful, non-anodyne way. We live in bleak times. I'm not sure AI-friendly filmmakers like the Russos should be in charge of a franchise that, overall, appeals to our sense of humanity. I'm hoping the heavy-handed trailers are a happy bait-and-switch. Let Deadpool and Wolverine cook.

#3514. A Look Inside the Scorpion Ball, Princess Grace Kelly’s Scorpio-Themed 40th Birthday Party

Grace Kelly always had a deep passion for astrology. Born on November 12, 1929, she was a Scorpio, and very proud of it. To celebrate her 40th birthday on November 15, 1969, the Princess of Monaco organized a party themed by her astrological sign, resulting in the extravagant Scorpio Ball, held at the Hôtel de l’Hermitage in Monte Carlo. For the occasion, she only invited celebrities who were also Scorpios. Among the 60 or so guests were Swedish actress Hjördis Paulina Genberg, American actor Rock Hudson, and Italian actress Virna Lisi.

Actor Richard Burton was also in attendance, accompanied by his wife Elizabeth Taylor, even though she was born under the sign of Pisces. An exception was made for the actress, who was granted special permission thanks to her husband’s astrological sign—Scorpio, born on November 10. For the occasion, Taylor chose to dazzle, wearing a Cartier diamond necklace with an estimated value of $1 million around her neck—a gift from Burton two weeks earlier. She also wore a spectacular evening cape by Tiziani, made of black velvet and adorned with two rhinestone scorpions on the front and a third on the hood.

Guests were required to adhere to a dress code devised by Kelly, inspired by the colors associated with the sign of Scorpio. Red, black, and white were therefore strongly recommended. The princess, for her part, opted for an off-the-shoulder black velvet dress by Balenciaga from the fall-winter 1967 couture collection. Two ruby brooches set with diamonds—a wedding gift from Prince Rainier III—completed her ensemble.

The decor also reflected the evening’s theme. Red candles, portraits of famous Scorpios, and a lavish cake adorned with golden scorpions set the tone. No detail had been left to chance: The waiters, wearing powdered 18th-century wigs, dressed in velvet suits embroidered with sparkling stars and held silver candelabras adorned with red candles.

Princess Grace was seen on numerous occasions alongside Carroll Righter, an astrologer and Hollywood columnist nicknamed “the astrologer to the stars.” According to People magazine, the princess’s birth chart also revealed a Scorpio ascendant, while her Midheaven was in Leo. In astrology, the Midheaven is associated with career, public image, and reputation. Some attributed her commanding presence and magnetism in the spotlight to this configuration.

Kelly embodied the mysterious aura that her admirers associated with her astrological sign. Unfortunately, that light was extinguished on September 14, 1982, when the Princess of Monaco lost her life in a tragic car accident on the hills above the principality.

Originally published in Vanity Fair France.

#3513. Aaron and Jordan Rodgers Share Rare Photo Together Amid Reunion After Feud

Aaron and Jordan Rodgers are continuing to put their past rift behind them.

The formerly estranged brothers posed in a photo together, putting their arms around one another in a happy snap shared via a joint Instagram post on Friday, November 13.

“Great to see little bro @jrodgers11 in his element tonight  @acrisurestadium. Really proud of how hard he’s worked to get to where he is now 👊🏻,” Aaron captioned the image.

Followers were surprised to see the pair together given how strained the dynamic between Aaron, 42, and Jordan, 38, had previously been.

“Got tears in my eyes over a reunion of two people who don’t know I exist,” commented one social media user, while another gushed, “The world is healing.”

Aaron had long been estranged from his parents and brothers throughout his NFL tenure. They recently reconciled thanks in part to Aaron’s wife, Brittani.

Appearing on the September 10 episode of Cam Heyward’s “Not Just Football” podcast, Aaron shared details of his recent reunions with his various family members.

“I went out to Nashville and met with my older brother,” Aaron said on the podcast, referring to his brother Luke, who lives in Tennessee with his wife and three kids. “A couple weeks after that, I met with my little brother. It was cool.”

Aaron further divulged that he and Jordan shared a “tough conversation” when they reconnected and explained Brittani was instrumental in helping him bridge the gap amid the lengthy family feud.

“I’m in a much better headspace, and I said it before, but my wife deserves a lot of the credit for that just to be even able to to get to that point where I could think about having the conversation,” Aaron said. “She was a big part of that, not that she was pushing anything, she wasn’t.”

He continued, “When you’re loved by someone in such an unconditional and beautiful pure way, it changes your perspective on all your relationships around that. That becomes your anchor point. It’s like, wow, if I can be made to feel like this by this person, it opens up your heart in a really deeper way, you know, that I never experienced before.”

Aaron reflected that there was a time that he could never imagine there would be a moment that an olive branch would be extended.

“I mean, a year ago, even two years ago, [and] five years ago for sure, I would have said, ‘No, I’m never going to reconcile,” he continued. “It’s just not going to happen. It’s not in the cards. I’m not ready for that. It was really built in judgment, just like ego and judgment. And ego and judgment gets in the way of any progress or evolution. I had to really put those aside.”

Aaron and Jordan had not been on speaking terms for years, which Jordan discussed when he was a contestant on The Bachelorette in 2016, where he met his now-wife, JoJo Fletcher.

“Me and Aaron don’t really have that much of a relationship,” Jordan said at the time. “It’s just kind of the way he’s chosen to do life and I’ve chosen to stay close with my family and my parents and my brother. Yeah, it’s not ideal and I love him and I can’t imagine what it’s like to be in his shoes and have the pressure he has, the demands from people that he has. Don’t have hard feelings against him, it’s just how things go right now.”

Aaron also discussed the estrangement with his family in his 2024 Netflix docuseries, Enigma.

“It wasn’t like I was super duper close with everybody in the family. I was close with my little brother,” Aaron said. “But in actuality, it goes back to stuff from high school that kind of made me feel distant. Stuff in college, stuff post-college. I was quiet about it. I thought the best way to do it was just don’t talk about it publicly.”

#3512. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

I’m very new to the NCIS franchise, but I think NCIS: New York, which debuted last month on the 2026 television schedule, is really fun. I love the characters and the actors playing them, and that is the most important thing for procedurals to work for me. I especially like Scott Caan’s character, even if it’s really similar to his Hawaii Five-0. There are two subplots that I’m really not digging, but they are easy to wrap up, and I hope the show does that quickly.

My first issue involves two special agents on the team: Addy Ross, played by Jacqueline Byers, and Wyatt Sellers, played by Shane Harper. There is a weird “will they/won’t they” thing going on between the two characters, and I don’t like it. It’s not the chemistry between the actors or the characters or anything like that. It’s just unnecessary. There doesn’t have to be a romantic angle in a show like NCIS: New York. It feels shoehorned in, and doesn’t feel organic at all.

They are the “other” two members of the field team, with Caan and LL Cool J making up the “A-team” as the two biggest stars on the show. Addy and Wyatt are great when they are doing their jobs, and I can even get behind the idea that Wyatt is trying to learn more about the personal life of his partner, who is very private about it. Hinting at a potential relationship is not believable. These are professionals! Keep them professional!

My other big issue with the character subplots is between the two “office” members of the team. Jennifer Beals plays Robyn Wells, the leader of the team, and she’s great! It’s so fun watching her in a new show. However, she has a consistent beef with the computer nerd, Sean Sullivan (Devon Druid). It stems from the reason Druid is employed by NCIS. His backstory hasn’t been fully fleshed out on the show yet, but we do know that he is there because he was a hacker who was facing a long prison sentence.

That’s all well and good, but every time Sean says almost anything about the job, Robyn reminds him that he has prison hanging over her head. Like, I get it. He’s there against his will and avoiding jail. Great! Fun concept! But do we really need to be constantly reminded of it? Let it just sit in the background and come up when it makes sense. The character’s backstory doesn’t need to be re-established all the time.

As I said, both of these stories can be wrapped up, or at least pushed way to the back burner without really causing any plot holes or other problems with the show, and I really hope they are soon. Otherwise, I’m looking forward to NCIS: New York's future

#3510. Rings Of Power Season 3 Features The Most Gruesome TV Scene Of 2026

The land of Mordor is where the shadows lie, and this article is where major spoilers lie. Read no further if you haven't watched the Season 3 premiere episodes of "The Rings of Power."

"The Rings of Power" is a tragedy. As far as prequels go, this one is not as full of doom and gloom as "Andor" — a show where audiences knew the main character was destined to die tragically — but it is still a show all about the rise of an evil that almost conquered Middle-earth. Indeed, though there are some surprising main characters in Season 3, the true star of "Rings of Power" is the Dark Lord Sauron (Charlie Vickers), who spends each season lying and manipulating his way to ruining everyone else's day.

This was especially prominent than in Season 2, which was all about Sauron making the elves believe he was an envoy of the Valar so that they'd help him make the titular Rings of Power. In particular, Sauron spent the entire season gaslighting the show's best and most tragic character, Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards). Episode after episode, Sauron used Celebrimbor's vanity and pride to his advantage, scheming and lying into making Celebrimbor his friend and ally, before stabbing him in the chest with a pike.

This leads to "Rings of Power" Season 3 featuring the most gruesome TV scene of 2026. When Sauron returns to his little office in Barad-dûr after failing to make the One Ring yet again, the Dark Lord gets a visit from the ghost of Celebrimbor, who mocks Sauron's failures at trying to replicate the dead elven smith's work.

And right there, in front of Sauron, is the rotting body of Celebrimbor, hanging on a wall like a trophy.

What makes this horrifying is not only that Sauron still keeps the dead body of Celebrimbor around, but the fact that it's a rotting mess with arrows sticking out of the torso. Making matters worse, Skelebrimbor is hung from a wall like a war banner

This, of course, is a reference to the actual books. As J.R.R. Tolkien himself wrote, Celebrimbor's dead body was "hung upon a pole, shot through with Orc-arrows" and turned upon Elrond's forces like a banner for Sauron's army. It's why fans affectionately refer to this act as "Celebrimbanner." It is arguably one of the cruelest things the Dark Lord ever did — which is saying something considering the untold number of people that died because of him.

Seeing the body of Celebrimbor hanging on a wall — the flesh rotting away, an expression of fear and shock on the skeleton — is horrifying, and easily the most gruesome piece of imagery in the entire "Lord of the Rings" franchise. There is no reason why Sauron needs to have kept the body of Celebrimbor, other than to assert his cruelty.

And yet, it leads to a rather hilarious scene of the ghost of Celebrimbor appearing only to taunt Sauron, ragebaiting the Dark Lord and mocking his inability to craft anything as majestic as the great smith Celebrimbor. He even tells Sauron that his orcs now pity him because of how pathetic his jewelry crafting skills are. It's a testament to Charlie Vickers for the subtle ways in which you can tell the insults are actually getting at Sauron. Meanwhile Charles Edwards reminds us why he is one of the best pieces of casting in this show, with this short but impactful scene in a third season that otherwise struggles to live up to hype.

#3509. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#3508. Jensen Huang’s Potentially Seismic Art Retreat

Welcome to True Colors. I’m in Manhattan. Lots to get into this week. There’s the matter of what to do about a major new San Francisco arts institution that was set to be named after Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang. Understandably, it’s a question whether that renaming will still happen given…everything. There’s my ode to the death of the Cybertruck. And there’s all the details from the star-studded MoMA Film Benefit honoring Steven Spielberg. Tom Cruise shocked the crowd with surprise remarks, and Bruce Springsteen roasted the director. It was a whole night.

MENTIONED IN THIS ISSUE: Donald Trump, Jason Calacanis, Brendan Dugan, Siniša Mačković, David Zwirner, Lorenzo Amos, Kate Capshaw, Zohran Mamdani, Jessica Craig-Martin, Dean & DeLuca, Indochine, Stanley Whitney, Marina Adams, Will Whitney, The Beverly Hills Hotel, Elon Musk, Lana Del Rey, Grimes, Travis Scott, Pharrell Williams, 21 Savage, Tyler, the Creator, Bad Bunny, Julia Wachtel, Todd von Ammon, Frieda Toranzo Jaeger.

The major arts institution named for Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, appears to be—shocker!—very much in jeopardy.

Just months ago, Huang was getting a phone call from President Trump while onstage at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles. “I’m here with the besties, Mr. President,” a laughing Huang said, putting his phone up to the mic. “Tell him I say hi!” said All-In cohost Jason Calacanis.

But Huang’s recent weeks have not been marked by good times with the besties. First, the Democrats took over Congress, throttling all the goodwill he built with the administration. Then he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by the US to be a Chinese spy—and then news of another affair, this time allegedly with a subordinate, came via a shocking New York Times bombshell. Amid rumors that yet another affair would soon break, he stepped down as CEO and, according to Forbes, has watched nearly $20 billion of his estimated net worth vaporize since Monday.

What’s unknown is the current state of his relationship with his wife, Lori Huang—and their ambitious plans for an arts organization that was set to bear their name. Earlier this year, the Huangs pledged $75 million to Vanderbilt University in order to help transform the soon-to-be-closed legendary San Francisco art school California College of the Arts into part of Vanderbilt’s SF campus. Vanderbilt announced that it planned to name a portion of its SF campus the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design.

Which is now a bit awkward, given the multiple alleged affairs, and the whole Chinese-spy thing. Plus, Huang is no longer affiliated with Nvidia, which teamed up with CCA in 2025 to form the CCA-Nvidia Incubator for Creative Intelligence. Will Jensen and Lori Huang still put their names together on arts organizations after all that’s happened? And if there is no Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design, what will happen to Vanderbilt’s SF campus when it opens next year?

The CCA was started in 1907, and Huang and his wife were expected to support its transition to a new chapter. It would be a shame if this is how it ends. Reps at Vanderbilt didn’t get back to me.

It’s a new era in Tribeca. Tonight, Karma, a burgeoning mega-gallery with spaces in New York’s Chelsea and LA’s Hollywood, opens its new gallery at 38 White Street. Founder Brendan Dugan and director Siniša Mačković took me on a tour earlier this week, and it’s easily one of the most generous spaces anywhere in the neighborhood. Plus, an outpost of Karma Bookstore—a much needed bookstore for a neighborhood shockingly lacking in one—is coming in right across the street.

This will be the latest big-tent blue chipper to take a space in the Triangle Below Canal, as they used to call this neighborhood. Something to consider: In the last few years, mega-galleries such as David Zwirner and Hauser & Wirth have shut their uptown townhouses and opened downtown.

Also opening tonight is a White Street outpost of Gratin gallery, which has a roster of incredibly exciting young stars, including Lorenzo Amos (whom we wrote about a year ago). I’m hearing about other younger dealers grabbing spaces in the neighborhood. The art market isn’t exactly on fire, but dealers are betting on one thing: the enduring power and capital of New York City.

Speaking of New York, guess who’s lived here full-time for almost a year? Steven Spielberg, that’s who. On New Year’s Day 2026, the GOAT American director—who is married to the artist Kate Capshaw—moved his official residence from California to New York, and has made the apartment in the San Remo his home base. You will not be surprised to hear that, post-move, Spielberg is doing extremely cool stuff in town. He’s walking around with a script and a Tracy Kidder book while slugging down an iced McCafé. He’s getting lunch at Benvenuto Cafe. He’s having Mayor Zohran Mamdani over to the crib.

The only thing left was for one of the city’s great museums to throw a big party for the Hollywood-royalty-gone-Gotham. Last night, Spielberg got just that: He was honored at the MoMA Film Benefit, sponsored by Chanel. I was there. Read the full report—with fun pictures!—here.

Also on VF this week: an exclusive excerpt from an uproarious new memoir by artist Jessica Craig-Martin, I Regret I am Able to Attend. Craig-Martin is a real treasure of the art world, a great photographer—and, as it turns out, a hell of a writer. The whole book is a compulsively readable blast. The chapter where Craig-Martin recalls working as an extremely inexperienced, occasionally larcenous teller at Dean & DeLuca is one of the funniest, most satisfying New York vignettes I’ve read this year. And of course, all the scuttlebutt from the ’80s art scene is fabulous. Read the excerpt, in which our narrator spills all the tea—and, um, stuff stronger than tea—about working as a waitress when Indochine opened.

Happy 80th birthday to the great painter Stanley Whitney. His wife, the artist Marina Adams, and son, dealer Will Whitney, threw Stanley a party to celebrate his octogenarian status on Nine Orchard’s roof, overlooking Dimes Square. Writers, artists, dealers, old heads, everyone was there. A fabulous Wednesday night.

#3507. Jamie Lynn Spears’ Daughter Maddie Pokes Fun at Her Mom’s Teen Pregnancy

Jamie Lynn Spears’ daughter, Maddie, is having a little fun at her mom’s expense!

Maddie, 18, poked fun at Jamie Lynn, 35, in a cheeky TikTok video shared on Friday, November 13, joking that she had managed to make it through high school without becoming pregnant.

In the clip, Maddie can be seen spinning around and dancing with her hands in the air as Jamie Lynn watches on. As the song continues, the Zoey 101 alum puts her hands on her hips before crossing her arms, seemingly playing along with the joke.

Maddie added the text, “Dance if you beat high school pregnancy,” over the video. She tagged her mom in the caption, writing, “lol @Jamie Lynn Spears.”

The playful post comes years after Jamie Lynn welcomed Maddie with her then-fiancé, Casey Aldridge, in June 2008. The actress was just 17 years old at the time, while Aldridge was 19.

Earlier this year, Jamie Lynn set the record straight as fans continue to speculate that her pregnancy was the reason her show, Zoey 101, was axed.

“If we’re talking about a concrete misconception, it would be that everybody thinks Zoey 101 ended because I got pregnant. And that is not true,” Jamie Lynne said during an August appearance on the “Momarchy” podcast.

Jamie Lynn shared that Maddie often gets comments on TikTok from fans of the Nickelodeon sitcom accusing her of being the reason it was canceled after four seasons.

“We laugh about it,” the Sweet Magnolias star continued. “But it’s just not the truth.”

The actress explained that Zoey 101 had already finished filming by the time she got pregnant, but the final season had not yet aired on TV.

“That’s how it is in entertainment. A lot of people who aren’t in the business don’t understand. They think we shoot it, it comes out,” she said. “No, you shoot it and it comes out maybe the next year or something. So I think that’s where people are confused. But we were wrapped, we were always wrapped, and there was never going to be another season.”

Spears concluded, “My beautiful Maddie is not the reason the show ended.”

Zoey 101, which starred Jamie Lynn as the titular Zoey Brooks, premiered on Nickelodeon in January 2005 and ran until May 2008. The fourth and final season ended production in August 2007 — two months before the show’s staff learned about Jamie Lynn’s pregnancy with Maddie. (The cast later reunited for a follow-up film called Zoey 102 in 2023.)
