#3487. Hillary Clinton Showed Up For Dinner at Gloria Steinem’s Townhouse

It’s a dark and stormy November night at Gloria Steinem’s townhouse, and Hillary Clinton has something to say about the 2026 election. “One of my most anticipated moments will be watching Donald Trump walk into the State of the Union through the now more than one hundred women members of the House of Representatives. I just want them all to stare at him and say, ‘You fired us from jobs we were qualified for. You insulted us. You demeaned our ambition. You undermined our place in government and society. And we’re here.’”

Huma Abedin, Busy Philips, and Paloma Elsesser.

The former Secretary of State and 2016 presidential candidate is a last-minute but highly anticipated arrival to this dinner honoring Steinem, the late activist. She passed away in September, but the feminist pathfinder was known for throwing these salon-type events (she called them “circles”) at her Upper East Side townhouse, which she bought for just $30,000 in the late ’60s. It’s overflowing with books (I spy Marilyn by Norman Mailer, Jane Fonda’s War by Mary Hershberger, and several Eleanor Roosevelt biographies on the shelves), pictures (there’s one framed of Steinem alongside Mariska Hargitay) and Indian art. (Steinem spent two formative years in the country.) There are magnets in her kitchen of Wonder Woman, Frida Kahlo, and a cloth finger puppet of Hillary Clinton. A political button is pinned to it that says “Another Bitch for Hillary.” The whole place smells like a Cire Trudon candle, and everyone’s drinking negronis. (Which actually isn’t technically very Steinem—her favorite cocktail was a margarita—but the negronis go with the night’s dinner, prepared by Lilia chef Missy Robbins.) Yet this is one of the first events at the townhouse that Steinem herself isn’t here to lead.

Jihae, Lux Pascal, Naomi Watts, and Bethann Hardison.

Amy Richards, a feminist activist whom many consider to be the daughter Steinem never had—a title Richards rejects because her mentor “didn’t want kids”—stood up at one point to tell the crowd that this is what Steinem would have wanted. Growing up with a transient father and a mentally volatile mother, the late activist took near-obsessive care in maintaining a welcoming home she could share with others. “As long as I knew Gloria, she always said, ‘I just want my home to be the way it’s always been.’ She wanted it to be filled with people,” Richards says. “She didn’t grow up with a home. She was traveling the country for the first 10 years of her life and then lived with her mother, who was not very stable.”

At least Steinem’s still here on the wall: Months before her death, she posed for a series of portraits by Paola Kudacki for Weldun, a platform that offers physically adaptive and functional fashion. It was a bit of a small miracle that Steinem said yes. “I will say, Gloria did not always love to be photographed,” Richards says. “Especially in her later years—not because of wrinkles or aging, but she was just like, ‘Aren’t there enough pictures of me?’” Weldun and the Gloria Steinem Foundation are presenting tonight’s dinner, and mementos of Steinem are everywhere. On the fireplace mantle sits a pair of her signature Ray-Ban aviators. But Gloria’s stuff isn’t the same as Gloria herself.

Former secretary of state Hillary Clinton hugging Melissa McCarthy.

Which is probably why, in a crowd of women that include Huma Abedin, Mariska Hargitay, Padma Lakshmi, Melissa McCarthy, and Bethann Hardison—who, at the ripe age of 84, shows up wearing Gucci—Clinton’s unexpected arrival feels seismic, like Gloria sent someone in her place. (Hardison tells me she thinks Steinem used whatever divine power she’s got up there to launch the Blue Wave: “She’s probably saying she helped it happen!”) Whatever your views on Clinton’s politics, she was the first woman to receive a presidential nomination from a major party. Paloma Elsesser and I sit crouched in a corner of the room, glued to the window. “There’s mother,” the supermodel whispers to me as Clinton exits her car into the pouring rain and walks up to the townhouse door.

Guests at dinner honoring the late Gloria Steinem.

“Hi, everybody,” Clinton says as she walks in. The entire dinner comes to a silent halt. “Hi,” the room responds in unison. Madame Secretary doesn’t seem to like the fuss, probably because 30 or so people intensely staring at you when you arrive at a party is objectively unsettling. “Go back to eating!” she says, motioning to the Missy Robbins meal on the table. Clinton sits down next to Naomi Watts and warmly greets Busy Philips, who stumped for Clinton back in 2016. Hargitay blows her a kiss across the table. All anyone wants to do is talk to Clinton about the 2026 election, in which Democrats won at least 55 seats in the Senate and 256 in the House to take both majorities in the US Congress. At the end of the meal—and after a proper catch-up with Shonda Rhimes—Clinton tries to leave, but she can’t. Guests block the door, clamoring to chat her up.

Amid the Clinton traffic jam, I ask Hargitay about the photo. She can’t remember exactly what it is from. “Was it Bravo? Was it with Andy…what’s his name?” But she can guess what she thinks Steinem might say about the blue wave: “There is a God!”

I watch Clinton finally make her exit. It’s late, so I wait several minutes before I descend the stairs to leave too. (I wait for Elsesser, Watts, Hardinn, and Lux Pascal to finish taking a selfie on the steps.) But I spoke too soon: Clinton’s stuck waiting for the coat check, another group of women crowded around her hoping to say something—or, more likely, hoping she says something. With the way this night is going, Clinton might be the last one at the party.

#3486. How to get mighty Pokémon in Pokémon Go

These Pokémon essentially come combat-ready

These Pokémon essentially come combat-ready

Mighty Pokémon are particularly strong Pokémon that you can find during the Pokémon Go Wild Area 2026 event on Nov. 14 and 15.

These monstrous beasts are just found in the wild as normal, but all is not what it seems — these fully-evolved Pokémon are beefed up stat-wise and are pretty hard to catch.

Below we explain how mighty Pokémon work, the schedule for mighty spawns, and what mighty Pokémon are the most meta-relevant.

Update (Nov. 13): We’ve updated this guide with the roster of mighty Pokémon available as part of the 2026 Wild Area event.

Mighty Pokémon are special strong Pokémon that spawn during the Go Wild Area event. It will have the following qualities:

Despite the difficulty in finding and catching, mighty Pokémon are made for combat right away, and are pretty powerful! You'll want to nab any you find during the Go Wild Area event — and you should use your Go Safari Balls to nab them. (There's a reason these two things exist as part of the same event at the same time.)

Different mighty Pokémon spawn depending on the days:

Alolan Exeggutor*, Scizor*, Flygon*, Walrein, Metagross, Empoleon*, Magnezone*, Conkeldurr, Haxorus

Azumarill*, Kingdra*, Aggron*, Ferrothorn, Hydreigon*, Goodra, Noivern, Tinkaton, Clodsire

*These Pokémon will spawn on both days via Incense.

Some mighty Pokémon will have special moves. Evolving the prior Pokémon into these will also give them their special moves:

If you’re trying to be more selective with your Safari Ball usage and don’t know which of these Pokémon fit into the meta, we've got your back.

Metagross is a top steel-type attacker, Hydreigon is a top-tier dark-type attacker, and Haxorus is a pretty good dragon-type attacker, too. Metagross is an especially good pick, as it also has a very powerful Mega Evolution. Set them up with these moves for success:

The rest of the mighty Pokémon are just fine. Notably, these also have Mega Evolutions, so if you want a strong one for that, grab some of these:

Notably, some of the other mighty Pokémon are good in PvP, but since they show up at a high level already, lots of them have been powered up too high, disqualifying them from their relevant leagues. (For example, Clodsire is a beast in Great League, but... it's definitely going to be over 1,500 CP here.) The only Pokémon on the mighty list that's good in Master League is Goodra, Metagross, and Hydreigon.

#3485. How To Rob A Bank Director Reveals The Real-Life Inspirations Behind The Movie's Influencers [Exclusive]

Of all the movies in 2026 that can claim to be the timeliest, none may have a better case than "How to Rob a Bank." Even setting aside the obvious social and political commentary behind director David Leitch's newest heist flick, in which a group of Robin Hood-like bank robbers team up to send a message to corporate bigwigs and capitalist vultures, the movie's timeliness is also apparent in the way it's shot and edited. The various trailers have made no secret of the content creator angle behind this crew, led by Nicholas Hoult's Ryan (aka The Wolf). When they're not sticking up banks and making thrilling getaways, they're busy editing their escapades into viral-ready YouTube videos to be consumed by the masses.

It's a novel approach that'll either work or not for audiences, many of whom are well aware of the online ecosystem that is influencer culture. It's a tall task for any mainstream Hollywood movie to tackle, but the creative team behind "How to Rob a Bank" clearly did their homework. During a recent press junket for the film, I spoke to both Leitch and producing partner Kelly McCormick about the deep well of influences they drew from in order to nail this specific element of the film — one that certainly attempts to feel true to our digital lives. According to McCormick:

"We were trying to go for what might be the next push for creators, if you know what I mean. Like, the wish fulfillment aspect from a creator's perspective of just pushing the envelope even more. So it was just really absorbing as much as possible to see what was out there and then using some of the prosumer cameras to make sure that we were just being even more wild."

The content creator footage depicted throughout "How to Rob a Bank" will inevitably leave an impression. No, we don't live in a world where adrenaline-seeking influencers actually put themselves and others in harm's way to pull off successful heists and robberies. (Not yet, at least.) But actually capturing those vibes in an authentic way meant resorting to some very specific filmmaking measures.

One scene shows Ryan and his friends fleeing the scene of the crime on motorcycles through a forest, with GoPros strapped to their helmets capturing footage in every direction. When this is filtered through the lens of the video they upload afterwards, well, that's where things get visually dynamic. As Kelly McCormick explained to me:

"The one [scene] in specific I always remember is when they're biking through the forest and you see it from above and we are pivoting the camera in editorial, because literally it's capturing [360 degrees] around [the action]. And so you can spin it around in editorial to get that vibe of this wild editing that I think would be a creator's dream, if they didn't have to hit deadlines and always be feeding as much as possible to their hungry, hungry followers [laughs]."

David Leitch name-checks "extreme sports" as one section of YouTube they paid particular attention to for sequences like that, while the idea of philanthropy and giving back to communities was taken out of the Mr. Beast playbook. Even podcasters get into the mix, like Scott Galloway or King Bach (both of whom make cameos in the film). Adds Leitch with a laugh, "We had a lot of influences in our influencers."

When you’re responsible for wiping out half the universe, people are going to keep bringing it up. So obviously, most fan questions Josh Brolin gets asked have to do with Thanos, especially from curious minds who want to know if the Titan will ever return. However, the actor was recently asked about an entirely different character in the Marvel universe. Now, I’m aware that Brolin still has love for Thanos, but the real question is: Would he ever come back as Deadpool 2’s Cable?

With the upcoming X-Men reboot, people want to know if we’ll be seeing him again. So while promoting his new survival thriller Whalefall at NYCC, The Direct asked what the likelihood of seeing Cable again is, and Brolin revealed:

Thanos to me is a very, very interesting role, and a role that I had a lot of fun doing. You know what I mean? A lot of fun doing. Joe Russo, Anthony Russo, those guys to me, they're just unprecedented, unparalleled... There's some practicality to it, but when you resort to your imagination, and they would come up and they would reference Scarface or something like that, something that I understood, then it made it even better. 'Deadpool 2', I'm glad happened. I'm glad [Cable] was isolated unto that experience, and it's a good memory.

In the movie, the character is a time-traveling anti-hero who was also the son of Scott Summers and a clone of Jean Grey. Some ‘timey-wimey’ stuff later, and he’s back in the present after living in a dystopian future. With various X-Men, including James Marsden as Cyclops, coming back, it makes sense that people want to know about Cable. However, it sounds like Brolin is happy to leave that character in the past. Although Deadpool creator Rob Liefeld has shared that he thinks there’s “much more meat on those bones” when it comes to Cable.

So, hear me out. In the spirit of reboots, they could cast a younger Cable and do an origin story as part of a grander X-Men plot. We have Mister Sinister in the upcoming reboot, which could lead to a Jean clone, and this could bring the story full circle to Cable earlier in his journey. Now that there’s a mergence of the mutant characters with our MCU, anything is technically possible.

While Brolin’s time as Cable seems to be “isolated” in the past, that doesn’t mean his time as the Mad Titan is over forever. The actor has shared that if the Russo Brothers ever asked, then he’d be open to returning. So maybe if the right person asked, he'd return (even for just a cameo) as Cable one day.

While we're all still thinking about his Marvel work, Brolin has been hard at work outside of the MCU. In addition to Whalefall in October, the actor also had The Dog Stars out this year, which he described as one of the “more creative, satisfying” projects he’s been part of. He also has a role in Dune: Part 3, which hits the 2026 schedule on December 18 alongside Avengers: Doomsday.

So even though we won't be seeing Cable or Thanos anytime soon, you can go see him reprise his role as Gurney Halleck in Dune.

#3483. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3482. Doctor Who Star Peter Capaldi Knows How To Save The Struggling Sci-Fi Series

As "Doctor Who" fans (aka Whovians) are no doubt aware, the show is in a bit of a bind. Since its debut way back in 1963, the series has sustained itself with a clever sci-fi concept that has allowed multiple actors to canonically play the title role of the Doctor. The character, you see, is a time-traveling alien known as a Time Lord, and when they die, they're able to regenerate into a new person. Each time the Doctor regenerates, their personality changes a bit, although they still have the same memories, intellect, and enthusiasm

Unfortunately, after running for so long, "Doctor Who" has developed a bad habit of falling back on stale tropes. A Whovian friend of mine has agreed that "Doctor Who" is in a bad place right now, and the franchise's future is uncertain in the wake of Disney ending its partnership with the show due to its relatively low viewership. As my friend put it, the series is, indeed, in a "tepid" place, and no one knows where it will go moving forward.

Peter Capaldi, however, has some suggestions. The actor, who played the Twelfth Doctor from 2014 to 2017, shared his ideas during his recent appearance on the "Half the Picture" podcast, explaining that he thinks the show needs to get back to basics. He added that it would do well to reorient itself by returning to its lower budgeted origins and tapping back into the shoddy charms of its earliest days.

In the same interview, Peter Capaldi clarified that he is fine with no longer being associated with "Doctor Who," as there are other ventures he would like to pursue. "Doctor Who," he noted, is the kind of show that takes over your life, adding, "You can't do it [...] as a part-time role." When it comes to the property's future, though, Capaldi is uncertain, stating:

"What it's got to be, I don't know. I was thinking about this [...] I don't know what people want from it. Because my love for the show was the old show. That's what I grew up with. And that's not going to work. I can't come in and say 'Let's set it in the '60s. Let's make it black-and-white with very wobbly sets. Let's make more cheaply. Or with less ambition.' I mean, 'Doctor Who' has always had ambition, it's just that budgets haven't always met that."

Capaldi then mused out loud if audiences might want "David and Kylie." He was, of course, referring to David Tennant's highly popular iteration of the Doctor appearing with a character played by Kylie Minogue on "Doctor Who" in the 2007 Christmas special "Voyage of the Damned" (which brought in an impressive number of viewers). Or maybe they're more interested in previous "Doctor Who" stars like Christopher Eccleston or Jodie Whitaker. Basically, Capaldi is very unsure what fans really want out of the series.

All he can say is that he enjoys "Doctor Who" the best when it experiences what he calls a "ripple" from the old show. Not a reused monster, necessarily, but a specific tone that sometimes breaks through. Something humble and old-fashioned.

Although "Doctor Who" is a time-travel series that involves aliens, monsters, major historical figures, and ineffable, universe-ending technologies, Peter Capaldi feels that it's actually a "small" show. It's about a small group of characters and their time-traveling TARDIS, which looks like a police box that, via advanced technology, is larger on the inside than on the outside. Capaldi added that if the series could focus on those basics, it could sing once again, explaining:

"It's the Doctor and the assistant-slash-assistants in the TARDIS. Quite contained. Kind of balming. And like in 'The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe,' they step out the door to this drama. And those dramas change shape, and they've got monsters in them. Magical, strange, weird, sad. It's that central core of that small group of people with the Doctor at the center of it."

I have personally watched enough of the show to know that most of the best "Doctor Who" episodes embody what Capaldi talked about. The problem, then, is that many of the series' seasonal storylines climax with some sort of supervillain threatening to destroy the universe, unwrite history, or commit some other kind of massive sci-fi cataclysm. And if those types of cataclysms are regularly happening, then it's no surprise that fans are experiencing a sense of fatigue (or that the show's creatives may be running low on ideas).

Time will tell if the minds currently behind "Doctor Who" take Capaldi's advice and scale the series back into a cheaper, more humble form. It certainly wouldn't hurt, what with the series being adrift following its short-lived Disney era and the planned 2026 Christmas special being canceled. Capaldi might just be onto something.

With the new Harry Potter series getting closer, Daniel Radcliffe has been getting a lot of questions about any advice he has for Dominic McLaughlin. The actor has previously said he didn’t have advice for McLaughlin and only shared advice for the producers. At the time, he asked them to “let [the young cast] be kids still,” especially in the age of social media. However, I was surprised by his take on why he doesn’t want to give advice.

While the actor was promoting his upcoming movie, Steps, he was asked by AP News Entertainment about handing down the wand. The actor doubled down on not sharing advice, but this time he explained why:

I’m really, truly in the business of not giving Dominic advice. He’s got it, he doesn’t need any advice from me. I don’t want to be like a — because then if I say something to you, then the next interview [with him], people will be like, ‘Oh, Dan said you should do this.’ And I don’t want to haunt this poor child through interviews.

It’s understandable that he doesn’t want to put even more on McLaughlin’s shoulders. It’s a little surprising, though I can see why he doesn’t want to put the young actor under pressure to live up to anything. Meanwhile, he’s not the only Harry Potter actor who has been asked to hand down advice. Bonnie Wright, who played Ginny Weasley, shares a similar opinion to Radcliffe when it comes to telling the next Ginny what to do. She has stated, “I think it’s so important for them to be in their world and their interpretation of it.”

This seems to be largely what the original cast thinks, with Tom Felton also veering away from giving advice on how to portray Draco. However, the Broadway actor focused on the sentimentality of his Harry Potter days and advises the new cast to take lots of pictures. It seems that Radcliffe isn’t the only one not wishing to ‘haunt’ the child actors. Though this take on advice is a little surprising, Radcliffe’s reveal that he’s not a big TV watcher is even more so:

I don’t know if I will [watch] honestly. I’ve been in a lot of Harry Potter already and also, not even because I don’t — I don’t watch any TV. I haven’t seen Breaking Bad, and I haven’t seen Mad Men. I haven’t seen some of the real classics. Eight hours is a lot of anything to watch.

I’m not surprised he hasn’t watched his own franchise, but he’s so behind on so many classics. Perhaps he’ll check out the Harry Potter series with his son. Hopefully, after Season 1 airs, someone will ask him. Though I doubt watching the series will change his stance on giving advice.

Meanwhile, this hasn’t stopped a few of his co-stars. Ralph Fiennes gave some practical advice to whoever takes his place as Voldemort: “Practice your long, flowing, robe walk” and advised him not to trip. Additionally, a pair of Weasleys have shared the sweet gesture they gave to the next Fred and George, up-and-coming actors Tristan and Gabriel Harland. Oliver and James Phelps sent the twins sweet notes wishing the next set of mischief makers the best of luck. They declined to give exact details about what was in the notes, stating they were private messages of encouragement.

The Harry Potter series will arrive on the TV schedule on Christmas Day. It is expected to have a weekly release and will be available with an HBO Max subscription.

#3479. ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters

Peacock‘s latest limited series “The Good Daughter” adds to the streamer’s solid run of women-led thrillers, though it’s best to interpret that label loosely. When stretched to include biographical mysteries, the streak dates back to 2022 with Nancy Oliver’s limited series “Angelyne,” showrun by Allison Miller and starring Emmy Rossum as the enigmatic ’80s era L.A. personality known only by her mononym (until some man decided that’s not good enough).

Then came a slight pivot into pulpy book adaptations with “Apples Never Fall” (2024) an adaptation of Lianne “Big Little Lies” Moriarty’s novel of the same name that was showrun by Melanie Marnich and centered around a wealthy family’s missing mom, played by Annette Bening. Not only did “Apples Never Fall” make the perfect amuse-bouche for Peacock’s next whodunit — “All Her Fault” (2025) the Emmy-nominated yet deeply unserious Sarah Snook showcase — it also teed up Jake Lacy, Hollywood’s leading expert in the field of “entitled douchebags,” for a meta-fun Keyser Söze moment as the devil hiding in plain sight (while his wife took on all of their family’s emotional and physical labor). Related Stories ’12 12 12′ Review: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Ticking-Clock Heist Thriller Runs on Broken Time ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

Two less successful entries, by viewership anyway, were this year’s jaunty critical favorite “Ponies,” from co-creator and director Susanna Fogel, which starred Emilia Clarke and Haley Lu Richardson as the CIA’s first female spies operating within the Soviet Union; and the jaundiced “Long Bright River” (2025), a limited series co-created by Liz Moore (who wrote the novel on which it was based) and Nikki Toscano (who served as showrunner), starring Amanda Seyfried as the only cop in a bad/pale part of Philly who cares about neighborhood sex workers and opioid addicts getting killed (one of whom may turn out to be her missing sister).

All of these shows share common tropes, despite disparate tones, topics, and objectives — not the least of which are their glorious feminist underpinnings. Within each of these thrillers lurk so many shady husbands, brothers, bosses, and dads. The patriarchy looms large enough to get name-checked, and the leading ladies are all fighting an uphill battle just to be seen, heard, and understood. “All Her Fault” was so attuned to the ways men routinely let down their families Vulture hailed it as a “misandrist masterpiece.”

But “Long Bright River” carries the most direct parallels with “The Good Daughter,” both by design and on accident. They’re both gritty and dark. They both follow leads whose careers connect back to their personal demons, and they both track working-class women fighting for their impoverished communities (and against the shitty men who run them). Where “All Her Fault” and “Apples Never Fall” could be carelessly devoured as melodramatic amusements, “Long Bright River” and “The Good Daughter” are too brutal and self-serious to constitute anyone’s idea of a “fun” binge, even if there is a morbid bit of fun to be found in the latter’s performances, dialogue, and many, many character quirks.

“The Good Daughter” is set in the fictional town of Pikesville, GA, where Charlie (Meghann Fahy) works as a public defender, adjacent to her sole-surviving parent, town pariah, and private defense attorney, Rusty Quinn (Brendan Gleeson). Her mother, lovingly referred to as Gamma (Olivia Williams), didn’t live long enough to be a grandma; she was murdered in front of her daughters when they were just kids, and the resulting assaults left Charlie’s sister Sam (Rose Byrne) with a lifelong motor speech disorder called dysarthria, as well as impaired vision and a notable limp.

Sam is also a lawyer, but she specializes in patent law (to avoid the anxiety that comes with criminal cases) and moved to New York as soon as she was old enough to get out of Georgia. She only returns to Pikeville when Rusty, for the first time, calls to say her sister needs help. Why now? Well, the list of Charlie’s hardships is nearly as long as her sister’s, but Rusty — who tends to speak in Flannery O’Connor quotes — is likely referring to the most recent trauma: a school shooting she witnessed that left the principal and a 13-year-old student dead.

Once Sam is back in town, the two sisters start mounting a defense for their dad’s client: the school shooter, Kelly Wilson (Shayna Benardo), an 18-year-old student with an intellectual disability. The maniacal powers that be are eager to kill her — first at the scene of a shooting, where a teacher (played by Jake McDorman) saves her from the trigger-happy cops, and then in court, where a self-righteous district attorney argues for the death penalty, competency laws be damned.

They’re all under the Coins’ thumb, a powerful family (with connections throughout the local government) who turned the township against Rusty and his family long ago. Everyone believes Charlie and Sam lied about who killed their mother, and they resent Rusty for defending so many “obviously” guilty parties. The only folks willing to help the Quinns are Rusty’s best friend and legal aide, Lenore (Harper Steele), and Charlie’s husband and assistant district attorney, Ben (Michael Dorman). Otherwise, they’re on their own, standing up for Kelly, standing up to the Coins, and standing against Bad Men™️.

Adapted by Karin Slaughter (from her own book) and directed entirely by Steph Green (“Duster,” “Dare Me”), “The Good Daughter” holds back too many revelations for the finale, creating an exposition-heavy ending that covers its bases but functions like an endless list of answers. It’s not as powerful as it needs to be in order to justify its upsetting subject matter, and it’s trauma-drama plotting skews into overkill well before it’s done doling out distress.

And yet, I have to say, much of it works. Credit goes to the cast, particularly Byrne and Gleeson, for internalizing their showy character quirks to such a degree that Sam’s limp, vision impairment, and sporadic stutter — yes, also a stutter! — never feel like her defining traits. The same goes for Rusty’s folksy banter, poetry quotes, and even his red-nose routine, in which the professional attorney pops on a clown nose whenever he feels the moment calls for a little levity. Such a strange, impractical choice, deployed as often as it is here, could spoil a curious character who’s always viewed from his children’s removed perspective. Maybe he’s unbelievable, maybe he’s too cute for the rest of the story, maybe he’s simply too silly. But Gleeson gathers it all up to form a heartbroken widower who just wants to give his traumatized children the light they need in an ever-darkening world.

Fresh bursts of creative Southern witticisms are similarly rewarding, like hearing Gleeson say, “Never kick a fresh turd on a hot day” or Byrne tell a patronizing windbag “to shit in both hands and start clapping.” The series ultimately rests on Sam and Charlie’s relationship, and their relationship is strong. Their dialogue, particularly when poking fun at one another, rings true, and there’s a buddy-cop dynamic to their investigation that demands to be extended into an ongoing series.

Not this series, mind you. Peacock should limit this limited series to its established, er, limits. But I know a streamer where Byrne and Fahy could pitch another thriller centered around two crusading women looking to crack a case, save their souls, and destroy the patriarchy in one fell swoop.

Just maybe base the next one on a slightly easier read.

“The Good Daughter” premieres Thursday, November 12 on Peacock. All six episodes will be released at once.

#3478. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

#3477. Ryan Phillippe's Two-Part Action Thrillers Have Been A Paramount+ Streaming Hit For Weeks

All you really need to know to understand what you're getting with the "One Mile" movies is a single line from Phillipe: "These guys don't know it yet, but they messed with the wrong dad." That's it. The movie is a guy unleashing his dad rage on a bunch of bad guys who took his daughter. The films are basically "Taken" in a forest.

But clearly there's something more to "One Mile" than your average B-movie actioner. After receiving a digital release back in February 2026, the films hit Paramount+ on October 1, 2026 and have been holding strong in the most-watched charts ever since. In fact, this has to be one of the strongest streaming runs of any release this year. Per viewership tracker FlixPatrol, "One Mile: Chapter One" and its sequel have now been in the Paramount+ movie rankings in the United States for 42 days apiece.

Before he rose to fame with roles in the 1997 slasher craze cash-in "I Know What You Did Last Summer" and 1998's "Cruel Intentions," Ryan Phillipe made his film debut in the submarine action thriller that pit Denzel Washington against Gene Hackman, "Crimson Tide." Three decades later, he's leading his own action thrillers that draw heavily on the tone and style of their '80s and '90s predecessors. The "One Mile" movies most obviously bear a striking resemblance to 1982's "First Blood" in terms of their one-man-army outnumbered in a forest story. Unlike in that seminal Sly Stallone outing, however, Phillipe's ex-soldier isn't opposed to racking up the kills.

The actor plays former special forces operative Danny Beckett, who has had very little time to connect with his teenage daughter Alex (Amélie Hoeferle). To make up for lost time, he takes Alex on a road trip to visit colleges ahead of her high school graduation. On their way, they make an impromptu stop in a remote area where they set up camp, only for a violent off-grid community to descend.

At first Danny uses his special forces skills to evade the group, but they eventually get their hands on Alex. Cue a violent rampage in which Danny runs through the survivalists one by one in a desperate attempt to get his daughter back. If you're wondering why such a straightforward action premise requires two movies, it's because Alex manages to get kidnapped twice. Yes, twice. Look, these movies might not measure up to the Denzel and Hackman effort that gave Phillipe his start, but they're a solid way to waste away a weekend and come with a ringing endorsement from Paramount+ users.

The "One Mile" movies are directed by Adam Davidson, who has a prolific career stretching back to the late-'80s when he made his directorial debut with the short "The Lunch Date." His filmography otherwise includes dozens of directing jobs on shows such as "Bosch" and Ryan Phillipe's former USA series "Shooter." "One Mile" chapters one and two represent a rare feature film project for the director, and thus far it's proven a worthy departure for him.

Per FlixPatrol, not only have both chapters been in the Paramount+ charts for over a month, until November 13, 2026, "Chapter One" was sitting at the very top of the U.S. movie charts, with "Chapter Two" occupying the second spot. At the time of writing, both have slipped to the second and third position respectively, but that's an impressive run for the duology. What's more, the films are clearly sticking around for some time to come, having thus far only succumbed to the might of "PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie," which only just batted Phillipe's thrillers down a slot to take number one.

The runtime for "One Mile: Chapter One" is 89 minutes while "Chapter Two" runs for 83 minutes. That means you're essentially getting an almost three-hour action epic, if you watch the films back to back. Why couldn't they just be one movie? Who knows, but Paramount+ viewers, who previously turned Aaron Eckhart's neo-Western "Thieves Highway" into a Paramount+ hit, don't seem to mind at all.

The big double feature of the year we’ve all been talking about is rightfully “Dunesday”. On the weekend before Christmas, movie theaters are going to be crowded, full of people excited to see Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part 3. But hold up, did you know there’s actually another worthy double feature coming next Friday, November 20?

This one is for the YA readers! The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is coming out on the same day as the premiere of Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3 on the 2026 TV schedule. For the former, you’ll have to go to the theaters, but the latter will be streaming for those with a Hulu or Disney+ subscription.

It’s kind of perfect because these are two book-to-screen adaptations based on series that are often discussed in the same circles since they’re both for the same audience and were first published in the 2000s. Sunrise on the Reaping is a prequel about Haymitch’s Hunger Games and Percy Jackson Season 3 adapts Rick Riordan’s third book in the Greek mythology-inspired fantasy series called The Titan’s Curse.

The first two episodes drop on Friday, making this double feature just over three hours. Dunesday, on the other hand, is going to be a much longer sit, considering both movies are expected to be around two and a half hours, bringing the double feature to over five hours.

While this double feature is a bit more niche than Dunesday, its respective stars have been asked about it, but they haven’t come to a consensus on viewing order. Here’s what The Hunger Games’s Joseph Zada thinks about it:

I think you watch our film, and then to get happy again, you watch a little bit of Percy.

See, I think this might be the way to go because if you’ve read Sunrise on the Reaping, you know it’s tragic and emotional. Whereas I don’t expect the first two episodes of Percy Jackson Season 3 to take too much out of me. But Walker Scobell (aka Percy Jackson) had different thoughts when he also spoke to Entertainment Weekly:

In my opinion you should watch the first episodes of Percy before you watch The Hunger Games. The sad parts of Percy don’t come until a little bit later in the season, and then I already know the sad parts of Hunger Games are just going to be there the whole time.

I guess he’s thinking you should start your day with some lighter fare and go downhill from there? Sunrise on the Reaping’s Whitney Peak also thinks fans will need some “levity” after the latest Hunger Games movies, but ultimately she had these thoughts:

There’s no wrong answer. Just see them both.

As a huge fan of both these franchises, I honestly didn’t realize this double feature existed either, but now I’m excited. I’m going to fully feel like I'm back in my middle school library on November 20, and I can’t wait.

#3475. Zelda Fans Who Loved Ocarina of Time Need to Play This Game Next

By now, you’ve probably had time to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on the Nintendo Switch 2. You’ve marveled at what a great job it does of bringing the classic Nintendo 64 adventure to a new generation, with visual improvements and quality-of-life changes to make it more palatable for that new audience. Maybe you’ve even run through it a second time.

As good as Ocarina of Time might be, however, it’s just one game. It can’t keep you busy forever. Once you’re finished with that grand adventure, you’ll need to decide what to play next. And assuming you’re not tired of Hyrule and Zelda just yet, there’s one game you definitely should consider for your next conquest. That game is The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, and it did a brilliant job of introducing key elements that players loved about Ocarina of Time several years later, including an intricate world that changes over the course of the epic adventure.

Incredible as it may seem, The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past is already 35 years old. It arrived in Japan on Nov. 21, 1991. How can so much time have passed already? I have vivid memories of terrific games I played before Link’s first Super Nintendo outing ever occurred. Time clearly flies as fast for some of us, every bit as readily as it did for Link in Ocarina of Time.

When A Link to the Past hit Japan in 1991 and then launched in North America five months later, it provided the most meaningful update the Zelda series would see for decades. Up to that point, there were only two console releases. Both of them were wildly different. A Link to the Past cemented what a Zelda game should be, offering its grandest open world yet, stuffed with thrilling dungeons built on a foundation of everything that came before them.

The game began with Link following his uncle out into the rain in search of the imprisoned Princess Zelda. He freed her and then began a search for three magical pendants, the better to someday vanquish an evil wizard. As his quest neared its apparent conclusion, Link learned that it had really only just begun. He soon found himself traveling frequently between two realms: the Light World and the Dark World.

The Dark World is A Link to the Past’s grandest innovation. Players spent hours exploring every corner of Hyrule, from the warm desert sands in the southwest to the cascading waterfalls and mountains in the north. They might have thought they knew everything. Then another dimension came along and turned all of that on its head. Sand dunes turned to fetid swamp. A lake became a glacier, and a thriving village turned into a hideout for bandits. Truly, the alternate realm lived up to its title.

But the Dark World offered more than just a dreary aesthetic. Actions Link took in one realm allowed him to make progress in the other, in ways large and small. A Heart Piece might rest on a ledge that lay out of reach. A trip between dimensions added a walkway that finally granted access. Or a dungeon entrance might lie out of reach, but a trip between worlds would reveal a new path. Players got to know the landscape more intimately than ever before, or else they could never reach some of the places where their greatest adventures waited. In the end, Link’s ingenuity and bravery provided the strength necessary to defeat a familiar foe: Ganon.

Ocarina of Time built on much of that same design, with just enough differences to make it all feel fresh. Link wakes to find an insistent fairy by his side, instead of having his dreams disturbed by a telepathic plea. He meets Zelda early in his adventure. Three dungeons later, circumstances force them apart. Instead of traveling to another realm, the lad simply wakes in a different time period. It is a dark one, every bit as disastrous as the Dark World in the previous game.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

If you’ve just finished exploring that structure in Ocarina of Time, the time is right to experience the Super Nintendo version that pioneered its best attributes. You’ll be able to better appreciate just how much impact a classic 2D game had on the series as it evolved into 3D. It should serve as a reminder that the best entertainment experiences of today don’t come from nowhere. They often represent an evolution of everything that came before them. For people who enjoy the evolution of a medium, there’s true joy in exploring those roots, even now. And few games deserve your attention as much as A Link to the Past.

Zelda's ability to endure over decades is a miracle

#3474. Miles Teller Opens Up About ‘Paper Tiger,’ Adam Driver, and Losing His Home Before Filming James Gray’s Movie

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release “Paper Tiger” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

An actor who started at 22, Miles Teller earned rave reviews out of the gate for his debut performance in “Rabbit Hole,” when he was signed swiftly by CAA, followed by “Whiplash” and “The Spectacular Now.” He has worked steadily ever since, with everything from auteur fare like “Whiplash” and studio franchises such as “Divergent” and “The Fantastic Four” to his name. Holding his own opposite Tom Cruise in the blockbuster “Top Gun: Maverick” pushed him into the limelight, but he was still playing Rooster, the son of radar intercept officer Nick “Goose” Bradshaw (Anthony Edwards). Related Stories After ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

His latest role in James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” which earned raves at Cannes, sees Teller play a real grown-up, Irwin Pearl, a Queens engineer and family man opposite Scarlett Johansson as his wife Hester, and Adam Driver as Gary, his older brother, a former cop. No longer the onscreen son of a leading man, Teller is now firmly in father roles. Irwin is slowly building a solid business when his brother offers a quicker route to success. Alas, the naive Irwin goes for the idea and, during an unscheduled night reconnaissance, blunders with the Russian mafia, seeing things he should not see.

I sat down with Teller at the Carlton Hotel in Cannes after the movie wowed in its world premiere. He was seeing it for the first time. We do not count fake standing ovations at IndieWire, but I was there and can vouch that it played well. The dynamic between Driver and Teller is powerful, with Johansson holding her own in the middle. Even though the movie did not land a Cannes prize, it will play the fall festivals and enter awards contention.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Anne Thompson: You’ve played the Cannes game before.

Miles Teller: I’m one of those actors [where] it’s pretty hard to watch yourself. I always have a hard time. I was here with Nic [Winding] Refn for this limited series that we did [“Too Old to Die Young”]; that was my first time at Cannes. I’ve done Cannes with “Maverick.” It’s truly an overload of the senses.

You’ve never given this kind of performance before.

Hopefully, your taste evolves as you get older. It struck me that on my first film, “Rabbit Hole,” I was playing the wide-eyed teenager, and we filmed the majority of that movie in a house in Queens. And now I’m playing the part of the parent.

That was your breakout. You revealed some strong emotions related to your own car accident. I’m so sorry you lost your home in the Palisades Fire.

When I met James for this movie, our house had just burned down. And I had just lost my grandfather. We were renting a place in Santa Barbara, and then I got the call saying James wanted to meet me for this. That infused this story and performance with a lot of love as well, because of that feeling of home that Keleigh [Sperry] and I had lost. I’d lost it with my grandfather, but then also just the physical place where you can have people come gather, where you have memories attached. We did not have that, so that probably came through.

Do you believe that you have to grow up a bit before you can find your way in Hollywood?

If you want to have a long career, the audience, hopefully, that you attract in your early 20s, as they get older, and they start having kids or not having kids, but just getting more life experience under the belt, you want to reflect that in your choices as well. And James makes movies for adults, he deals with characters. I’ve loved every one of his films, and I’ve always felt like he gets incredible performances, so I was excited to play a man at this point.

Every actor is going to get to a place where you know it’s tough because you do something that has some success to it, and then people want you to keep doing that same thing, whether that’s from the studio side or you keep getting scripts that are that same kind of thing.

When I started out with “Rabbit Hole,” and then I wanted to audition for comedy, they’re like, “he’s not funny.” And then you do comedies, and you want to be going back to drama, and they’re like, “Willard from ‘Footloose,’ what are you talking about?”

I remember “Bleed for This.” [He gets up to close the shutters to block the noise for my audio, and pours me some water.] That was a point where I was 27, and I said, “OK, I want to step up and play, not the funny friend. Playing Vinny Patz, as a five-time world champion boxer, very much a man’s man, absolutely, that was something. But it always comes down to a director, oftentimes taking what I feel is a chance on me, casting me in a role that I haven’t necessarily shown those abilities before, but believing that I could do that.

You had to carry the TV series “The Offer,” in which you play Al Ruddy, who produced “The Godfather,” running interference between Francis Ford Coppola, Robert Evans at Paramount, and the mafia. That must have been tough.

I was intimidated by portraying Al, to be honest with you, not just his bravado and accomplishments, but it felt like I was playing somebody who had more life experience than I had at that point, and there was a certain maturity to that. I enjoyed that Al, being a man of action, if he takes a step back, he’s taking two steps forward. Typically, there’s five or six different producers doing all these things: that was all Al.

In “Paper Tiger,” there’s one scene between you and Adam Driver where you get into a fight. Your face was shaking with anger.

I know. I saw that. Yeah, there was a twitch going on there. At least in my own life, your family can get to you in a way that nobody else can. Those feelings are so deeply rooted and established from childhood, so I guess in that moment, and neither one is fully aware of the ramifications of the Russians, this deal going bad, and how it’s affecting that person in their life. In that particular scene you’re letting out. It’s not just about what they’re talking about right there. It’s an entire lifetime of misgivings — he’s going to let him have it. When that’s happened to me in my personal life, you feel so bad afterwards. It’s a horrible feeling when you’re not talking to a sibling or your parents, and often it’s hard to make amends.

How did James Gray base this film on his own father’s experience?

With his father, that was the biggest regret. He took it to his deathbed, the fact that he brought this [danger] into his home, and his family became collateral damage for his business ambition. [In the movie] the venture that he went into, to go into business with his brother, he makes a mistake that was very naive. I think it’s easy to forgive this mistake. When I read this script, I had a ton of empathy for this family in this situation, and then also what Hester is going through.

Did you have any models for your character in this movie? Your own father was an engineer.

No, he was a project controls manager, but worked nuclear. The men that I grew up around, my father and my grandfather, were strong men, but very sensitive, and were dependable, reliable. My grandfather was married to my grandmother for 60-something years. I never saw her open a door for herself. I never saw her carry her own bag. He was a Marine, but he also was well-versed in world history, and he was a sweet man who was never afraid to show that side of him, but he also would stand up for himself, or his wife, or his kids, whatever it is. He took a lot of pride in that.

I found it refreshing, even comforting, to watch a movie about a kind, loving family man who’s good at his job, who’s competent. He’s a good dad. You haven’t shown that side to such a degree.

I felt immensely for this father and husband. It was clear he loves his kids, and he’s trying to lead by example, and to show them that success in life is not based on the car you drive. He wants to show them that you can build something on your own merit, and if you work hard and treat people right, that you can earn it.

Those values are no longer as respected as they once were. So, if you were to look back at your career, you did some studio work, like the “Divergent” series. Have you made a course correction? That comes with maturity, too, when an actor recognizes what they want to do rather than doing what people tell them to.

Early on, I didn’t want to feel like I was repeating what I had just done. I didn’t want people to be able to expect what I was going to do next. I always want to defend young actors in their careers, because people say, “Oh, why did you make that choice? Why did they make that choice?” You’re just hoping to get a role, and it’s less than 10 percent of people in SAG who pay their bills off acting alone. We all want to work on the best material with the best directors and the best actors. There’s an ebb and flow. I used to be more critical of work other people were doing, because you get thrown into this rat race when you’re first starting out.

Who were you competing with? Who was in your class?

It was me, and Michael B. [Jordan] and [Robert] Pattinson and Shia [LaBeouf] and [Zac] Efron was big, “The Hunger Games” stuff was blowing up. As I’ve gotten older, I appreciate and have respect for longevity, if you can hang around. I always wanted to contribute. When I was going to the Lee Strasberg Institute at NYU, and looked on the wall, there’s all these incredible actors that went through there. I hold acting and actors in such high regard, whether it’s theater or film or TV.

You seem to be delivering performances at such a level that you keep getting more work. The work itself is selling you. You had to counteract some bad press. Did that hurt you in terms of getting roles?

That was so mishandled. The reason why I have not done profiles is because I said, “Wow, if I’m not doing this interview on camera, this person can misquote things or put things out of order or say things that didn’t happen.” It felt like such a violation of what actually transpired. I told my team, “Guys, I don’t think I’m doing this again, because I’m reading this and this doesn’t sound like me to me. This is not life, so why would I ever want to be a part of something where they can just put that in?” So it’s unfortunate that being a good person, that doesn’t sell. People want to click on the negativity. If you go to bed and put your head on your pillow and how you treat people truly, that’s what matters. That [2015] interview was like 12 years ago.

Some people still remember. Well, casting directors know who you are and what you can do.

The actors, the directors, the crew, the producers, you can’t hide who you are when you’re on set.

Legal questions surround the Michael Jackson estate and his lawyer, John Branca, who you play in “Michael,” which has grossed $707 million worldwide. What’s going on with the sequel?

They had to rework the third act of the last movie. As far as the sequel goes, I know they’re working on it. I haven’t had any direct discussions, other than the team is excited to complete that story.

#3473. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3472. I'm Usually A Ross Complainer, But My Friends Rewatch Has Me So Mad At Rachel
