#3459. 5 Best New Movies And Shows To Stream This Weekend On Netflix, Prime Video, HBO Max, And More (Nov. 13-15)

Can you believe we're halfway through November? Wild. 2026 is passing by alarmingly quickly, and we're about to hit full holiday mode as we approach Thanksgiving ... but you don't need to get your turkey and stuffing recipes out of storage just yet. We've still got some time, and you should consider using that time to watch a whole bunch of stuff.

Yes, it's time to round up the buzziest, best, and biggest streaming releases for the weekend of Friday, November 13 to Sunday, November 15, which does include releases from earlier in the week as well. As always, the list is limited to releases new to major streamers entirely (case in point: though the hit Colleen Hoover movie adaptation "Reminders of Him" only just came to Netflix, it was already available on Peacock, so that's a nonstarter here), but between a killer dinosaur flick, a new thriller starring an Oscar winner, a drama with an innovative structure, a fresh literary adaptation, and the continuation of a massive fantasy series, you've got plenty of options.

If you didn't get enough Jessica Chastain in this year's admittedly silly horror movie "Other Mommy," you're in luck — she has a new film coming to Netflix this weekend. Written and directed by Shana Feste (the filmmaker behind "Country Strong," "Run Sweetheart Run," and "Boundaries," to name a few), "Heartland" stars the Oscar-winning Chastain as Misty Jones, a country singer who's retired from show business but has to come out of her self-imposed solitude to find her niece Charlie Heart (real country singer Carter Faith), who's gone missing. As Misty tries to locate Charlie, other family secrets come to light, and she tangles with a criminal underbelly in Nashville in the process ... and the fact that Misty is notoriously prickly and was nicknamed the "queen of mean" in her days as a country star certainly doesn't help matters.

"Heartland" also stars John Hawkes, Garrett Hedlund, Jennifer Nettles, and Ross Lynch in supporting roles, but Chastain is the real draw here, and whether or not you saw or loved "Other Mommy," you should check this pick out. "Heartland" drops on Netflix on November 13, so stay in this Friday and have a movie night.

If you, like me, love dark and twisted thrillers, you're probably familiar with the name Karin Slaughter. (Incredibly, I'm pretty sure that's her actual name.) Even casual TV fans are aware of her, even if they think they're not. Indeed, ABC's massively successful procedural "Will Trent" is adapted from Slaughter's novel series about an Atlanta detective (though it tones down some of the more depraved stuff found in the books), and in 2022, Netflix released a series adaptation of Slaughter's novel "Pieces of Her" starring Toni Collette and Bella Heathcote in its lead roles. Now, Slaughter's book "The Good Daughter" is getting an adaptation from Peacock, and it stars two of the most talented women acting today: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy.

The premise of "The Good Daughter" is enticing on its own: Decades after a brutal and violent incident in the Quinn family, sisters Samantha and Charlotte (Byrne and Fahy) still reside in their hometown of Pikeville, Georgia, with Charlotte working in law enforcement. Hence, when she starts looking into a particularly violent crime, Charlotte is struck by her own experiences, as is Samantha — and new family secrets come to light. Byrne and Fahy are both excellent on the show, and they're joined by Brendan Gleeson, Harper Steele, and Paula Malcomson, just to name a few. So, whether or not you're already a fan of Slaughter's body of work, you'll definitely want to get acquainted with "The Good Daughter," which dropped all of its episodes on Peacock on Thursday, November 12.

Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" film trilogy was a cinematic triumph when it released over the course of three years in the early 2000s, and it stands the test of time (though, the same can't really be said of his interminably drawn-out three-part "Hobbit" prequel). So, if you've already watched the extended versions of every single "Lord of the Rings" movie thousands of times, I've got great news: Amazon Prime Video has a "Lord of the Rings" TV show, and it's entering its third season.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power," which has been running since 2022, takes its lore from the appendices of J.R.R. Tolkien's massive fantasy tomes (but notably not Tolkien's "The Silmarillion" due to rights issues, so that has yet to be fully adapted). There are some "familiar" faces here from the Jackson movie trilogy, like Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and Elrond (Robert Aramayo), but "The Rings of Power" admirably expands the world of Tolkien during the second age of Middle-earth. This is also, incidentally, when the Rings of Power (that's the title) were forged, which led to the rise of the Dark Lord Sauron (Charlie Vickers). As such, there's plenty to explore as this series forges ahead.

The first four episodes of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 dropped on Amazon Prime Video on November 11. Two more will arrive on November 18, and the season will wrap up one week later on November 25.

I truly cannot believe a movie as delightfully weird and ambitious as "The End of Oak Street" got made in the first place, but I sure am happy that it did. David Robert Mitchell ("It Follows," "Under the Silver Lake") helmed this ode to dinosaur movies, summer blockbusters, and 1980s Steven Spielberg classics, which stars Ewan McGregor as Greg Platt, Anne Hathaway as his wife and aspiring writer Denise, Maisy Stella as the couple's eldest child Audrey, and Christian Convery as their son and youngest Brian. (There's also a family dog, Starbuck, and don't worry — nothing bad happens to him. That's as close to a spoiler as I'll get.) The Platts are an everyday family with everyday problems — Greg is secretly working as a pizza delivery driver after losing his job, while Denise is growing dissatisfied with their suburban life — but one night, a storm hits and traps them all in a bizarre prehistoric playground full of dinosaurs. This sounds almost magical, but here's the thing: those dinosaurs are starving.

On one level, "The End of Oak Street" is the only movie in existence, as far as I'm aware, where you can watch Anne Hathaway wreak havoc on dinosaurs with a shotgun. On another level, it's a treatise on the importance on family, and on another level, it's an audacious science-fiction story with a little bit of time travel and a lot left unexplained. What "The End of Oak Street" is above all else, though, is fun ... and it's streaming on HBO Max as of November 13.

In the aughts, "24" innovated a new style of episodic television by using a real-time conceit as a spy tries to save the world. Decades later, "The Pitt" used that same structure to great effect for its real-time experience of working a busy 15-hour emergency room shift. Apple TV's new drama series "12 12 12," though, is even stranger. Created by creative partners Jim Keeble and Dudi Appleton, "12 12 12" stars Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan as Jack Strickland and Bobby Galvin, two men involved with a high-risk heist in Zürich.

So, how does "12 12 12" tell its story? As former FBI agent Strickland and master criminal Galvin circle each other in Europe, the heist in Zürich is where they eventually meet ... and Keeble and Appleton use three timelines within each episode. First, you get the 12 months of planning the heist, followed by the 12 hours required for said heist — and finally, the 12 days' worth of heist-related aftermath. "12 12 12" also stars Jack Kesy, Kali Reis, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, and Patrick Fabian in supporting roles, and its first two episodes are streaming on Apple TV as of November 13.

#3458. David O. Russell’s ‘Madden’ Biopic Is Out Next Week — Does Anybody Know or Care?

Once upon a time, a new David O. Russell movie would be a must-see cinematic event. But did you know Russell has a new movie opening next week from Amazon MGM Studios? That would be “Madden,” his biopic starring a physically distended and hair-pieced Nicolas Cage as the iconic NFL commentator. When I told an IndieWire colleague about this story, they had heard of “Madden” the movie, yes, but had no idea that Russell directed it. Doesn’t bode well. Related Stories After ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

The film co-stars Russell perennial collaborator Christian Bale, strapped back into the hair and makeup chair for another grotesque transformation, as Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis, receding bleach-blond hairline and all, plus a wigged-out Kathryn Hahn as Madden’s wife Virginia, and poor Sienna Miller as Davis’s wife Carol. Reports have claimed the sports biopic carries a $75 million budget, making it one of the “Spanking the Monkey” director’s most expensive movies next to the critically flayed COVID release “Amsterdam,” which, not adjusted for inflation, cost a reported $80 million and earned a paltry $14 million domestically. That’s a movie that entirely vaporized from the cultural imagination — though you may recall a much-memed excerpt of a blink-and-you’ll-miss-her Taylor Swift being thrown under a car to her doom.

The “Madden” release strategy does not inspire confidence, either, suggesting a classic case of bag-and-tag on the part of Amazon MGM Studios: a day-and-date release on Prime Video globally with a perfunctory, subterranean-level theatrical bow, both on Wednesday, November 18. The critics’ screening takes place Monday, November 16, with the embargo lifting about 15 hours later. Muted marketing only further intimates Amazon wants to take the latest Russell joint gently into that good night — but why? Is it that bad? The trailer has more than 8.6 million views and counting, though that’s largely explained by the prolific fanbase behind Madden, who died in 2021, and the NFL. Less so by any fanbase of Russell’s.

To be fair, the studio has its hands full trying to position “Project Hail Mary” in the Oscar race and back into voters’ consciousness after opening theatrically six months ago. Amazon MGM’s social media heist movie “How to Rob a Bank” opens in theaters this Friday, while another awards hopeful, “I Play Rocky,” is in limited release. While “Project Hail Mary” was a box office juggernaut for the company, the tech giant has yet to master juggling multiple tentpole-scale projects theatrically at once — though they’ve had a banner year with considerable successes “Verity” and “The Sheep Detectives” spread out throughout 2026.

Co-scripted by Russell and Cambron Clark, “Madden” centers on Madden’s Super Bowl-winning partnership with Al Davis and the Raiders that led to the “NFL Madden” games. The film wrapped production well over a year ago, in late spring 2025 in Atlanta. A TMZ report from May 21 claimed several actors walked off set after Russell allegedly used a racial epithet during a scene. A reputation for volatility has followed Russell across projects, from the widely seen behind-the-scenes footage of the filmmaker chewing out his “I Heart Huckabees” star Lily Tomlin, to Amy Adams’ confessional interviews in which she revealed the filmmaker made her cry throughout the “American Hustle” shoot. George Clooney has called Russell “a miserable fuck” and swore never to work with him again after his experience making “Three Kings.”

The five-time Oscar nominee has built a career on quirky, sprawling ensembles and pushing actors toward extreme physical performances, like Christian Bale, who went gaunt (again) to win an Academy Award for “The Fighter,” then put on the pounds for “American Hustle.” Back in October, Russell and producer Todd Black appeared at the Virginia Film Festival in Charlottesville to present four clips from “Madden” — which showcased Cage in prosthetic padding that’s more January Jones in “Mad Men” Season 5 than Kazu Hiro Oscar-level effort, plus an exasperatingly accented Bale with bleached eyebrows, and the women, including Hahn and Miller, in insane wigs. Clearly, this is Russell operating at an 11, with characters, based on these clips, squawking over each other like the most strident ensemble scenes out of “Silver Linings.”

During the panel, Russell described the casting process as “trippy,” noting that Cage gained weight for the role along with the prosthetics.

“We were scared because we weren’t telling a documentary, but we were honoring John Madden and honoring Al Davis,” Black said. “We were trying to make it an entertaining story without making it a documentary. So some stuff was inspired by, some stuff was true, and a lot of stuff we made up, not wildly, but just for entertainment value.”

The producer added, “I think when you see the movie, you’ll see it really is an incredibly positive film that when you watch it at Thanksgiving time, I think you’ll watch it with your family, hopefully, and you’ll walk out feeling really happy about it and telling people it’s such an inspiring film.”

He might be onto something. With three NFL games scheduled for Thanksgiving — including the Kansas City Chiefs at the Buffalo Bills on NBC and Peacock — “Madden” could prove apt counter-programming to sports spectacle. That’s if enough people know where to watch it, or that it’s available at all.

#3457. This 3D Pet SIM You Never Played Has Over 12,000 ‘Overwhelmingly Positive’ Reviews

Have you ever wanted to raise your own genetically mutated pup? Well, there's a Steam game focused on exactly that, and it probably deserves more success than it's managed in the four years since it launched. Wobbledogs, from developer Animal Uprising, is described on Steam as "a 3D pet simulation where you raise your own hive of mutating dogs."

It's as much a comedic game as it is a simulator, for two reasons. Firstly, the dogs look ridiculous. They're made up of an amalgamation of shapes, including lengthy, cuboid torsos and enormous tails, somewhat reminiscent of the creatures in the early noughties British children's show Bamzooki.

Secondly, Wobbledogs has some wacky physics in play, which means it's a good laugh just observing your pets. "Two dogs with separate body structures will experience the world in different ways," reads the "about this game" section on Steam.

Impressively, each Wobbledog also has a simulated genetics system. "As they age, they periodically enter a pupal state and physically mutate. The foods they eat fill their guts with different flora… [which] influence the dogs' mutations, letting you craft and mold them to fit your own idea of canine (im)perfection!"

Wobbledogs is very much a make-your-own-fun sort of game though, so there are no explicit goals other than enjoying yourself. You can create and design habitats for your dogs, and you'll unlock more cosmetic decorations and objects as you play. "Give your dogs a relaxing place to sleep, set up a maze, or even cultivate a garden."

"I fed a family only Doritos for like eight generations to try to give them long legs and they ended up incredibly orange," reads one positive review. "This game is absolutely amazing. I get struck with waves of happiness every time I play," reads another.

It can also be an alarming game, however, as this review explains: "Got my first dog Pancake. Played with him, fed him, loved him. Got some more dogs for Pancake. Pancake played with them. Was best friends with Randy. Watch Pancake grow older & change with the minutes. Always happy and playful. I loved Pancake.

"Proceeds to die right in front of me. My other 4 dogs then come over & eat his dead body right in front of me, all while I'm still in shock that dogs can die in this game."

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Rest in peace, Pancake. Wobbledogs is currently $19.99, but regularly goes on sale for as little as $4.99, so I'd recommend putting it on your wishlist and holding fire until it drops again.

#3456. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3454. 23 Years Later, Love Actually's Most Romantic Line Is Still The Greatest Christmas Quote Ever

It's an annual tradition for some people to watch "Love Actually," the 2003 Christmas "classic" written and directed by Richard Curtis that puts several seemingly separate love stories together to explain why love actually is all around. (That's the way the film phrases it, okay?) So, if there's one line that people remember from this movie, it's probably one of its famous confessions of love ... but let's back up.

"Love Actually" marries (pun intended) several vignettes about love in different stages (longstanding marriages, the newlywed phase, people flirting in workplaces, you name it), all of which eventually converge, and to call its cast star-studded is ... an understatement. Keira Knightley, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Martin Freeman, Bill Nighy, Andrew Lincoln, Laura Linney, Emma Thompson, Alan Rickman, Colin Firth, Hugh Grant, Thomas Brodie-Sangster, and Rowan Atkinson, just to name a few, appear in various configurations throughout the film, whether Brodie-Sangster's youngster Sam is pining after one of his classmates, Linney's Sarah wants to pursue a relationship with a coworker despite family troubles, Rickman's Harry considers stepping out on his wife Karen (Thompson), Freeman's John meets his eventual girlfriend while working as a nude stand-in on a movie, and Grant's David, the Prime Minister, romances one of his junior staff members. (He also does a very silly dance that Grant was not keen on performing.)

Let's talk about the love triangle between Ejiofor, Knightley, and Lincoln to illustrate why the love found in "Love Actually" might not be healthy, actually. At the start of the film, Juliet and Peter (Knightley and Ejiofor) have a glorious wedding attended by several of the movie's other characters ... and throughout the festivities, Peter's best friend Mark (Lincoln) seems sort of miserable. Why? Well, he's in love with Juliet, which brings us to the quote itself.

Here's the deal. Mark shows up at Peter and Juliet's door, tells Juliet to pretend that it's a group of carol singers, and unveils a series of notecards confessing his feelings — one of which says "To me, you are perfect." After he tells her, via notecard, that he loves her, he walks away ... and Juliet follows, gives him a kiss, and then runs home to her husband.

"To me, you are perfect" is a genuinely beautiful thing to say to someone you love. There's a problem, though. "To me, you are perfect" would be a lovely sentiment under any other circumstances than the ones depicted in this movie. Mark, that is your friend's wife! This sort of thing happens quite rampantly throughout the film, too, with this particular "Love Actually" scene being but one example.

Case in point: In a moment that Alan Rickman did not love filming, Harry buys a necklace for a woman who is, notably, not Karen (instead, it's for his walking HR violation of a secretary, Heike Makatsch's Mia). Similarly, David, ends up falling head over heels in love with his employee Natalie (Martine McCutcheon), and despite that being extremely inappropriate, I'll admit that they're cute together. Meanwhile, Colin Firth's Jamie has a whole storyline where he falls in love with a woman who does not speak any English — Lúcia Moniz's character Aurélia — and by the time they get engaged, they still can't functionally communicate. To be sure, "Love Actually" is chock full of unhealthy entanglements, and Juliet, Peter, and Mark are no exception.

... Sorry if you really love "Love Actually." It has its moments! Anyway, what are some other great quotes from this beloved holiday film?

#3453. Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

The term that comes to mind most is “ambulance-chasing.” Earlier this week, just one week after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault and two days after he was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for his crimes, word spread that Netflix was prepping a documentary on the comedian-turned-criminal.

Olivia Isaacs’ documentary has been in the works for a while. Deadline’s initial story on the project even noted that it “was referenced during the trial” and that while “giving evidence at London’s Southwark Crown Court, Mark Pinheiro, a former friend of Brand, said he had been approached by a producer about the Netflix show.” Related Stories David O. Russell’s ‘Madden’ Biopic Is Out Next Week — Does Anybody Know or Care? In Shana Feste’s Films, Gender-Flipping Cinema’s ‘Tradition of Celebrating Damaged Men’ Is Its Own Reward

But that the project — “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” a slim and unfocused documentary feature that clocks in at just under 90 minutes — was being dropped on the streamer to ride the wave of interest after Brand’s conviction and sentencing felt distasteful. How essential, after all, could this be? And what could it tell us about Brand’s actual trial, sentencing, and conviction?

Turns out, not much. Isaacs’ film doesn’t get into the trial until its final five minutes (counting its end credits to boot), when it uses title cards to share the conviction news, note that all of the allegations contained in the film itself “pre-date” those that led to the conviction, and make clear that Brand’s legal team was contacted after the Monday conviction and chose not to respond. That’s perhaps the most interesting part of the film’s literally tacked-on final moments: a desire to show its work when it comes to the journalism and attendant standards behind Brand’s long-simmering takedown.

Other elements are far less successful, as Isaacs’ film leans hard on tired tropes and cloying conventions. Captions frequently mention “[unsettling music playing]” or “[dramatic music playing]” during the most benign moments. Old footage of Brand, from home video to early stand-up gigs, is played slowly, all the better to maximize the sense that something is wrong with this man. Far more effective are interviews with those who were allegedly victimized by Brand, but those are often drowned out by played-out techniques.

The film opens with a typical “rise and fall” style montage, charting Brand’s humble beginnings, meteoric rise to fame, profound injection into the cultural consciousness (he met the queen! and also Tom Cruise!), stumble into right-wing ideology, and eventual criminal convictions for horrific acts the film posits everyone knew about forever.

It is, after all, called “Russell Brand: Open Secret.”

Isaacs’ film lacks a thesis beyond the general idea that everyone knew Brand was a creep from the jump. She assembles a hodgepodge of talking heads to hammer that home, including fellow comedians, some genuinely freaked out ex-girlfriends, a handful of accusers (including one who, reticent to appear on camera, is replaced with an actress, one of the film’s most thoughtful choices), and some bizarrely starry-eyed commentators (journalist George Monbiot comes across particularly badly here, zipping from talking about his early delight in Brand and his now-held belief that Brand’s far-right switch is the most horrifying aspect of all of this, oof).

Most compelling are Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, who worked tirelessly to investigate myriad accusations against Brand for years (Urwin first began to look into Brand in January of 2019). Even smushed up against a herky-jerky timeline and a loose sense of purpose, the way that Urwin and Wace talk about the precise nature of their work, what they can and cannot report, the women they spoke to, and the ways in which they were nearly shut down (and, in fact, many other investigations of its ilk were allegedly turned off) is both gripping and necessary.

With more time and better access, the film could have focused more on the police and legal minds that helped build the case against Brand, but in the rush to get this out in the world, that was surely not a major aim.

By its midpoint, Isaacs’ film turns its lens on the culture that helped give rise to Brand, the wild “noughties” when “ladette culture” ruled and being overtly sexy and crude was de rigueur. Women were into Brand! Being ruthlessly unfunny and breathlessly boorish was hot! Also, his dad was mean to him! Diddy and David Walliams jump scares! These are some of the insights on offer in “Open Secret,” and the only thing truly revealing about them is how huge of a mistake it was to let someone as outwardly disgusting and deeply unwitty as Brand get into a place where he could pick and choose his “damsels” or his “whores,” depending on who is talking about them.

The film speed-runs through the last few years of Brand’s life and career, as he pivots into far-right shock politics and Christianity just as the walls are starting to close in on him. Brand may have alleged that his former cadre of famous friends and stalwarts won’t “touch him with a barge pole” these days, but the film’s distinct lack of bigger talking heads stands out. That could stand some further interrogation, too, but there’s simply no time for that. (Well, there is, but not if you want to be a part of this news cycle.)

The four-day gap between Brand’s conviction and the film’s release is zippy, even for Netflix, which has gotten progressively speedier with its true crime joints. In July of 2024, it was announced that Netflix would release a multi-part Karen Read documentary, just days after her first murder trial ended in a mistrial due to a hung jury on July 1, 2024. Three episodes dropped earlier this month.

In January of 2026, the streamer announced a Lucy Letby project with “unprecedented access” after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced it would bring no further criminal charges against the former nurse, who was sentenced to life imprisonment for a slew of charges of murder and attempted murder of infants in her care following a review of additional allegations. “The Truth and Tragedy of Moriah Wilson” was first publicly announced in February of 2026, almost three years after Kaitlin Armstrong was convicted of first-degree murder of the cyclist in November of 2023.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” will surely capture lots of eyeballs as this part of the news cycle winds down, but what the film trades for immediacy, it more than loses in actual insight. Part two can’t be far behind. Let’s just hope it takes far more time to make and far more consideration to craft.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” is now streaming on Netflix.

Your burning questions about GTA 6 pre-order bonuses to Rockstar’s many official events, all in one place

These bonuses offer a classic sedan with its own storage area, vintage looks and hairstyles for Jason and Lucia, and some special weapon patterns inspired by Tommy Vercetti. You can take a closer look at all of these here.

The catch is that the game is fully digital. If you pre-order and pick up GTA 6 at, say, GameStop, all you'll get is a code in a box. And while the pre-order bonuses don't give players a gameplay advantage, many fans believe cosmetics are a core part of GTA 6's appeal.

There's the standard edition of GTA 6 ($79.99) and the Ultimate edition ($79.99). The Ultimate Edition comes with a retro-futuristic sports car, two special types of guns for Jason and Lucia, a fancy motorcycle and kayak, and some version-exclusive locations. These areas include, among other things, two car customization shops, a salon, a clothing store, a tattoo parlor, a Mud Club vehicle and hideout, and a contraband store.

No — GTA 6 is a stand-alone single-player experience. If you're on PS5, you can't play with folks on Xbox and vice versa. GTA Online is a separate experience, but one that Rockstar appears to be prepping for a new era. This next iteration of GTA's multiplayer will offer more ways to roleplay, and those features are being developed in partnership with FiveM, the modders at the forefront of that scene. GTA Online will be playable on GTA 6's launch day ... but it's also accessible right now!

If you're lucky enough to own both consoles, it may come down to preference. Rockstar and Sony have repeatedly insisted that GTA 6 "plays best" on PS5, and indeed, the platform comes with a few exclusive features. The DualSense controller will offer high-fidelity haptic feedback and improved spatial audio rendering. The Xbox version can be played via the Cloud, and on previous-generation hardware.

PS5 Pros are expensive and difficult to find right now. GTA 6 does have some PS5 Pro enhancements, such as Spectral Super Resolution as well as ray-traced shadows. No matter where you play it, GTA 6 will be capped at 30 frames per second.

Some people evidently think so. Red Dead Redemption 2 rendered at 30 FPS and that didn't deter it from being a critically acclaimed game.

If you want it! The controller and its chromatic blue and purple decals are quite nice, but the peripheral costs $84 and won't be available until Nov. 19. For now, you can pre-order it.

Rockstar has not announced a release for the PC version of the game, though many expect a port down the line.

No. While both games are set in the same universe, Jason and Lucia's story is a self-contained narrative. If you already have the game, Grand Theft Auto 5 could be a good way to kill some time before GTA 6. Some players are planning a final drive through Los Santos before the sequel drops, which could be a nice sendoff to the game.

If these leaks are true, you sure can! Fun fact: GTA 6's map is supposed to be three times bigger than Red Dead Redemption 2.

If GTA 6 is anything like its predecessors, it will be a game you could ostensibly play forever. If you want to go through the story, though, completion times will depend on how distracted you get along the way. For now, we know that it took at least one Rockstar developer around 80 hours to clear GTA 6's main story.

While it is your god-given right to mow down pedestrians on a busy day at the beach, you'll probably have to play through some initial tutorial or story bits, like the apparently early segment where Lucia is still in prison. The good news is that Leonida's map opens up earlier than in previous GTA 6 games.

Based on early previews, GTA 6 sounds like a harsher game that won't make it easy for you to rob everything and get rich right away. The better the car, the harder it will be to steal. The amount of money you can hold at one time appears to be limited. The new Wanted system sounds intense!

Whoa, there. Uh ... Jason and Lucia can be intimate with one another during tastefully rendered cutscenes. While leaks made it seem like characters could just walk around buck naked, that gameplay might've been achieved via a cheat menu. There is, however, a nudist colony where players might be able to go commando. And of course, GTA 6 will still have its signature strip clubs.

Based on ratings, players will apparently have plenty of opportunities to ogle digital male genitals throughout the game. If that's what you're seeking, there's probably a game out there that's a better fit for you than GTA 6.

There are a few! In addition to Rockstar's music festival event in Miami on Nov. 21, there are also a few pop-ups in places like London with some expensive GTA 6 merch. If you're in Miami, you might've already seen a number of advertisements for in-game brands, or noticed hot neon pink Vice City lights around places like the airport. Rockstar's also unleashed a handful of cars from the game around Miami that were crafted by West Coast Customs. You might remember them as the same cars from that recent realistic gameplay video that fans initially didn't believe was real.

On Nov. 18, basketball fans will be treated to a partnership between Rockstar and the Miami Heat. The basketball team's stadium will host concessions based on food brands from GTA 6. The Miami Heat itself will wear GTA 6-themed jerseys, and they'll play their game against the Milwaukee Bucks on a special pink hardwood court. Fans who visit the Kaseya Center on this day can purchase the jerseys worn by the team that was designed by Travis Scott's brand, Cactus Jack.

Cardi B is going to take over a strip club in Miami in honor of GTA 6 as well ... but that's not a Rockstar-sanctioned event, as fitting as it might seem.

#3450. Ronald D. Moore Has Found The Perfect Outlander Replacement

For almost 12 years, Ronald D. Moore’s epic romantic fantasy series Outlander has been the mainstay of his TV career. Now that the show has drawn to a conclusion, however, he’s already found a replacement for it, against a different historical backdrop. Anyone who enjoys Outlander will undoubtedly find plenty to love in this new series, which is also adapted from a major franchise in another medium.

There are few more exciting upcoming fantasy shows set to debut in 2027 than Moore’s next project, which features spectacular world-building and a lead actor who would have been the number one pick of many franchise fans. Most likely premiering on Prime Video at the backend of next year, it’s almost certain to take the streaming charts by storm.

If Outlander is a fantasy TV series worth the commitment, then this new release fronted by Dave Bautista will probably move a little faster, as it tells the story of a traditional hero’s journey. God of War is being adapted from the hugely successful video game franchise of the same name, which follows a mythological hero by the name of Kratos across the ancient world.

A swashbuckling warrior who’s somewhat larger in build than Jamie Fraser, Kratos straddles Ancient Greek and Norse mythology in his gaming iteration. However, Ronald D. Moore’s God of War will pick up his story in the Norse realm of Midgard, as he and his son Atreus attempt to climb the highest mountain in any known land.

Just as Outlander ostensibly ends in tragedy for Jamie and Claire, a tragic event shapes the premise of Prime Video’s God of War. Kratos is undertaking his quest following the death of Faye, otherwise known as Laufey the Just, who is the mother of Atreus. It’s this tragedy that ultimately motivates the journey of father and son to try and reach the highest peak of the nine Norse realms.

Steeped in real ancient mythology and the traditions of the fantasy genre, God of War is set up to be every bit the pseudohistorical epic that Outlander has become over the past decade. There are key similarities between the two shows when it comes to family dynamics, world-building on a colossal scale using extensive source material, and a visually compelling mix of gritty realism and fantastical phenomena.

Dave Bautista has already gone through an incredible transformation to play Kratos in God of War, which proves all the critics of his casting wrong.

Only an adaptation of this scope could have moved Ronald D. Moore to dive into another fantasy project following eight seasons of Outlander. Moore is the main developer, executive producer, and showrunner of God of War, which we can also expect to span several years, in not quite as many episodes as the story of Claire and Jamie Fraser.

Instead, the show will likely have fewer, shorter seasons, but look even larger and more cinematic onscreen. After all, there’s surely a higher visual threshold for the suspension of disbelief when depicting Norse mythology than there is for depictions of 17th century Scotland.

The confirmation that God of War has recast Dave Bautista as Kratos following an on-set injury to the original choice for lead actor, Ryan Hurst, has taken expectations for the series up a notch. Bautista’s magnetic screen presence and physical attributes will help convince viewers of the series protagonist’s godlike qualities on the battlefield.

Meanwhile, the likes of Teresa Palmer and Ed Skrein stand out in an impressive supporting cast, while early images of the show suggest that we’re in for a fantasy story grounded in visual naturalism, much as Outlander is. God of War is shaping up to be one of the genre’s biggest new releases of the 2020s, and fans of Ronald D. Moore’s work should be counting down the days until its release.

#3449. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3448. 5 Forgotten '80s Sitcoms That Still Hold Up Today

The 1980s were stacked with classic sitcoms. "Cheers," "Taxi," "The Golden Girls" and so many more had us pinned to our couches during primetime. Of course, there was also formulaic garbage like "Who's the Boss," "Full House" and "Growing Pains." This is always the state of play in television. But the quality-to-trash ratio was pretty favorable throughout the entire decade.

Nevertheless, there were many terrific '80s sitcoms that got axed before they had a chance to flourish. In most cases, they were flouting formula, which meant viewers had to adjust to different comedic rhythms. Audiences proved malleable with variety shows like "The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour," "Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In," and "Saturday Night Live," but the sitcom structure was sacrosanct: set-up and punchline all the way to a tidy finale in 30 minutes. Every minor crisis got resolved with a closing laugh (unless it was "a very special episode"). Deviating too far from the norm was typically fatal.

The '80s sitcom graveyard is littered with coulda-been classics, most notably "Police Squad!," which died a quick death after six episodes, but later spawned the wildly successful "Naked Gun" franchise. Alas, there are others that were so unsuccessful and/or controversial that they're only streamable on YouTube via old VHS rips (if they're streamable at all). Here are five '80s sitcoms that undeservedly got a quick hook.

Martin Mull was a brilliant comedic performer whose television career got off to a promising start in the 1970s. He was a scream as the detestable Garth Gimble on Norman Lear's "Mary Hartman, Mary Hartman," which earned him a spinoff as his character's brother Barth Gimble on the influential talk show spoof "Fernwood 2 Night." The show was something of a lark, but got a second season as "America 2 Night." After that, it seemed to be only a matter of time before he got another network show.

It took six years after the end of "America 2 Night," but that opportunity finally arrived in 1984 with "Domestic Life." The show had a seemingly can't-miss pedigree with Steve Martin as a co-creator, but CBS lost confidence in it quickly when it got off to a rocky ratings start as a mid-season replacement. Mull starred as Martin Crane, a Seattle TV news commentator who — along with his wife, rebellious 15-year-old daughter, and business-whiz 10-year-old son — encounters a variety of stock sitcom complications.

"Domestic Life" wasn't a parody per se, but, for 10 whole episodes, it was a hilarious vehicle for Mull's droll sensibility. Robert Ridgely was a delight as pompous anchorman Cliff Hamilton, and the series upended expectations at every turn. One of the best episodes found Mull scrambling to come up with $4,000 due for a balloon payment on his house, and being forced to ask his investor son for a loan. Mull plays the scene with an uproarious mix of flattery and outright shame. "Domestic Life" should've run for many seasons, but, despite critical acclaim, the ratings were never there.

When I watched the premiere of "Frank's Place" on CBS in 1987, I was simultaneously grateful that such an idiosyncratic sitcom could exist on network television and saddened that it was almost certainly destined for an early cancellation. The show reunited "WKRP in Cincinnati" creator Hugh Wilson with Tim Reid, who played DJ Venus Flytrap on the hit series, and was blessed with a nifty premise. Reid stars as Frank Parrish, a Boston college professor who's inherited a New Orleans restaurant. Frank wants to sell the restaurant, but is forced to stay on when one of the eatery's waitresses puts a voodoo curse on him. How will this erudite New Englander adjust to life in the Big Easy? On one level, this is basic fish-out-of-water stuff, but it goes places racially and culturally that no series dared to explore during that era.

Wilson adopted a single camera approach, and eschewed a laugh track. The latter threw a lot of viewers at the time, but, judging from solid Nielsen ratings over summer reruns, people were getting used to this approach. That's probably because the show was dripping with New Orleans atmosphere; it was every bit as lively and enchanting and delicious (oh, the food porn) as the city itself. Why was it canceled? According to Walter Kronkite, the legendary CBS newsman (who was a huge fan of the show), then-CBS CEO Laurence Tisch took offense to an episode that was critical of junk bonds (a major source of Tisch's wealth).

Why isn't this beloved series available via streaming or physical media? Much like "WKRP in Cincinnati," the music licensing is crazy expensive, and soundalike zydeco would rob the show of its soul. So the blurry VHS rips on YouTube are, sadly, the best we're going to get.

Three years before they brought the mean-spirited "Married... with Children" to the upstart Fox network, Ron Leavitt and Michael G. Moye caused a caustic stir with the blithely nasty "It's Your Move." The show starred Jason Bateman as a conscienceless teenager who scams everyone in his orbit, but takes particular pleasure in torturing his neighbor (David Garrison), a struggling writer who commits the cardinal sin of dating Bateman's mother. The two quickly engage in a tit-for-tat battle intended to discredit each other, but, until the series veered away from this format, their petty battles always ended in a stalemate.

Bateman landed this leading role on the strength of his smarmy work as Ricky Schroeder's friend on the NBC sitcom "Silver Spoons." He's matched every step of the way by Garrison, who toes the line between decency and sheer malevolence. There wasn't a nastier sitcom on network television at the time, and that, in part, proved to be its undoing. NBC found itself inundated with letters from concerned parents, who were alarmed to see their children mimicking Bateman's corrupt/criminal behavior. Pair this with the show trying to compete in the same timeslot as ABC's popular nighttime soap "Dynasty," and NBC opted to cut bait.

In the end, it worked out for everyone: Bateman smoothly segued from slappable kid to flustered adult (shining in "Arrested Development"), while Garrison turned into a confidante for Ed O'Neil's Al Bundy on "Married... with Children." But "It's Your Move" was a sharp (perhaps unintentional) satire of the greed-driven Reagan era. The characters on this show are either naive dopes or venal predators.

For five weeks in the spring of 1982, ABC burned off episodes of a sitcom that must've melted the brains of people who stumbled across it in a crowded time slot. Created in part by Michael Jacobs, a sitcom machine who would reach high highs with "Dinosaurs" and deep lows with "Boy Meets World," "No Soap, Radio" aimed to turn an inside-baseball comedy non-sequitur (on par with "The Aristocrats") into a successful sitcom. Had it debuted on HBO, it might've become a sustainable critical sensation. As a network series, it was dead on arrival.

The very loose premise of the show revolved around Steve Guttenberg as a manager of a failing Atlantic City hotel. These segments present the series as a slamming-door farce a la "Fawlty Towers," but it detours into absurd bits that, like its title, have nothing to do with whatever threadbare narrative it's trying to advance. People have compared the show to "Monty Python's Flying Circus," but it's clearly inspired by "Kentucky Fried Movie." The intermittent news breaks are straight out of the chaotic David Zucker-Jim Abrahams-Jerry Zucker classic. I'd love to talk to the creators of this show, because I simply don't understand how it was greenlit in 1982. "No Soap, Radio" is a shotgun spray of silliness. As a late-night show, devoid of the Guttenberg anchor and with a better recurring cast, it could've been a sensation. Instead, it's a fun little show that couldn't.

When Clint Eastwood's "Dirty Harry" film series sunk to a vile level of self-parody with the putrid "Sudden Impact," the conditions were perfect for a straight-up, ZAZ-type spoof of the star's judge-jury-executioner shenanigans. Comedy wunderkind Alan Spencer, who broke into the industry at the age of 15 as a joke writer, delivered the goofy goods in 1986 with the splendidly silly "Sledge Hammer!" The series starred David Rasche (Karl Muller from "Succession") as a trigger-happy San Francisco cop who's carrying on a near-relationship with his .44 Magnum. He sleeps with the gun (which rests on a satin pillow"), showers with it, and talks to it. Unlike Dirty Harry, Sledge Hammer is generally an affable guy, who, despite his extrajudicial bent, is liked by his partner Detective Dori Doreau (Anne-Marie Martin). He drives his supervisor Captain Trunk (Harrison Page) nuts, but typically gets the job done — albeit messily at times.

"Sledge Hammer" received mostly positive reviews and initially posted solid ratings. This changed when ABC began moving it around the schedule. When the show's numbers plummeted, ABC placed "Sledge Hammer!" squarely on the chopping block. Knowing they were doomed, Spencer and his writers ended the series finale with Hammer botching the disarming of a nuclear warhead, thus leading to the destruction of San Francisco. Amusingly, this episode did surprisingly well in the ratings, so ABC greenlit a second season (set five years in the past). The network promptly did "Sledge Hammer!" dirty by pitting it against "The Cosby Show." This was the end, but unlike the other shows on this list, you can currently stream "Sledge Hammer!" on Prime Video (it also received a physical media release). It's still a riot 40 years later.

#3447. Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

Look, it’s only November, but we know we’re not the only people getting excited about Christmas already. In fact, we know that some studio executives have been thinking about the holiday season a lot for a while now. That’s because they know as well as anyone that they have two juggernauts to contend with: “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday,” which open on Dec. 18 in true clash of the titans fashion.

There’s a question that if those movies take up so much oxygen, will there be room for anything else? The last “Dune” movie surpassed $700 million globally at the box office, and “Avengers: Doomsday” has already sold over $60 million in pre-sales. Those top two titles create enormous competition for everything opening on Christmas weekend itself. Those include the Dwayne Johnson threequel “Jumanji: Open World” from Sony, the football biopic “Mr. Irrelevant” from Paramount, Robert Eggers’ horror film “Werwulf” from Focus, and Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” from Neon. Paramount’s “The Angry Birds Movie 3” is also opening on December 23 just ahead of the rest. Related Stories Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go David O. Russell’s ‘Madden’ Biopic Is Out Next Week — Does Anybody Know or Care?

Anyone will tell you the Christmas holiday is always crowded at the movies. And there’s usually room for multiple blockbusters to draw crowds. Despite the onslaught of new titles, U.S, distributors are confident they’ll be able to secure the screens they need to be successful. For instance, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” this year opened at the end of July to $360 million domestic, and “The Odyssey” in its third week in theaters still made $50 million. Even during the “Barbenheimer” weekend, “Sound of Freedom” in its third week managed to bring in another $19.8 million. There’s always opportunity if the demand is there.

Recent Christmases have been similarly crowded. Last year had “Avatar: Fire and Ash,” “The Housemaid,” a new “Spongebob,” and “Marty Supreme” open the weekend before Christmas, then “Anaconda” and “Song Sung Blue” over the holiday itself. 2024 had “Mufasa: The Lion King,” “Nosferatu,” “Sonic the Hedgehog 3,” “A Complete Unknown,” “Babygirl,” and “The Fire Inside” all in a short span just before Xmas.

But this Christmas does bring some unique challenges that studios are preemptively working around for their titles that are not “Dune” or “Avengers.” Both of those films have had tickets on sale for months, and both are locked in a fight for premium large format screens that distributors would be lying to say they didn’t want, even if it’s for a family film that doesn’t need it. Warner Bros. and Legendary’s “Dune: Part Three” specifically will exclusively be on IMAX screens, which has famously left “Doomsday” without them, leaving Disney to create its Infinity Vision certification to drum up excitement.

To compete, “Angry Birds 3” is still opening in 3D if on otherwise standard format screens. “Werwulf” won’t have IMAX as Focus did for “Nosferatu,” but it has pre-sold select 35mm screenings of the film that have already done quite well (they went on sale on the full moon last month). The hope, too, is that titles like “Jumanji” and “Mr. Irrelevant” appeal to crowds that are distinctive from the male, fanboy-heavy audiences for “Dunesday.”

One source IndieWire spoke with argued that even though this Christmas is top heavy, it’s arguably lighter in sheer quantity than we’ve seen in recent years. What we’re not seeing is a movie like “Marty Supreme” or “Uncut Gems” getting a run in a more mid-size or limited number of screens. Universal doesn’t have a movie opening in that window, nor does Amazon MGM. Other awards titles like “The Debut” from A24 are going earlier in the month and aren’t doing the limited, Christmas day, qualifying run before going wide in January (GKIDS’ “Look Back” may be an exception, opening December 30).

There are some potential holdovers that could generate money well into Christmas. Rival studio execs are keeping an eye on movies like Disney’s animated “Hexed” or Universal’s “Focker-in-Law,” and Focus’ “Elsinore” will also be going wider shortly before the holidays.

The hope now is that all of these films get their flowers and collectively put an exclamation point on a stellar 2026, with the box office now projected to finish far above $10 billion domestic, a number that might’ve been a pipe dream this time in 2025. That’s reason for holiday cheer, indeed.

#3445. Rings of Power Just Changed the Nazgul in 1 Terrifying Way: ‘They Still Have a Human Side’

Sauron's Nine Rings offer healing and unimaginable power, but the price is far worse than death

Sauron's Nine Rings offer healing and unimaginable power, but the price is far worse than death

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 sees Sauron begin to recruit the nine lieutenants that will one day become the Nazgûl, or Ringraiths. While details in J.R.R. Tolkien’s lore are a bit scarce when it comes to the gradual transformation of the Ringwraiths, Rings of Power initially presents the rings as miraculous gifts that transform the Men who wear them into Nazgnagôl, or "Ring-servants.” Rather than immediately enslaving their wearers, Sauron's rings heal their injuries, cure terrible afflictions, and grant them extraordinary power. The catch is that every gift brings its recipient closer to surrendering his freedom.

For Rings of Power co-creator Patrick McKay, depicting that transformation is one of the biggest reasons to make the series in the first place.

"Part of the opportunity of this show is to dramatize what the introduction of these powers, the rings, mean to all these peoples in this world," McKay tells Polygon.

As part of the series, McKay and his fellow showrunner J.D. Payne wanted to establish why anyone would willingly accept a ring from Sauron, the self-proclaimed Dark Lord, in the first place.

The LOTR showrunners and star reveal why now is the perfect time to feature an essential character

"It was very important to J.D. and I that there was a reason you would want to wear one, which is that it would give you wealth and power," McKay says. "The idea that, in the lore, thousands of years from now, they're enslaved to Sauron's will, they've lost their humanity, and they're ghost-like wraiths, that's a long way off."

"That's the bill coming. Right now, it's the good times."

Note: Spoilers follow for the first four episodes of Rings of Power season 3.

Executive producing director Charlotte Brändström wanted the Nazgnagôl to feel recognizably human while also possessing an unsettling supernatural presence. That begins right at the start of season 3, when a Nazgnagôl shows up in a battle between Elves and Orcs where Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) confronts the Nazgnagôl — and is handily defeated before escaping.

"I slowed down everything around them," Brändström says, explaining that she filmed the characters at either 36 or 48 frames per second. She also introduced echoes and reverberation into their movements and voices.

The Nazgnagôl's unnerving composure is just as important as their supernatural abilities. "We could feel their power by the fact that they never needed to hurry," she says. "They know the power they have."

Despite their terrifying appearances and abilities, Brändström emphasizes that the Nazgnagôl haven't completely transformed into the monsters audiences recognize from The Lord of the Rings.

"They still have a human side to them at that moment."

That distinction is crucial. Tolkien's Nazgûl are terrifying precisely because they have become so thoroughly enslaved to Sauron that almost nothing remains of their former identities. The Rings of Power is exploring how that happens, beginning with men who have understandable reasons to accept the rings and gradually revealing the price of their newfound power.

By the time season 3 begins, Sauron has already recruited three kings of men to become Nazgnagôl. Early in the premiere episode, we’re given a look at the brutal audition process when five leaders from Rhûn sent by the Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) arrive in Mordor to forge an alliance between the two kingdoms. Sauron recounts how their ancestors ruled Rhûn for a thousand years before the wizard showed up and cursed their flesh and that of their descendants.

After an orc kills the two that are most loyal to the Dark Wizard, Sauron reveals a small box holding the remaining Rings of Power but says he can only spare one. Then he drops a sword on the ground, implying that the last man standing can claim it. The victor is Khamûl the Easterling (Zubin Varla). After he undergoes a painful transformation, the wizard’s curse is cleansed, and Sauron dubs him “the fairest of the Nine.” Newly empowered, Khamûl is later able to confront and overpowers the Dark Wizard to effectively seize control of Rhûn.

Khamûl is also a significant figure in Tolkien's mythology. He's the only Nazgûl identified by a personal name, apart from the title of the Witch-king of Angmar. As detailed in Unfinished Tales, Khamûl is associated with the East and ranks second among the Nine. That makes his connection to Rhûn fitting, although the specific circumstances of his recruitment and his confrontation with the Dark Wizard are unique to Rings of Power.

We later see the same violent ritual play out with Men from the Southlands, which includes Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin). After Theo wins the contest, Sauron conducts a dark ritual that supposedly identifies his lineage: according to the Great Deceiver, Theo is descended from “a noble house of old” that were “the sworn servants of Mordor” supposedly born with special powers. Sauron rationalizes that this is why Theo was previously drawn to the sword hilt that essentially unlocked Mordor at the end of season 1. Whether or not all of this is true, Theo does accept the ring.

In an interview with Nerdist, Muhafidin described Theo's growing resentment toward Arondir, whom he holds partly responsible for failing to protect Bronwyn. “I think we find him at the beginning of the season kind of void of that hope and angered by the pain the world has dealt out to him,” he said. Sauron manipulates that desperation and offers Theo great power. By the time Theo really starts to question what the ring might cost him, it’s already too late.

The most devastating demonstration of the Nazgnagôl's predicament comes during the climactic battle at Gundabad in episode 4. After Arondir discovers the long-lost Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) in a cell, they attempt to escape the Orc stronghold with Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) on the back of a Great Eagle. But then a Nazgnagôl confronts Arondir, and Theo takes off the mask.

Rather than immediately attack, Theo urges Arondir to leave. Unlike the Nazgûl, Nazgnagôl like Theo here still have their autonomy to an extent. Sauron’s influence and corruption have yet to completely take over. Arondir refuses to abandon Theo, and for a moment, it seems like he might actually take the ring off. Then Sauron arrives and forces Theo to kill Arondir as if he’s already exerting total control.

Arondir's death is doubly heartbreaking because Theo recognizes the man standing before him. But whatever humanity remains inside him isn't enough to prevent the Dark Lord from asserting control. We all remember the Nazgûl as these terrifying, faceless, and inhumane wraiths. Are the Nazgnagôl more or less frightening when we can still see the people beneath the mask long before they’re totally destroyed?

#3443. 7 Major Movie Twists That Happen Shockingly Early, Ranked

Major spoilers ahead for all seven movies.

Most movies save their biggest surprise for the end. The audience suspects the wrong person until a final-act revelation upends everything. It's a tried-and-tested arrangement, and the best plot twists in crime movies demonstrate how satisfying a properly timed disclosure can be. But there's something especially audacious about dropping the bombshell while most of the story is still ahead.

Alfred Hitchcock knew that better than almost anyone. In Psycho, he spent nearly half a movie encouraging viewers to follow Janet Leigh's troubled heroine before disposing of her in the shower. The scene was horrifying, but the real trick was what happened afterward: a story that appeared to be about stolen money suddenly had no thief to follow.

An early twist creates a problem for the filmmaker. Once the surprise is out, there has to be enough compelling material left to justify the decision. Killing someone in the opening minutes doesn't automatically qualify, either. Plenty of horror movies do that. The more interesting question is whether the reveal forces viewers to reconsider the kind of film they're watching.

That's the principle behind this ranking. Timing matters, but the entries aren't ordered by a stopwatch. What counts most is how radically the reveal changes the story and how convincingly the film follows through. A clever genre switch can be tremendous fun without being as consequential as losing the character we've been encouraged to treat as the lead.

Some of these surprises were practically advertised in advance, which complicates matters. Others remained closely guarded secrets. Either way, the best early twists don't finish the puzzle. They make audiences realize they've been trying to solve the wrong one.

Fresh starts like a romantic comedy. Noa (Daisy Edgar-Jones), defeated by dating apps, meets a charming doctor named Steve (Sebastian Stan) at the grocery store. Then, about half an hour into the film, he drugs her and reveals that he sells women's flesh to wealthy cannibals. Well, that explains why the first date went so smoothly.

Director Mimi Cave makes the transformation part of the film's design. The opening credits don't appear until around the 30-minute mark, as though the seemingly agreeable romance has been a feature-length practical joke on Noa. Suddenly, Steve's earlier charm looks less like flirtation and more like the sales technique of a man who knows exactly how to gain someone's trust.

The turn is brilliantly staged, and the rest becomes a nasty exercise in survival horror. Yet the marketing and growing unease have hinted that something dreadful is coming. Fresh conceals the nature of its horror without making audiences rethink whose story they're watching. That's a terrific trick, but the movies above take bigger structural risks.

Wes Craven put Scream's biggest star in the opening scene, then killed her before the story had properly begun. Drew Barrymore's Casey Becker is murdered by Ghostface roughly 12 minutes in, despite the actress's prominence in the marketing. Anyone assuming her celebrity came with plot armor was in for a very unpleasant surprise.

Craven builds the sequence around a phone call that stops being playful. Casey's horror-movie knowledge offers no protection, and Barrymore makes the ordeal frightening. The opening established the tone that helped make Scream one of the essential '90s horror movies. It also made a promise the franchise still works to keep: knowing the rules won't necessarily save anybody.

The distinction from Psycho matters. Scream dispatches its supposed star before viewers have settled into the main narrative; Casey's murder effectively launches Sidney Prescott's story. Hitchcock waits long enough to establish another movie before taking its protagonist away. Barrymore's exit is an ingenious opening ambush, but it doesn't overturn an entire story already in progress.

Imagine paying for a whodunit and being told who did it before you've formed a theory. Rian Johnson comes close in Knives Out. After novelist Harlan Thrombey (Christopher Plummer) is found dead, a flashback reveals that his nurse, Marta Cabrera (Ana de Armas), apparently gave him a lethal dose of morphine by mistake. Harlan takes his own life to protect her.

That supposed solution turns the mystery inside out. Detective Benoit Blanc (Daniel Craig) is still investigating, but the audience knows more than he does. Johnson persuades viewers to side with Marta, turning a delightful detective into the person they desperately hope will fail. Every innocent question Blanc asks carries the threat of ruining her life.

Johnson's sleight of hand is more sophisticated than a simple early reveal, because the film later complicates what we thought we witnessed. He uses the apparent answer to make us emotionally invested in a possible culprit. The twist powers much of the movie rather than simply launching the plot.

It's cleverer than an opening ambush, but the revelation ultimately becomes another layer of misdirection. The remaining films leave their characters with consequences that cannot be undone.

Arnold Schwarzenegger spent The Terminator trying to murder Sarah Connor. When he returns as another T-800 in James Cameron's sequel, her son John (Edward Furlong) seems equally endangered. Cameron encourages that assumption by introducing a second time traveler who looks like a police officer. Then the two machines converge on John in a shopping mall.

The T-800 protects the boy. The officer, played by Robert Patrick, is the real killer: an advanced T-1000. In a moment, the monster from the original becomes the sequel's unlikely hero. The reversal creates room for the relationship that gives Terminator 2 its emotional force. John begins teaching a machine why humans matter.

There's a fair argument against placing the twist higher. Cameron deliberately showed Schwarzenegger as the protector in the trailers, deciding that the reversal was a selling point rather than a secret to preserve. Plenty of 1991 moviegoers knew the truth before entering the theater.

Even with that disadvantage, the first-act reveal rewrites the franchise's central relationship. The boy who would have fled from Arnold in the original now refuses to abandon him. Few sequels have repurposed an iconic villain so successfully.

Ryan Gosling is the face of The Place Beyond the Pines, and for nearly its first hour the movie belongs to him. Luke Glanton is a motorcycle stunt rider who begins robbing banks to support his infant son. Derek Cianfrance suggests a crime drama about a flawed man trying to become a father.

Then rookie police officer Avery Cross (Bradley Cooper) shoots Luke dead. The film doesn't invent a way to bring Gosling back or hurry toward a conclusion. It follows Avery, then jumps ahead to the lives of both men's sons. Luke's death transforms a familiar rise-and-fall narrative into something much more unsettling about inheritance.

Cianfrance has explicitly credited Psycho with inspiring this approach. Hitchcock's ability to pass the story from one apparent protagonist to another stayed with him, and he adapted the idea to a film about the effects of choices across generations. There's an unusual confidence in asking an audience to keep investing after the marquee star disappears.

Gosling's removal is genuinely irreversible, and the movie becomes richer because he's gone. Luke never knows the harm his decisions will cause, but every subsequent chapter bears their imprint. The twist supplies the film's underlying argument rather than simply jolting the audience. Few early revelations reshape a story so completely.

The most frightening moment in Hereditary arrives long before the full nature of its supernatural threat emerges. Ari Aster directs the audience's attention toward Charlie (Milly Shapiro), the withdrawn daughter of Annie Graham (Toni Collette). Her behavior seems central to the family's mystery. Then, roughly 30 minutes in, Charlie suffers an allergic reaction at a party.

Her brother Peter (Alex Wolff) races toward a hospital, but Charlie leans out of the car for air and is killed when her head strikes a roadside pole. Peter drives home in shock and leaves his sister's body for his mother to discover. The silence is almost unbearable.

Charlie's death doesn't merely remove a character who appeared important. It changes the film's emotional temperature. Annie's grief becomes a destructive force within the family, and Peter's guilt turns ordinary encounters into acts of psychological torture. By the time the occult elements become clearer, viewers have already been living inside an intimate domestic catastrophe.

That sustained aftermath is what places Hereditary above the other modern films here. Among cinema's bleakest movies, it's particularly ruthless about making grief feel inescapable. The shock arrives early, but that grief poisons nearly every scene that follows. Only Hitchcock's earlier, genre-changing act of narrative betrayal edges it out.

Alfred Hitchcock spends nearly 45 minutes making Psycho seem like Janet Leigh's movie. Marion Crane steals $40,000 from her employer and flees, fearing arrest. Her arrival at the Bates Motel seems like another complication for a woman who has made a terrible decision. Even her conversation with Norman Bates (Anthony Perkins) appears to belong to Marion's journey.

Then she steps into the shower, and the entire film changes. Hitchcock kills the apparent heroine before the halfway point, discarding the stolen-money plot along with her. Viewers who identified with Marion suddenly find themselves watching Norman clean up the crime scene. They may even catch themselves hoping he won't be caught.

That was an extraordinary gamble in 1960, when Leigh's star status would ordinarily have guaranteed her survival until the final act. Hitchcock even required theaters to refuse late arrivals, protecting the carefully timed experience. The shower murder is now one of cinema's most recognizable sequences, but familiarity can obscure how radically it disrupted storytelling conventions.

Other movies have killed prominent characters earlier. Some have delivered bloodier surprises. Psycho remains the standard because the revelation changes whom audiences follow and what they want to happen next. Its influence runs directly through Scream and The Place Beyond the Pines, yet the original still feels audacious.

Hitchcock doesn't wait to pull the rug out from under his viewers. He takes away the floor while they're still getting comfortable.
