#3441. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

#3440. Every GTA 6 Actor Rumored and Confirmed by Rockstar Ahead of Launch

Rockstar hasn't confirmed anything, but online detectives are on the case

It's been an excruciatingly long wait, but we're just days away from the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6. Ahead of the game's launch for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, Rockstar Games has yet to reveal any official details about the actors who will appear in GTA 6, including the central couple, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos.

Even so, eagle-eyed fans on social media have been speculating for months about who's playing the lead duo, as well as prominent supporting characters featured in trailers, previews, and promotional materials, including Brian Heder, Cal Hampton, Raul Bautista, and Boobie Ike. While we wait for Rockstar to make it official, we've rounded up all the most credible rumors about the GTA 6 cast below.

Manni L. Perez has been rumored to be playing the female lead in GTA 6 for three years now, since Rockstar shared its first trailer for the game. Over on the game's subreddit, you'll find dozens of posts about her from over the years, often comparing her appearance to that of the in-game character. (There is, indeed, a striking resemblance.) Perez has previously appeared in Law and Order: SVU, Chicago P.D., and Jessica Jones. She also provided the voice for a nightclub patron and a blackjack dealer in GTA Online. Neither Perez nor Rockstar have confirmed her involvement in the project.

The male lead of GTA 6 is widely rumored to be portrayed by actor Dylan Rourke. He has previously appeared in one episode each of Grey’s Anatomy and Modern Family. A number of YouTube videos have compared Jason's dialogue with some of Rourke's previous work. Though the two sound quite similar, neither Rourke nor Rockstar have confirmed his involvement in the project.

Back in September, Emmy-winning actor Stephen Root confirmed longstanding rumors he would be playing Brian in GTA 6 during a red-carpet interview with the Associated Press. "Yeah, you’re going to see me in there,” he said. “I think from the first rollout of GTA that they were doing almost a year ago they had my character in there, and there were too many people that knew me from King of the Hill and my voice. So, I think that secret kind of got divulged then.” Rockstar Games has not yet confirmed that Root will be playing Brian.

For several months, fans have speculated that Saturday Night Live alum Bobby Moynihan will be playing Cal Hampton, a chill friend of Jason Duval who never met a conspiracy theory he didn't like. On social media, fans have highlighted the physical resemblance between the actor and the character, Moynihan's previous experience with motion capture work, and the fact that he recently started following Dylan Rourke as evidence in favor of his casting. Neither Moynihan nor Rockstar have confirmed his involvement in the project.

The GTA fandom is less certain about who is playing Raul Bautista, an older mentor to Jason and Lucia who featured prominently in Netflix's Extended Look back in August. Several netizens honed in on the actor's Dominican accent, leading them to speculate the character was being played by actor Manny Perez, known for his roles in independent films and TV shows like Blue Bloods and

Law and Order: SVU. Other online rumor-mongers claim he will be played by Spanish actor Óscar Jaenada, who shared an Instagram post that appears to show him wearing a T-shirt with a picture of Raul. Rockstar Games has not confirmed whether either actor will appear in GTA 6.

Of all the GTA 6 characters that Rockstar has revealed so far, Boobie Ike is the biggest mystery of the bunch. The game's official site describes him as "one of the few to transform his time in the streets into a legitimate empire spanning real estate, a strip club, and a recording studio — Boobie's all smiles until it's time to talk business."

However, the character has yet to appear in a single trailer. Jason and Lucia were working for Boobie during the drug deal gone wrong at the start of the Netflix Extended Look, but the character didn't appear in that preview, either. That means we still don't know what he sounds like, which has made it difficult for the fandom to reach a consensus on who's playing the character. (That hasn't stopped redditors from making some wild speculation about T-Pain and Kanye West, though.) Some folks on social media think Boobie could be played by actor Johnny Ray Gill due to a cryptic social media post he made hinting at an upcoming project, but there's not much meat on that bone. Rockstar Games has not confirmed who will play Boobie Ike in GTA 6.

In past GTA installments, Rockstar looked to well-known movie and TV actors to fill out the cast. 2002's Grand Theft Auto: Vice City included a number of big names, including Ray Liotta, Tom Sizemore, Dennis Hopper, Danny Trejo, Debbie Harry, and Jenna Jameson. In 2004, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas starred Ice-T, Samuel L. Jackson, James Woods, Charlie Murphy, and David Cross, among many others. A longstanding (but unconfirmed) rumor claims that Liotta might have reprized his role as the Hawaiian shirt-loving protagonist Tommy Vercetti in San Andreas, but he asked for more money than Rockstar was willing to pay.

Instead, the cast of GTA 6 bears a closer resemblance to that of GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2: less widely known, yet very accomplished voice actors who are less likely to demand a massive payout. Still, given the stratospheric levels of hype surrounding Rockstar's latest, we suspect these new cast members are about to become household names.

Grand Theft Auto 6 will be released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X on Nov. 19.

#3438. IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

IndieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Friday, November 13 the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

The event will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well. The ceremony’s host will be announced at a later date. Related Stories Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas? Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

“It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” said Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”

“It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” said James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:

The fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for new talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

An early release for new distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

The most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she said uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

All sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

There is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she says. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

As the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

#3435. Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

From the misty seaports of Massachusetts seaports to the otherworldly town of Twin Peaks and even the distant shores of Troy, Ruth De Jong has spent the past twenty years transporting audiences into the unforgettable worlds created by auteur directors like Paul Thomas Anderson, Terrence Malick, Kenneth Lonergan, David Lynch, Jordan Peele, and Christopher Nolan.

“My goal in my work is to always paint the most authentic pictures,” De Jong shared with IndieWire at the Virginia Film Festival, where the production designer received the festival’s Craft Award. The town of Charlottesville has a special place in De Jong’s heart.

It’s here where legendary production designer Jack Fisk, father of De Jong’s high school friend Schuyler Fisk, suggested she forgo attending the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts for grad school in favor of working on the set of Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2007 Oscar-winning film “There Will Be Blood” instead. Recalling that fateful conversation, De Jong said that Fisk told her he saw the younger version of himself in her, sharing, “I think what the world continually needs are mentors [like Fisk] showing up.” Related Stories IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

De Jong fell in love with filmmaking as she continued to work with Fisk on Anderson’s “The Master,” and a handful of films by Terence Malick, including his Palme d’Or winner “The Tree of Life.” Eventually she spread her wings and took on her first film as production designer: Kenneth Lonergan’s “Manchester by the Sea.” Looking back on these early days and everything she learned on those sets, De Jong said that she believes “a body of work like that is built upon itself. I think I’m constantly pulling from the past, but also pulling from the future.”

Whether designing a fishing village in modern-day Gloucester, recreating the White House Oval Office, or crafting the iconic Trojan horse, all of De Jong’s work comes in service of the characters and story being told. While crafting a film’s world, De Jong asks herself, “How do I make this tangible and alive and real and authentic?”

To capture undertones of the real working-class people in the fishing community at the center of “Manchester by the Sea,” this meant spending time with local fishermen. “We asked if we could go into their houses. We asked if we could use their fishing boats. We asked if we could use their lobster cages and rope everything, and then we would,” De Jong recalled. All of this research helped De Jong nail the subtle nuances and layers of the region. “You’re always striving to not make it cliché,” De Jong told IndieWire.

The first step involves breaking down the script. At this phase of her process, De Jong attaches an image to each scene. “It may be a piece of art. It could be a photograph. It could be a texture. It could be a piece of cloth. It could be anything,” she shared, adding, “Then from that, I add physical locations, and we start putting the whole thing together and seeing our film.”

Sometimes these images come from the director themselves. While working on “Twin Peaks: The Return,” David Lynch gave De Jong some of his own artwork for inspiration. “He would hand me some of his paintings, his drawings, his work, and say, ‘Here, this is this set. Build that,,’” De Jong revealed, adding that even if it was “a flat 2D painting, the colors were wild and it’s textural.” These came in handy for the new worlds of the series, like the landmark Episode 8 (also known as “Gotta Light?”), in which De Jong designed the radio station and other eerier riffs on the atomic age 1950s.

For the more iconic aspects of “Twin Peaks, ” De Jong also dug up the original plans for the Red Room from the 1990s. “David remembered in his mind’s eye,” De Jong said, “and I’m there to continue to be David’s conduit on the new work. It was just a beautiful, beautiful dance.”

Along with reviving iconic sets from pop culture’s past, De Jong herself has created work that has become part of the entertainment firmament. The set she created for the “Jupiter’s Claim” theme park in Jordan Peele’s “Nope” has been added to the Studio Tour at Universal Studios Hollywood, a unique feat for an aspect of filmmaking that is often binned as soon as a production wraps. On the honor of her set being preserved in such a way, De Jong said, “It’s pretty incredible, because in the act of doing it, you aren’t thinking about what this is going to turn into.”

After receiving her first Oscar nomination for her work on Christopher Nolan‘s Best Picture-winning biopic “Oppenheimer,” De Jong re-teamed with the writer-director this year for his ambitious take on Homer’s epic poem “The Odyssey.” For this film, her process began at Nolan’s home, where she spent hours reading the script. Afterwards, De Jong asked for the parameters. “He said, ‘There are none,'” De Jong recalled.

This allowed the designer the freedom to “take the audience on the same journey that Odysseus (Matt Damon) was on,” she said. Starting with seven countries, De Jong and Nolan began searching for the film’s faraway locations, the only edict being that Nolan wanted the film to start in the Mediterranean and end in the Mediterranean. Without the barriers of realism, De Jong found inspiration in locations across the globe. “We didn’t care that we were shooting the Laestrygonians in Scotland. It didn’t matter. It just had the topography we were interested in. Same with Iceland and the same with Morocco,” De Jong said. Once the locations were determined, then came building sets that reflected the characters who inhabit them.

For the ominous stone house owned by Circe (Samantha Morton), who beguiles Odysseus’ men and turns them into pigs, De Jong shared that Nolan “was very clear about not wanting Circe’s home to be a Hansel and Gretel in the woods type cottage. She’s so peculiar and unique and bizarre and a witch.” With this in mind, the duo decided she should live on the edge of a cliff, finding the perfect craggy rocks in Scotland. Soon, a whole backstory informed the building of her dwelling. “She formed her house out of those craggy rocks,” De Jong said, adding, “We just made up all these stories and created the sets from there.”

The same attention to character informed the creation of the iconic Trojan horse, an imposing image of which opens the epic film. Nolan envisioned a rearing horse, telling De Jong that “it has to be iconic and it has to be larger than life.” For Nolan, De Jong said, the question at the center of this opening scene is, “Are the Trojans going to accept the gift?” Thinking about what kind of horse would be accepted, Nolan wanted their horse to be “the antithesis” of the one in Wolfgang Petersen’s 2004 film “Troy.” “We didn’t want the clunky wheels,” she said, adding that “these were master shipbuilders.”

“They’re master craftsmen,” De Jong insists, “If they collected all this wood, why don’t we shiplap the entire body, shiplap the tail? They hand-carved the legs and the head. That leaves the body all hollow like a ship, so all the men could all go inside and cut a trap door.” Once they agreed on the backstory for the building of the horse, the next step was figuring out how to make multiples out of fiberglass (and later out of plastic as one of the summer’s hottest collectible popcorn buckets).

As “The Odyssey” marches its way into awards season, De Jong is looking towards her future – and her next gig. With every project she takes, De Jong is looking to push herself as an artist. “It’s that space of being uncomfortable that is how you know you’re in the right place,” she said, adding, “The minute I find comfort, I realize I’m in the wrong place. So I’m always pushing to get back into that area of discomfort.”

Thinking back to her conversation with Fisk all those years ago, De Jong feels that what he taught her was “The act of physically doing and going and staying in momentum,” adding, “That’s something that Christopher Nolan has. All of these directors; They don’t stop producing work. They don’t do it in vain. They do it because that’s their language and their medium. They’re all artists at heart.”

Although De Jong looks back at her past fondly, she doesn’t regret forgoing art school to join the movie business. What she learned after all these years is that, “You need to go forward, and even if you go forward and you hit a wall, then just keep pivoting a little bit. Stay open and don’t be fearful. You can’t fear. I’d rather screw up royally and have tried than not tried at all.”

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H—and with Black Friday approaching, this 2026 model is already seeing a $500 discount, bringing its price down to $1,497.99 from $1,997.99. That's its lowest price to date.

Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ.

The system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That said, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

#3433. I hate how most smartwatches look, but I'll happily wear the Withings ScanWatch Light every day and with any outfit

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’re after a beautiful smartwatch with all the basic fitness and health features you need, and which won’t ruin your outfit, look no further than the Withings ScanWatch Light 2. This elegant watch is pricey given its basic functionality, but still offers strong battery life and lots of insight via the companion app. If it’s bang for your buck you’re after, rivals offer more, but none can match the ScanWatch Light’s sheer pizzazz.

Auto activity detection didn’t work for me

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

I hate most fitness trackers. Although I love what they do, I really don’t love how they look. For ages now, I’ve been pining for a smartwatch that does all the stuff I need it to when I’m at the gym or on a walk, yet looks like a normal, classic watch. I know, I know, you can set analog watch faces on many smartwatches, but we all know that’s not the same.

Enter the Withings ScanWatch Light. This thing is beautiful. It looks like a classic watch and fits in with even my smartest outfits. And it does all the basic fitness-y things I need it to, although not much more — the “Light” part really does mean light. This is not a feature-packed smartwatch, and certainly isn’t designed for athletes. Instead, it’s a smartwatch for people who want core health features without sacrificing style or ruining the cohesiveness of their outfits.

Find out whether this is the best fitness tracker for you in my full Withings ScanWatch Light review.

White/gray; rose gold/white; black/silver

The Withings ScanWatch Light costs $249 / £229 at Amazon. If you buy direct from Withings, you can choose a metal or leather strap for an extra $49, or a fabric strap for $39.

It certainly isn’t cheap, but look: Withings gear is always pricey. I don’t mind something being expensive if it can back up the price tag somehow. And most Withings products do so by combining charming design, solid build quality, and decent core functionality.

On the first two counts, the ScanWatch Light ticks the boxes. However, this is a stripped-back watch, so price versus functionality is pretty poor. You’re going to get more features for the money with the $249 Apple Watch SE 3. Or the $169 Amazfit Active Premium 3. Or heck, even the $79 Amazfit Bip 6. None match the ScanWatch Light’s elegant looks, though, so my question is: how much is style worth to you?

If you have the extra cash and want similar styling but more features, check out the ScanWatch Light’s bigger siblings: the $369 Withings ScanWatch 2 or $599 ScanWatch Nova.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In my opinion, the best thing about the ScanWatch Light is its design. I really appreciate the huge array of fitness features of smartwatches like my Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro. But I much prefer wearing a traditional analog watch when I’m not working out — giant AMOLED slabs and ugly silicone straps don’t really go well with my daily outfits. So, up to now I’ve switched between my analog watch and smartwatch when going to/from the gym, which has been a pain.

The ScanWatch Light is the perfect solution. It looks just like a classic analog watch: simple, elegant, beautiful. The face measures 1.4 inches, which fits my wrist nicely without feeling too bulky.

The watch comes in three different colorways (white/gray, rose gold/white, and black/silver). I chose the black model and love its effortless style and sophistication. It pairs well with all my outfits, from casual daily and smart casual fits up to suits and even my black tux. And the silver bezel and accents pair nicely with the silver and white gold rings I wear on my left hand. Obviously, though, the ScanWatch Light is also a fitness tracker! Which means I have a single watch for both gym, work, and leisure. I never have to switch again.

The standard strap is fluoroelastomer (a type of rubber), so it doesn’t absorb sweat or go gross when working out, and doesn’t chafe either. That said, while I usually dislike the look of rubber/silicone, the ScanWatch Light’s strap is finished with a matte effect, meaning it doesn’t look tacky like my (much cheaper) Amazfit Active. Again, you’re getting the best of both worlds.

I found the strap either a little snug or slightly too loose. In other words, I’m between sizes. This depends entirely on the individual anatomy/width of your wrist, though, so I’m not moaning. And besides, it still wasn’t uncomfortable at all, either when exercising or wearing all day — helped by the ScanWatch Light’s low 0.9-ounce kerb weight.

The buckle is dual-sided, meaning it also serves as a fixed loop to hold the strap tail in place, and there’s a sliding free loop for a second securement point. It’s a solid system and keeps the strap tail from flapping around. It can be a bit fiddly getting the strap through the second buckle opening, though.

As I’d expect from a Withings product, the ScanWatch Light is built extremely well and feels premium. The case is made from stainless steel and the face is covered by Gorilla Glass (the kind used on smartphone screens) so should stand up to daily wear and tear without scratching. It’s waterproof down to 5ATM (five atmospheres) of pressure, so you can take it swimming.

The digital grayscale OLED display is very small, but deliberately so — this is designed to be as minimalist a smartwatch as possible. When you press the digital crown, the watch hands move out of the way of the screen automatically if they need to, which I love. When it’s not in use, the display stays off and thereby blends in nicely with the black watchface, thus not spoiling the analog aesthetic. On the lighter models, though, the black display is always visible.

You control the watch entirely via the steel digital crown. Navigating the menu is fairly clunky, especially when you want to go back through menus. However, the menu system and features aren’t complex to begin with, so it’s fine. You don’t need to use the crown to set the time or date, as it’s all done digitally by pairing the watch to your phone and the Withings app.

As I mentioned up top, this watch bears the “Light” moniker for a reason. If you’re after highly detailed tracking and plenty of on-wrist control/info, the ScanWatch Light isn’t for you.

Don’t get me wrong, there’s a decent array of activities on offer. All the basics are there, of course: running, cycling, rowing, etc. There are indoor versions for treadmills and exercise bikes, as well as some specific activities like badminton, muay thai and more. There’s even a dog walking activity — I’m not sure how much that differs from ordinary walking.

None of the activity modes I used were particularly in-depth, though. Weight lifting, for example, had no interval functionality. They all seem to just measure BPM as you work out. Still, that’s all I really need. (And to be honest, I find the interval weight lifting function on my Amazfit watches a bit fiddly anyway.) You have no real control over the activities on-watch either — you simply use the digital crown to pause and then either resume or stop activities. Nor do you get any detailed info on the watch itself as to your performance or progress.

If you’re a serious fitness enthusiast and want something for hardcore training, you’ll want more in-depth measurements and onboard controls. Check out the Apple Watch Series 12, Withings ScanWatch 2 or Amazfit Active Premium 3. Or the Apple Watch Ultra 3 if budget is no constraint.

What the ScanWatch Light measured was pretty accurate. I compared the BPM analysis and calorific burn to several different machines at my gym and got essentially the same results each time, usually within just a couple of BPM and a couple of dozen calories. The ScanWatch did tell me I had mild bradycardia at first, measuring 52BPM resting. Look, I’m not in terrible shape, but that’s athlete levels, and I was highly stressed at the time due to a bereavement. So go figure. Since then, though, BPM reads have stayed more realistic and consistent. There’s also a VO2 max assessment available via the app — arguably the most important metric to track, generally speaking.

Unfortunately, the ScanWatch Light’s automatic activity detection simply doesn’t work on my test sample. Anything I did at the gym just went completely undetected. I cycled hard for 8 minutes. I ran for 10 minutes. Nothing, until I started the activities manually. I thought it might use GPS movement to detect activities, but when I walked or jogged outside, nothing happened. Weirder yet, on two occasions I've woken up in the night to find the watch has started detecting a run while on my bedside table.

I’ve reached out to Withings to find out why this may be and whether it’s an isolated incident on my test sample. This isn’t a gamechanger for me — I often find automatic detection results in false starts on my Amazfit Active and T-Rex 3 Pro, so I typically disable it anyway. But if a product has a feature, I still expect it to work.

The ScanWatch Light doesn’t have built-in GPS, instead relying on your phone for location services. This means you’ll need to keep your phone on you when you exercise if you want to view routes.

Health tracking-wise, it’s a similar story. The ScanWatch Light doesn’t track much. It’ll measure your BPM as I mentioned above, but there’s no ECG, blood oxygen, or body temperature tracking — you’ll have to upgrade to the pricier ScanWatch 2 or ScanWatch Nova for those.

Aside from BPM, the ScanWatch Light can track your sleep quality and give you an assessment of your breathing quality during sleep — both found on the pricier ScanWatch 2. There’s also menstrual cycle tracking. It’s more of an app feature, but you can add cycle tracking to the watch menu to input your stages. As a dude, I obviously didn’t use this, but it’s still a fundamental feature I expect to see in a fitness tracker.

There’s also a relaxation mode, which is pretty cool. You set a time interval, then how many breaths per minute you want to take. The watch then vibrates to prompt your breaths in and out. It’s a cool little feature for quickly taking a wellbeing break. And there are standing prompts when the watch detects you’ve not stood for a while — all pretty par for the course.

The Withings app is usually one of our favorites. It allows you to customize the ScanWatch Light’s menus and offers lots of information and data based on your measurements, inputs and watch readings. You can track your activities, progress and health data, with lots of graphs for visualization. The app provides a strong basic level of insight for all of this, explaining what terms mean and often linking out to informative articles for detailed explanation. As you can see in the screenshot below, I've tapped through from my BPM graph, to a basic explanation and second chart, and again through to a full detailed heart rate explainer article.

Via the Withings app, all your health data can be synced from centralized apps, like Apple Health, Google Health, or Samsung Health. Withings also partners with major tracking apps like Strava and MyFitnessPal, although if you’re using an iPhone like me, all this is routed through Apple Health to begin with anyway, so I didn’t need to set up any specific connections.

After one week with constant use and workouts 4-5 times per week, I still had 33% of battery left. So you can reasonably expect around 10 days with normal usage. A full charge takes around 2 hours on average, and charging via a 15W charger from 30% took me around an hour and 15 minutes, which tracks with Withings’ claims.

I’m not a fan of the ScanWatch Light’s charging dock. It’s just an awkwardly long piece of thin, bent plastic with an ostensibly meaningless lip on one side. It doesn’t sit particularly well on my bedside table, looks ugly, and struggles to stay in position. Great.

I much prefer the small, unobtrusive dock of my T-Rex 3 Pro, and Apple’s sleek little magnetic dock. But in fairness to Withings, I resent using all docks equally as much — they’re just a sad reality given that sticking a USB-C port on a watch would seriously compromise pressure- and waterproofing.

Look, the Withings ScanWatch Light is overpriced and under-featured for the money. I can admit that. It’s not for athletes or serious fitness enthusiasts. But it isn’t meant for those people. It’s for people like me who want a stylish all-round watch that can track all the basics for general day-to-day fitness and wellbeing without getting too serious. And importantly, for people who don’t want an ugly square hunk of AMOLED display on their wrist, clashing with their outfit.

It’s also built beautifully, has solid battery life and offers lots of visualizations and information via the Withings app. And did I mention it looks fantastic? I know the ScanWatch Light isn’t perfect, but damn, do I love it.

#3432. Diablo: Legacy Of Terror Officially Announced

The Diablo franchise has been around for a long time and continues to grow and evolve to give its players a fresh experience in the classic dungeon-crawling genre. Despite Diablo 4 being out and the announcement of Diablo 5 in development, the 2000 game Diablo 2 received the remaster treatment with Diablo 2: Resurrected​​​​​​ in 2021, and its players are now getting even more as part of Diablo's 30th anniversary celebration.

Starting on November 13, 2026, and running for only six days, Diablo 2: Resurrected will host the Legacy of Terror event to celebrate the 30th anniversary of the series. This comes only months after the popular Warlock class was added to the game, as well as several quality-of-life updates that prove that this game is alive and well. In fact, it has a player base that could easily rival that of the more recent Diablo 4 title, particularly as Diablo 2 has often been heralded as the best entry in the series.

Diablo 2: Resurrected - Legacy of Terror event launches Season 16 of the competitive, seasonal Ladder system experience. However, this special anniversary event is available for both Ladder and Non-Ladder players.

The event brings numerous perks for players and unique gameplay experiences. A quick breakdown of the information you need to know about the Legacy of Terror event is as follows:

On the Hell difficulty, players will have the chance to face off against the Diablo Clone once every six hours. This Uber Diablo is a more challenging variant of Diablo from Diablo 2.

After players defeat Baal in Normal, Nightmare, or Hell difficulty, that difficulty will then feature simultaneous Terrorized Zones in every zone. Terrorized Zones are an endgame feature where random areas will become high-level hunting grounds, offering better loot and a chaotic experience.

The Terrorized Zones can be disabled in the Game Creation menu if you choose, and turning it off will not affect any other features of the Legacy of Terror ​​​​​​event.

The Cow Level has always been one of the most ridiculous and popular features of Diablo 2, and Blizzard is leaning into the experience for this anniversary celebration. During the Legacy of Terror week, players can enter the Cow Portal in the Rogue Encampment any time they want after defeating Baal once on a difficulty level.

The Cow Portal will then remain active at all times during the event. Additionally, after slaying monsters, you have a rare chance to reanimate them as Hell Bovine Minions.

As if all that wasn't enough, during the Diablo 2: Resurrected - Legacy of Terror event, players can also enjoy 100% Magic Find and a 15% discount on all vendors, including Gamblers, on every difficulty level.

Although it would be nice to get even more classes since the addition of the Warlock earlier this year, for now, having this special event to enjoy is exciting and sure to bring many players back into the game.

On a side note, someone at Blizzard is clearly a Dungeon Crawler Carl fan, as the official statement regarding the Diablo 2: Resurrected Legacy of Terror event ends with the line, "Now get out there and slay, slay, slay!" which I, for one, absolutely love.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3431. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3430. After ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

With Cannes entry “Bitter Christmas,” Oscar-winning Spanish auteur Pedro Almodóvar (“Talk to Her”) is back. My bet: he will not shoot another film in English and will stick to making movies in his native language. Since his debut “Pepi, Luci, Bom and Other Girls Like Mom” in 1980, Almodóvar has written singularly identifiable, heightened, rhythmic, and mellifluous Spanish dialogue.

While Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore adeptly wrangled his translated English in Golden Lion-winner “The Room Next Door,” which deployed his bright Almodóvar colors and exacting mise-en-scène, the director did not enjoy dealing with the unions in New York. “In Spain everything is much more immediate, and also it is my language, it’s my culture,” he told me during the New York Film Festival. While he doesn’t rule out making another English-language movie, it would have to be small-scale. “I don’t find myself, anymore, capable of dealing with a production that is chaotic with a lot of people and a lot of characters.” Related Stories Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

Now he’s back to his self-referential, meta autofiction mode in full force. The results are exhilarating. “Bitter Christmas” offers a movie within a movie, as writer-director Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia) crafts a script that lifts some key story points from his friends’ experiences. Even though Almodóvar considers the movie one of his riskiest, it’s the filmmaker’s biggest hit in Spain since “Volver.”

Almodóvar considers “Bitter Christmas” to be “twins” with Oscar-nominated “Pain and Glory,” which starred his old favorite Antonio Banderas as his alter ego. “‘Pain and Glory’ is more about the physical pain, right?,” he said. “The character [Raul] has had a lot of surgeries, and his fear is about that the fact that he’s not going to be physically able to to handle another another film shoot. Whereas in this film I deal with a different pain, which is the pain of writer’s block, of the blank page, or writing something that doesn’t quite come together for you. The character of Aitana in the film says to Raul, ‘you know we are all losers, you have lost grace.’ And by grace it means inspiration, something that is equally painful to that writer-director as the physical pain was to the writer director in ‘Pain and Glory.'”

Mostly when Almodóvar sits down to write, he’s making things up. He’s gotten into trouble in the past for raiding his friends’ stories. “There is not any law that creates the limits of the autofiction,” he said. “There is no law that’s going to define the limits of what you can appropriate and what you can’t appropriate. But if I’m inspired by the life of someone who’s close to me, who’s going through a difficult time, as a writer, you are selfish, because what propels you is the idea, even if it means going against the relationship. I don’t feel comfortable the two or three times that I did it. This is the limit: not to hurt anyone. But it’s normal that writers are influenced by everything in life you see, you talk to with others, you read, you see movies. So it’s impossible to renounce the influence of the life of others.”

And he’s passionate about making movies. As Raúl says in the film, “This is all there is to my life.” But Almodóvar has never suffered writer’s block. “I inspire myself because this is the profession that I know better than anyone, than any other,” he said. “The only thing that separates me from this alter ego is that I never lived a creative crisis. The experience I have had is more scripts that have taken me a long time to find the solution and to get them to gel together. But I’ve always succeeded ultimately.”

And he only recently discovered panic attacks, which took him by surprise. “I hadn’t previously experienced panic attacks, but now I have,” he said. “At that moment I was unconscious, and it was something awful, awful.”

Needless to say Almodóvar spends most of his days sitting at his desk at the computer. (Hence his legendary bad back.) Mostly he enjoys writing but also feels the clock ticking. “You always feel like time is lacking, right?” he said. “Especially that moment when you get that idea that’s going to become the motor of your story, you feel like there’s no time to breathe, because you want to get it all down as fast as possible. They’re quite intense days as we’re trying to get this. And then once I’ve started the story, my process is to get up in the morning and start writing. Those are some of the most pleasurable days in my life because you know where you’re going. But also, I have to pay attention to everything, because in that moment that you are possessed by the idea, you experience everything in your life filtered through the sensibility of the story that you’re writing.”

Listening to music feeds his creative beast. While he was writing “Talk to Her,” he listened to Caetano Veloso’s “A Kukuku Paloma,” a song that he had heard thousands of times, “but then it was like an epiphany. I discovered the song, and you feel it in a different way.” And in “Bitter Christmas,” his two actresses in the movie-within-the-movie listen to “Weeping Woman” from the filmmaker’s longtime muse, Mexican chanteuse Chavela Vargas.

Finally, the filmmaker had fun making himself the bad guy. “This was a new structure for me,” he said. “What I liked about it was that I could talk about myself as a writer-director, but mostly I also enjoyed the part of becoming the villain in a sense of that story. But the spectator does have to pay a lot of attention because if they go to the bathroom for two minutes, they’re going to miss something and be lost.”

In one scene, the filmmaker offers a close-up of the cursor on the computer screen. “Even though the cursor itself is not a very cinematic thing to see,” he said, “it’s his call to creativity, right? It’s the thing that calls him and pulls him in to have to tell his story. So it’s autofiction.”

Going forward, Almodóvar has no plans to put himself at the center of another film. “I promise not to talk about me anymore,” he said. “I was interested since the beginning of my career about the origin of creation and the relation with reality. Inspiration and life together, like the two sides of a coin. This mysterious question that so fascinates me is about not just where does creativity come from, how does it come, when does it come, how does it manifest? I have reached the end of my exploration around this.”

Up next: He’s writing, he said. “This is almost the opposite of this one. The new one will be very different.”

A Sony Pictures Classic release, “Bitter Christmas” is now playing in theaters in New York and Los Angeles. It expands nationally on November 25.

#3428. The ‘Godzilla’ Movie That Divided Fans Is Officially Getting a New Streaming Release

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

By the time Madison Square Garden becomes the most dangerous building in New York in Roland Emmerich’s Godzilla, the military has spent much of the movie trying to find one enormous animal. Then the eggs hatch, and Matthew Broderick has to get out of an arena full of mini-Godzillas. If this was your first Godzilla movie, there’s a decent chance you remember the scramble to get out of the Garden better than you remember what the big guy himself looked like.

Twenty-eight years later, Takashi Yamazaki’s Godzilla Minus Zero is heading into its second North American weekend after opening to an estimated $31.6 million. The sequel picks up two years after Godzilla Minus One, with Japan still rebuilding from the last attack. Yamazaki is asking what it takes for a country to get back on its feet after Godzilla comes through, while Emmerich had a more immediate question for New York: how do you get everybody out before the rest of the eggs hatch?

Godzilla (1998) is now streaming free with ads in the U.S. on Pluto TV. Fandango at Home also added it to its free lineup on November 1, timed to Minus Zero’s theatrical release. Broderick plays Niko Tatopoulos, the scientist who figures out what brought the creature to Manhattan, while Jean Reno, Maria Pitillo, and Hank Azaria round out the cast.

Emmerich makes Godzilla fast enough to lose in traffic and gives his human characters a problem that gets worse the longer they spend chasing him. Niko realizes the creature came to New York to reproduce, which means the military has been looking for one animal while an entire nest is about to hatch. It’s a fun setup for a creature feature, and the design sells it. The long snout and hunched posture make him look like he could outrun a cab, so it’s at least fun to watch right up until you realize you’re watching Godzilla run from the army, when a lot of fans showed up to watch the army run from him.

Of course, plenty of people met Godzilla in the middle of that chase. The movie made $376 million worldwide, and for some viewers it was their first Godzilla movie. That’s part of what makes it fun to revisit alongside Minus Zero. If you came in expecting a monster who could walk through everything an army threw at him, watching him duck around a corner was a hard sell. If you were eight years old hoping nobody would open the wrong door at Madison Square Garden, you’ve probably been defending this movie ever since.

Godzilla is available to stream now on Pluto TV, while Godzilla Minus Zero is still in its theatrical run.

#3427. After 30 Years, Luffy’s Faith In The Straw Hat Pirates Breaks With One Big Twist

WARNING: SPOILERS FOR ONE PIECE CHAPTER #1198The Straw Hat crew’s continuous faith that they put in each other is one of their most admirable traits, but One Piece's Elbaph arc features a betrayal of that trust between Luffy and his crew. The World Government's covert mission to kidnap Giant children from their homeland has evolved into a battle so large and grand that Usopp seems convinced he's witnessing the end of the world. While he’s normally exaggerating, several new transformations of prominent characters might be capable of such chaos.

Almost as soon as it looked like the Straw Hats and the Giants had successfully defeated the Holy Knights threatening Elbaph, the tables suddenly turned. The World Government's secret ruler, Saint Nerona Imu, descended on the island in an attempt to regain control of the island, enslave its inhabitants, and steal hidden ancient technology. But he never expected Luffy and Loki to push him to exert so much effort in a battle that has also forced the Straw Hat captain to evolve his Devil Fruit to a level that threatens to change him and his relationship with his crew.

As the battle against Imu raged, Sanji and Zoro were increasing their powers to a level closer to Luffy's in their fights against the enhanced and nearly immortal Holy Knights. The crew and all of Elbaph were counting on the two to take care of Imu's subordinates in charge of securing the children and a means of escape. But after the two Straw Hats finally learned how to control their Conqueror's Haki, they were able to overwhelm their foes, sabotaging Imu's plans.

Both Zoro and Sanji were trusted to complete their objectives, and just as they seemed to have things under control, Luffy in his new beast form suddenly arrived and made short work of the Rain God construct that had been summoned by one of the Holy Knights. However, there were several signs in chapter #1198 that this version of Luffy is not the same person who's led the Straw Hat crew all this way, but a much more chaotic figure that's willing to betray the Straw Hats.

Luffy's crew has gone through several changes throughout One Piece, but it's original Monster Trio has regained their standing in a big way.

Throughout One Piece's many arcs, Luffy has consistently counted on his crew mates to accomplish important tasks while he focused on confronting the enemy leader. With Saint Nerona Imu wreaking havoc in his colossal, god-like form, there couldn't be a worse time for Luffy to ditch the fight to go interrupt the situation that Zoro and Sanji had under control. And that interruption is a betrayal of the faith Luffy normally places in his cherished crew.

It's been previously established in One Piece lore that when a Zoan-type Devil Fruit user fully awakens their abilities, they run the risk of the fruit's animalistic spirit overtaking the user's mind. In the worst cases, awakened Zoan users permanently become extremely powerful humanoid animals devoid of logical thought and the user's original personality. With Luffy being the user of the Mythical Zoan Human-Human Fruit, Model: Nika, chapter #1198 finally explored what it looks like when Luffy's fruit fully awakens. But after seemingly losing control, there is no telling what he might do next.

One Piece has revealed a myriad of Devil Fruits thus far, but these 30 are stronger than the rest by a pretty wide margin.

Luffy has consistently been a character who has extremely high levels of emotional intelligence and acts on instinct rather than thinking of a complex plan. Because of this, author Eiichiro Oda rarely gives the character internal dialogue represented with thought bubbles. After Luffy's awakened into his full Nika form, he's shown using thought bubbles that are completely blank and speech bubbles that have reduced his vocabulary to "oookee ookee" monkey sounds. And now, Luffy more closely resembles a tumultuous monkey god who laughs at the laws of logic and physics than the captain of the Straw Hat crew.

The following chapters will undoubtedly see whether Luffy’s new form will fulfill the prophecy that described Nika as both a liberator and a God of Destruction, and if he will be a danger to Elbaph and the Straw Hats. Keeping those facts in mind while also taking into account his interruption of Zoro and Sanji's current situation, it's clear that One Piece's main character is now more monkey than man, and I have a feeling that will lead to some unwanted consequences.

#3424. Apple Intelligence completes regulatory registration for iPad and Mac in China

Apple has completed an important regulatory step ahead of Apple Intelligence’s expected launch in China this December. Here are the details.

In late October, Apple published a press release on its Chinese Newsroom website confirming its intention to launch Apple Intelligence in China this December, as part of iOS 27.3.

Apple went on to release the first iOS 27.3 developer beta a few days later, allowing users in China to test Apple Intelligence ahead of its public launch.

In its press release, however, Apple also noted that the initial rollout would be limited to iPhones, as support for other platforms was still pending regulatory approval.

Now, as spotted by Reuters, Apple Intelligence “has been ‌registered for use on tablets and laptops in China, Shanghai’s cyberspace regulator said on Monday.”

For context, generative AI services must complete a regulatory registration process before they can launch publicly in China.

Apple Intelligence, which, in China, relies on Alibaba’s Qwen model to power certain AI features, had already received regulatory approval for iPhones in July, following months of delays and negotiations with Chinese authorities.

With today’s registration, Apple has cleared another regulatory hurdle ahead of Apple Intelligence’s launch in China. However, the company has yet to confirm whether iPad and Mac support will also arrive in December.

#3423. Ridley Scott’s 153-Minute Historical Thriller Officially Removed From Streaming

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

Ridley Scott is coming off a major setback in the form of The Dog Stars, his first sci-fi movie in nearly a decade. The film underperformed at the box office, grossing around $40 million worldwide against a reported budget of around $100 million. As big a flop as it was, The Dog Stars isn't the biggest bomb that Scott has directed this decade. That unenviable honor goes to a period epic released five years ago with a budget similar to several of the filmmaker's recent movies. The period epic is currently streaming for free in the United States, but not for much longer.

Not only was it marketed as Scott's return to Gladiator-style filmmaking, but it also marked an on-screen reunion of Ben Affleck and Matt Damon. More interestingly, the two also worked on the script, making this their first new project as writers since 1997's Good Will Hunting, for which they won an Oscar. This time around, they collaborated on the script with filmmaker Nicole Holofcener and crafted a movie that owes its structure to the Akira Kurosawa classic Rashomon.

The movie features Damon as one of the three leads, along with Jodie Comer and Adam Driver. Affleck, on the other hand, plays a villainous supporting role. The movie is based on the true story of the last recorded duel in history, which was fought over a woman's honor. The film presents the same incident from three different perspectives, asking the audience to arrive at their own judgments.

Four houses, four completely different theories about how you survive a world like this one. Here is where your banner belongs, what the name would cost you, and what it would buy.

You belong in the North, where the weather does most of the arguing and nobody is impressed by a title. The Starks are the only great house on this list who genuinely believe that being right matters more than winning, which is exactly why the show spent eight years punishing them for it.

You belong to the house that worked out early on that gold moves faster than armies. Casterly Rock runs on leverage, reputation and the certainty that everybody at the table owes you something, and you are perfectly comfortable with all three.

You belong to the house that conquered a continent and never quite got over it. Targaryens do not ask for a seat at the table, because in their version of events the table was theirs to begin with, and that certainty is either magnificent or catastrophic depending on the week.

You belong to Highgarden, where nobody raises their voice and everybody gets exactly what they came for. The Tyrells feed the realm, charm the realm and quietly steer the realm, and they have never once needed to win a battle to get their way.

We're talking, of course, about The Last Duel. Produced on a reported budget of $100 million, the film grossed $30 million at the worldwide box office. Ironically, it happens to be the best-reviewed film that Scott has made since The Martian. The movie holds a "Certified Fresh" 85% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, where the consensus reads, "The Last Duel's critique of systemic misogyny isn't as effective as it might have been, but it remains a well-acted and thought-provoking drama infused with epic grandeur."

The Last Duel will remain available on Tubi until December 1. Meanwhile, Damon and Affleck recently collaborated as producers on the political thriller Animals, which Affleck also directed and starred in. Like The Last Duel, the movie effectively serves as a reimagining of a Kurosawa classic. In this case, Affleck adapted the Japanese filmmaker's High and Low, which was remade by Spike Lee only last year. You can watch both The Last Duel and Animals at home, and stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3422. Chicago P.D. Begins A New Era With Halstead & Erin’s Modern Replacement

Laura Hurley has been writing about the entertainment industry for more than twelve years, after a decade as a content producer and editor at CinemaBlend after writing for WhatCulture and Examiner. Attending events like SCAD TVfest and San Diego Comic-Con over the course of her career, she has been immersed in the world of network, streaming, and cable TV.

Warning: this article contains spoilers for Chicago P.D. season 14, episode 6, "The Thin Grey Line."Chicago P.D. shifted focus from one of One Chicago's most well-established relationships to what seems to be the beginning of a new one in the latest episode of season 14. After the previous installment delved into Burgess and Ruzek's family unit, which evolved slowly but surely over nearly a decade and a half, "The Thin Grey Line" showcased the cop drama's two newest series regulars. The relationship already has shades of Halstead and Erin from the early seasons of P.D., but it's missing some of what made that romance work.

By this point, Chicago P.D. is all but infamous for how members of the Intelligence Unit regularly date each other. The workplace romance complications that cause problems for Severide and Kidd on Chicago Fire generally don't apply to the cops working under Voight in the CPD. That started with Erin and Halstead early on, as well as Burgess and Ruzek; now, the latest incarnation appears to be Torres and Imani.

The two formed a bond early on as the two newest and youngest regulars, and "The Thin Grey Line" dropped some obvious hints that more than friendship is brewing. While romances in this installment of Dick Wolf's TV universe generally add serialization to a format that could otherwise be painfully procedural, a modern version of Linstead may not be what Chicago P.D. needs just yet, especially not out of Torres and Imani.

In early seasons of Chicago P.D., Halstead/Erin and Burgess/Ruzek were the only two main romances within the Intelligence Unit, so a little flirtation between colleagues was still novel. By the sixth episode of season 14, however, there have been so many relationships within Voight's team that there weren't many degrees of separation between them all by the time Upton left. Even Atwater finally got a CPD romance before the end of his time. At this point, sparks flying between Torres and Imani feel like just another Chicago P.D. partnership turning romantic. Something has to change.

Admittedly, "The Thin Grey Line" didn't explicitly give them romantic moments, but there's a reason why the episode focused on reaction shots from Burgess and Ruzek whenever Torres and Imani shared a moment together. If Chicago P.D. wasn't building their partnership into something more, their closeness wouldn't seem any more romantic than One Chicago's best platonic pairing was over the years. The obvious reaction shots, combined with a heart-to-heart before the final credits rolled, set the stage for more.

Chicago P.D. season 14's premiere saw a tough case with Intelligence under siege, and the beginning of the end for one of the unit's best officers.

The problem with Torres and Imani, compared to earlier Chicago P.D. romances, is that the show hasn't invested enough time in their relationship yet for fans tobecome invested as well. Even though both Arienne Mandi and Benjamin Levy Aguilar are series regulars, Imani and Torres usually get the kind of screen time expected of the most junior members of the team. Even the episodes that focus on each of them in particular usually focus on something other than their partnership.

Romances don't necessarily have to heat up as quickly as Halstead and Erin did, or burn as slowly as Halstead and Upton did, but they need more time to feel like they could rank among One Chicago's best relationships.

Even though Erin and Halstead's relationship only evolved (and devolved) over the first four seasons of Chicago P.D., it remains one of the most important romances from One Chicago's first several years. Some of the appeal comes down to Sophia Bush and Jesse Lee Soffer's early chemistry rather than the writing in every episode, but P.D. deserves credit for giving the pairing regular screen time. The highs were exciting, the lows could be devastating, and the show kept their storylines interesting by investing in them.

Linstead was so key to Chicago P.D. that Halstead unraveled for a hefty chunk of his first season without her and didn't bond with Upton as his new partner right away. Their relationship wasn't always healthy, but Chicago P.D. always made it important. The drama didn't hesitate to fan the flames between Erin and Halstead, and it didn't hurt that Bush and Soffer were arguably the lead actors in the Intelligence Unit, behind Jason Beghe as Voight.

In fact, Halstead's two main romances worked well in different ways. With Erin and Halstead, Chicago P.D. wasted no time elevating their relationship into one of the show's most important elements. With Upton and Halstead, Chicago P.D. burned long and slow, to the point that One Chicago's 2026 crossover event was basically a three-hour Upstead reunion special.

Chicago P.D. hasn't made either Torres or Imani important enough for a potential romance to become one of One Chicago's best, although both characters have parallels to Erin and Halstead. Imani's closeness with Voight isn't unlike Erin's, except for Imani and Voight having considerably less history. For Torres, Halstead was actually his first mentor when he joined the Intelligence Unit.

None of this means the procedural is doomed to fall short on an Imani/Torres romance if the drama delivers on the seeds that "The Thin Grey Line" clearly planted. Still, they need more time to feel like more than just another instance of Chicago P.D. hooking up two single members of the Intelligence Unit.
