#3421. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3419. Keychron just ended the magnetic vs. mechanical keyboard debate: the V6 Ultra Hybrid proves you can have both with literally no compromises and even a magnetic tactile switch

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Someone had to do dual MX/HE compatibility properly, and Keychron stepped up to the mark. The Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE offers dual magnetic and mechanical switch compatibility, plus the widest array of magnetic hot-swappability I’ve yet seen. It’s formidable for gaming, beautiful for typing, built well and reasonably priced. It’s a little bland-looking, but that’s a minor point, and we had a small QC issue, although I’d expect that to be fixed in full production units.

Minor QC issues (hopefully fixed by full production)

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE (catchy name, right?) attempts to forge ‘The One Ring’ of keyboards. One keyboard to rule them all, to do and be everything for everyone. The master keyboard.

As such, it’s the latest in a very small selection of keyboards that offer dual mechanical and magnetic capability. If you want to hot-swap from magnetic back to mechanical switches, you can. But the V6 takes things further with, as I alluded to above, an altogether more holistic approach. The V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE also packs everything else Keychron has to throw at a keyboard — which essentially means every feature that actually exists right now.

8K polling, tons of magnetic features and customization in the Launcher app, gasket mounting for comfortable typing — all with a reasonable price tag. It also offers my holy grail feature at checkout: a magnetic and tactile switch, for elite gaming and typing without even needing to hot-swap in the first place.

So, like, is this legitimately the perfect hybrid board? The best gaming keyboard and the best mechanical keyboard all rolled into one? I think so. Keychron has done it. Find out more in my full Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE review.

Where to even start? Proper MX/HE hot swap, bags of gaming and productivity performance, reasonable price — this is a Goldilocks keyboard.

The V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE’s main feature is denoted by the “Hybrid” part of its (terribly convoluted) name. This board is dual mechanical/magnetic switch compatible, meaning you can swap between the two.

The V6 Ultra Hybrid takes any standard 3-pin or 5-pin mechanical switches. It also supports a wide range of magnetic switches with the N Pole facing downwards — that means Gateron x Wooting Jade switches, Gateron KS-20 switches, and any of Gateron’s ever-growing line of dual rail magnetic switches. Neat.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Now Keychron isn’t the first to do dual MX/HE. Glorious did it a while back with the hilariously overpriced GMMK 3 HE. More recently, Lofree had a pop with the Hyzen, but with typically Lofree results: great looks and typing but rank amateurism in the software department (pivotal to a magnetic board). Keychron, in usual Keychron fashion, is the first to do a proper job of it, with the widest magnetic hot-swap scope while still keeping things affordable.

The long and short is that the V6 Ultra Hybrid has more actual hot-swap potential than any other magnetic board that I know of. Most magnetic boards claim to be hot swappable, but only support a couple of switch variants from the same specific magnetic switch line — often the variants available at checkout. In reality, that usually makes hot-swap claims severely hamstrung at best; meaningless at worst. Not so here. Again, the Lofree Hyzen also supports an impressive roster of compatible magnetic switches, but lacks the professional polish of Keychron’s boards.

The “hybrid” moniker also has another related meaning. The V6 Ultra Hybrid is a hybrid board for both work and play, offering powerful gaming performance while capable enough to handle the rigors of work and heavy typing.

The bit that excites me most are two of the magnetic switch choices available from stock. The V6 Ultra Hybrid ships with one of four Gateron Ultra Fast Lime magnetic switches, two of which are tactile. Yes, tactile magnetic switches — this is the biggest news in my opinion.

All magnetic switches up to now have been linear in operation. Sure, being able to hot-swap those is fine, but swapping out 108 switches from a full-sized keyboard is a ginormous time suck. So it’s not like you can just quickly switch from tactiles for work to magnetic for gaming. If, like me, you enjoy tactile switches but want magnetic gaming performance, you’ve so far been left out in the cold. Not anymore.

The V6 Ultra Hybrid also packs plenty of Keychron’s productivity heritage. There’s a gasket mount, for bouncy and comfortable typing; Keychron’s steeply-raked and deeply-sculpted OSA profile keycaps, which I find ideal for fast typing; and screw-in stabilizers for minimal big key wobble. As you can see, my typing speed and accuracy were both above average on the V6 Ultra Hybrid, helped by paring back the actuation to 2.6mm — my personal sweet spot and where I type-test all magnetic boards. I could (and indeed did) type on this thing all day.

Thanks to Gateron’s magnetic switches, you also get every elite gaming feature under the sun right now: adjustable actuation; rapid trigger; dynamic keystroke for multiple commands per actuation; custom SOCD resolutions for last key prioritization (A.K.A. ‘Snap Tap’). There’s 8K polling too, although on a keyboard this is tantamount to snake oil, if you ask me. All of this is customizable through Keychron’s fantastic web launcher.

I used the board for everything, from competitive gaming on “Counter-Strike 2” and “Wardogs,” through to more relaxed titles like “Total War: Rome II,” “Valheim,” and “Dune: Awakening.” It never put a foot wrong.

Admittedly, if you want a board purely for competitive FPS gaming, you’re probably better off with a plate-, tray-, or top-mounted magnetic board like the NuPhy Air60 HE, NuPhy Field75 HE, or Keychron Q16 HE 8K — these mount styles aren’t as comfortable, but move around less than a gasket mount, making them less likely to cause accidental inputs at super low <0.5mm switch actuations.

If you need an all-rounder for both work and play, though, I seriously can’t think of a better board than the V6 Ultra Hybrid.

As this is a Keychron board, you get all the expected goodies. Aside from some QC issues I’ll cover later, the board is built well, using premium materials. The case is sturdy ABS plastic with very little bend and flex — impressive given this is a long board.

The keycaps are doubleshot PBT, which will stand up well to wear and tear without going shiny, unlike ABS keycaps. PBT is also grease resistant. I did my usual test, typing on the keyboard after eating Monster Munch (a fried corn snack here in the U.K.), and the V6’s keycaps picked up a lot of grease but were easy to wipe down. Not quite as impressive as the caps on the Logitech G Pro X2 Rapid, which completely resisted the same grease altogether — like not even a single smear.

The V6 features a decent 4,000mAh battery, plus triple Bluetooth, 2.4G and wired connectivity, toggleable via a switch on the case. There’s a macOS/Windows toggle, too, but Keychron still supplies separate sets of Windows and macOS command keys rather than dual-labeling its keycaps. This is a longstanding frustration of mine. I switch between the two OS’ constantly for work. It’s great to have the toggle, but it undermines the ease if I have to switch keycaps too. A small issue, but one that’s so easily solvable by dual labelling — as proved by the Lofree Hyzen and Lofree Flow 2.

When I reviewed the original Keychron V6, which I awarded a full five stars, one of my favorite features was the price. It offered major performance for a very reasonable sum. The V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE is pricier. It costs $164 versus the $99 basic V6 and the $119 V6 Ultra (which has faster polling, better internal damping, nicer switches, etc — just an all-round upgraded package).

However, the V6 Ultra Hybrid packs a lot more functionality than the lower-tier V6 models thanks to the dual MX/HE switch compatibility, and way more gaming features when using HE switches. An extra $45 over the standard V6 Ultra is fair game for all that, at least in my book.

Let’s look at the hybrid MX/HE competition, too. The Lofree Hyzen costs a whopping $279 — sure it’s made from aluminum and is beautiful to behold, but the software is janky as hell. The Glorious GMMK 3 HE starts at $179, but you can easily get up to near $500 for choice productivity upgrades (and to make it look less ugly than stock). By those two yardsticks, the V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE is the best value-for-money hybrid board on the market, and it ain’t even close.

At the time of writing, the V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE is in pre-order, after its Kickstarter campaign, with estimated shipping starting December 2026.

As I’ve mentioned in previous reviews, I absolutely hate that Keychron floats its new boards on Kickstarter. Keychron is a major keyboard brand (arguably the dominant productivity market force) that absolutely does not need to crowdfund its boards. Besides, as someone who has tested several of Keychron’s crowdfunded boards, I can tell you they’re already developed and practically finished by the start of the campaigns (because most Keychron boards are 95% the same under the hood). Oh well. That’s just unfortunately how Keychron chooses to operate, but you can rest assured that there’s usually very little chance of a crowdfunding rug pull from this brand.

There’s very little I don’t like about the V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE, aside from its ridiculously long-winded name. It’s a little boring to look at, I guess, and I saw some QC teething issues, but nothing that should seriously dissuade you.

Ah, look: black plastic case, gray rounded keycaps, a tiny bit of color on the ESC key. It must be a Keychron! Yawn. I’m not saying the V6 Ultra Hybrid is bad-looking, but it’s the same old Keychron design we’ve seen for years now. And it’s getting kinda boring.

Now, as someone who has owned, tested, used, or edited the reviews of literally hundreds of keyboards, this probably affects me more than you. I see a lot of Keychrons; you’ll probably only see the one you buy.

But man, I wish Keychron would make some more exciting decks in its more affordable V- and K-series sometimes. Pretty boards with plenty of color, like the NuPhy Halo75; or handsome futuristic designs like the Lofree Hyzen and Lofree Block. Come on, Keychron, spice it up a bit.

As Keychron has grown, I’ve seen firsthand its once stellar reputation for build quality start to drop. A few years ago, every single Keychron board we tested was built like a tank. Now we’re seeing frequent issues with sticky switches or other build quality concerns. Not all the time, I must say. And Keychron is always keen to hear from us when this happens, so we always tell its representatives and receive a replacement in quick order. But it’s getting to the point now that I’m seeing a pattern I can’t ignore.

My first V6 Ultra Hybrid review unit suffered both a sticky switch (solved by adjusting debounce time) and a USB dongle port that was far too large with no magnet inside, meaning the 2.4G receiver would fall out. Keychron’s representative has assured me this was a pre-production teething issue, and issued me a full production unit where the problem has been fixed. But as I said above, similar issues are becoming too common now from this once wholly reliable brand, and it’s a problem I need to call out. Keychron, if you’re reading, please step your game back up.

I utterly adore this keyboard. I won’t be using it long-term because I prefer a 75% layout (so I‘m eagerly waiting for a V2 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE). But I absolutely love what this deck signifies.

As is so often the case in the productivity keyboard arena, it takes Keychron to turn its attention to an innovation to truly bring that feature into the mainstream and make it work. Dual MX/HE compatibility is now here, with proper wide-ranging switch support for both mechanical and magnetic. And there’s a tactile magnetic switch on offer to boot.

If you want one keyboard that excels for literally every purpose, without breaking the bank, it’s the Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE. End of story.

#3418. Canadian court certifies class action against Apple over Google search deal

A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has certified a class action against Apple over allegations that its search agreement with Google stifled competition and inflated advertising prices. Here are the details.

In recent years, Apple’s deal with Alphabet to make Google the default search engine on Safari has drawn regulatory attention in the US, the UK, and Australia, while related search competition concerns have also come under scrutiny in the EU and Japan.

While the details of each investigation differ, they all raise concerns about the impact of Google’s dominance in search, as well as the extent to which its agreements with other companies might be limiting competition.

More recently, Apple’s agreement with Google received significant attention during the US Department of Justice’s antitrust case against the search giant, which included testimony from Apple executives Eddy Cue and John Giannandrea. The latter joined Apple from Google in 2018 and led its AI efforts until stepping down earlier this year.

As a result of the US case, a federal judge ruled in August 2024 that Google had illegally maintained its monopoly in online search through anticompetitive agreements, including its deal with Apple.

Now, evidence presented during that trial has become central to a class action against Apple in Canada, which a British Columbia Supreme Court judge recently certified.

The case was initially brought in 2021 by Spark Event Rentals Ltd., an event rental company based in British Columbia. The plaintiff alleged that Apple and Google conspired to limit competition in the search market, allowing Google to charge advertisers artificially inflated prices.

Apple, meanwhile, argued that its agreement with Google was a legitimate distribution arrangement rather than an unlawful conspiracy. The company also maintained that Google was the appropriate defendant, describing itself as an “innocent bystander.”

Interestingly, the lawsuit originally named both Apple and Google as defendants, but the plaintiff later dropped Google from the case following a dispute over an arbitration clause in its advertising contracts.

With Apple now the sole defendant, Justice Thomas has allowed the case to proceed as a class action, finding sufficient grounds to examine whether Google’s payments discouraged Apple from developing its own search engine.

The lawsuit seeks financial compensation for advertisers who allegedly overpaid for Google search ads, and the court has also allowed the question of punitive damages to proceed.

The class action covers Canadian residents who purchased search ads from Google since 2005, when Apple and Google first agreed to make Google the default search engine on Safari in exchange for a share of advertising revenue.

Importantly, the ruling does not establish that Apple engaged in anticompetitive conduct, but simply allows the allegations to proceed as a class action.

The central proposition raised by these pleadings is that Apple could have used its resources and distribution network to enter the search engine market, but chose not to because Google paid Apple billions of dollars in revenue-share payments to make Google the default search provider on Apple products. This arrangement gave Google market power, enabling it to charge supracompetitive advertising prices on search engines.

In my view, this pleads a common purpose to perform an act prohibited by s 45 of the Competition Act, such that it is not “clear and obvious” that the plaintiff has not pleaded an agreement between Google and Apple not to compete in the search engine market.

At one point in his decision, Justice Thomas cites Giannandrea’s testimony and directly quotes Cue’s from the US antitrust trial, before concluding that “this provides some basis in fact, supporting the inference that Apple did not compete with Google in the search engine market because of its Agreement with Google.”

Interestingly, the judge also acknowledges Apple’s objections to the evidence, agreeing that “the plaintiff has cherry-picked evidence to support his case,” but adding that, in his view, “it is appropriate to do so at this stage in the proceedings.”

With the class action greenlit, the case can now move forward toward trial, though no date has been announced yet.

#3417. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3416. Daniel Radcliffe Officially Admits He May Never Watch HBO's 'Harry Potter' Reboot

For an entire generation, Daniel Radcliffe is Harry Potter. The British star spent a decade bringing J.K. Rowling's famous wizard to life across eight movies, growing up alongside Emma Watson and Rupert Grint as the franchise became a global phenomenon. Now, 25 years after the first movie arrived in theaters, HBO is preparing to introduce an entirely new trio of Hogwarts students. But while millions of fans are counting down to the reboot's Christmas premiere, the original Boy Who Lived might not be joining them.

Radcliffe has admitted that he may never watch HBO's upcoming Harry Potter series, despite previously expressing his support for Dominic McLaughlin, who is taking over the title role. Speaking with the Associated Press at the New York premiere of his Netflix project Steps, however, Radcliffe clarified that it was more down to the fact that he didn't have the time to spare, and that, in case you didn't realize, he's already done this. Oh and also, he's missed out on some of the finest television ever made.

I don't know if I will [watch], honestly. I've been in a lot of Harry Potter already… and also I don't watch any TV. I haven't seen Breaking Bad. I haven't seen Mad Men. I haven't seen some of the like the real classics. So, you know, eight hours is a lot of anything to watch.

That's not to say he's not for the new series doing well. Although Radcliffe might not be watching, he has been supportive of McLaughlin, who will lead the new adaptation alongside Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley. Radcliffe previously explained that McLaughlin doesn't need advice from him, and he expressed his concern that his own comments could follow the young performer throughout his career. #3414. 10 Best Scrooge Performances In A Christmas Carol Movies Ranked, Including Johnny Depp's Ebenezer

Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol has been adapted countless times, with dozens of iconic stars playing the legendary miser, Ebenezer Scrooge. Scrooge is a particularly compelling role because he is considerably more than a miserable banker who shouts "Bah! Humbug!" A truly effective Ebenezer must be thoroughly unpleasant without becoming totally irredeemable. Importantly, his eventual transformation needs to be the culmination of a genuine emotional journey.

While some actors have portrayed Scrooge as a terrifying embodiment of Victorian greed, others have emphasized his loneliness, bitterness, or capacity for childish enthusiasm. Some surprisingly successful musical and animated interpretations also show that the character doesn't need to be played traditionally to make an impression.

Cinema's very best Scrooges have managed to balance each of these characteristics while also offering something a little bit unique.

Tim Curry is famously brilliant at playing unpleasant characters, and the 1997 animated A Christmas Carol makes excellent use of his distinctive delivery. Curry gives Scrooge considerably more personality than the modest production might suggest.

Curry's naturally expressive voice makes Scrooge's festive contempt entertaining without undermining the character's nastiness. The film also features original musical numbers, giving Curry additional opportunities to insert some theatricality into the character.

Curry earns a place on this list because his interpretation has a distinctive personality, but it doesn't have the emotional depth or lasting impact of the performances higher up. Unlike other understated performances, Curry leans into his familiar, sickly eccentricities. He’s a fun Scrooge, but not quite an essential one.

Seymour Hicks had considerable experience playing Ebenezer before 1935’s Scrooge, having portrayed Dickens' miser on stage for decades. His familiarity with the material is evident throughout, particularly in how he balances Scrooge's outward hostility with the character's underlying vulnerability.

Scrooge is historically significant as the first feature-length sound adaptation of Dickens’ novella. However, its limited production resources mean it has been overshadowed by subsequent versions. Nevertheless, Hicks makes particularly effective use of Scrooge’s physicality, presenting him as an irritable, almost grotesque figure whose misery is reflected in his cramped surroundings.

Hicks’ performance is an essential foundation in the character's cinematic evolution. However, the limitations of the 1935 production prevent him from reaching the emotional complexity of the performances higher on this list.

Reginald Owen's interpretation of Scrooge in 1938’s A Christmas Carol is considerably more approachable than some of the nastier versions that followed. That said, Owen makes an unforgettable initial impression as the banker. His Scrooge is particularly entertaining when confronted with people who refuse to share his cheerless outlook.

Vitally, Owen also gives the character enough vulnerability to make his redemption particularly convincing. His interpretation has a sprightliness that distinguishes it from the more intimidating performances, and his transformation on Christmas morning is genuinely infectious.

Owen ranks above Hicks because he brings greater warmth and comic energy to the character, contrasting Scrooge's initial misery and eventual happiness, which is particularly satisfying. However, he lacks the psychological intensity and the dynamic emotional range of other actors.

Johnny Depp brings a distinctly theatrical interpretation to Ebenezer Scrooge in Ti West's Ebenezer, leaning into the character's eccentricities and grim disposition. His performance is particularly convincing during the earlier scenes. His petulant delivery, exaggerated expressions, and distinctive comic timing make the character entertainingly unpleasant.

Unfortunately, Depp's bad-tempered eccentricities as the unreformed miser were much more effective than the redeemed Scrooge. The Christmas morning Scrooge is underwhelming and doesn’t feel significantly warmer.

This contrast is important because the character's transformation is ultimately what makes a memorable Scrooge performance. Depp's comic timing and exuberance are great, but the more emotionally complete performances ahead of him ultimately have the advantage.

Disney's A Christmas Carol gives Jim Carrey an unusual opportunity to play several characters, including Scrooge at different stages of his life and all three Christmas spirits. It's an ambitious approach that makes excellent use of the actor's physical comedy and expressive facial movements, particularly when Scrooge finds himself desperately attempting to escape the spooky visitors.

Carrey is especially effective during the Ghost of Christmas Past sequence, when the miser is forced to confront the loneliness and disappointments that contributed to his increasingly bitter personality. Carrey's transformation into an exuberant, generous man on Christmas morning is therefore even more compelling.

Playing the younger Scrooge allows Carrey to explore the character's history and psychology in ways that others don't quite match. He also makes the transition from fear to joy particularly convincing. Sadly, the digital animation occasionally distracts from his performance, limiting him from ranking higher.

Patrick Stewart's interpretation of Scrooge benefits enormously from his background as a Shakespearean actor. He approaches Dickens' dialogue with considerable authority, making the character's lengthy speeches and confrontations with the Christmas spirits feel natural rather than unnecessarily grandiose.

Stewart’s benefits from a particularly strong adaptation, which retains much of Dickens' original dialogue and narrative structure. Stewart had performed A Christmas Carol as a one-man stage production, portraying approximately 30 characters during the performance. That experience clearly informed his understanding of Scrooge, particularly the distinction between the miserable old man and the lonely young boy he once was.

Stewart offers one of the most complete and faithful portrayals of the character, and his command of Dickens' language makes the character's emotional journey particularly persuasive. Despite this, he doesn't quite possess the intimidating screen presence of other cinematic Scrooges.

Scrooge's musical format means that Albert Finney could explore the character in ways that more traditional adaptations cannot. His performance of "I Hate People" is a particularly effective introduction to Scrooge's personality, capturing his contempt for practically everybody around him.

Finney is equally effective during the quieter sequences, particularly when confronted with memories of his younger self and the relationship he sacrificed for financial security. His eventual performance of "I Like Life" is a wonderfully exuberant contrast to his earlier misery.

Finney manages to make an inherently theatrical interpretation feel remarkably human. His performance has an infectious comic energy, but he also captures the sadness beneath Scrooge's behavior. His Golden Globe-winning performance is one of the most unusual and entertaining screen Scrooges – but still one that doesn’t quite feel quintessential enough.

George C. Scott offers one of the most intimidating interpretations of Scrooge in the 1984 television adaptation of A Christmas Carol. His considerable screen presence makes the miser genuinely unpleasant, particularly during his interactions with Bob Cratchit. Scott doesn't need to exaggerate the character's cruelty because his imposing delivery and naturally stern expression make even relatively ordinary exchanges feel confrontational.

Vitally, Scott gradually exposes Scrooge's vulnerability. Scott is especially convincing when confronted with the Cratchit family's circumstances, making Scrooge's eventual concern for Tiny Tim feel like a genuine emotional breakthrough.

Scott ranks high because he finds the most convincing balance between Scrooge's cruelty and vulnerability. His imposing presence also gives the opening scenes a sense of menace that few other actors can match. The result is one of the most dramatically complete Scrooge performances ever filmed.

Michael Caine's performance in The Muppet Christmas Carol is a masterclass in commitment. It surrounds the actor with talking frogs, pigs, rats, and bears, but Caine approaches Scrooge with the seriousness of a dramatic production. He treats the Muppets as wholly legitimate characters, allowing their comedy to shine through while he carries the seriousness of Dickens' story.

Caine flaunts considerable emotional depth in the scenes involving the Ghost of Christmas Past, most notably when confronted with his lost relationship with Belle. Caine’s greatest achievement, though, is the Christmas morning transformation, when Scrooge's newfound enthusiasm becomes infectious without ever feeling like an entirely different performance.

Caine’s straight-faced approach is the most perfectly judged interpretation of Scrooge in any adaptation that’s deliberately comedic. He never competes with the Muppets for attention, and his complete commitment makes the humor even more effective. Only one actor ultimately edges Caine out in Scrooge’s cinematic history.

Alastair Sim’s impeccable performance in 1951’s Scrooge remains the definitive on-screen Ebenezer. Sim is simultaneously frightening, funny, pathetic, and deeply moving, making his eventual redemption feel like a genuinely transformative experience.

His reaction to the Ghost of Christmas Present's revelation about Ignorance and Want is genuinely affecting, while his encounter with the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come brings an appropriately terrifying sense of finality to his journey. However, the actor's greatest achievement is the sheer exuberance of Scrooge's Christmas morning transformation.

Sim's laughter, frantic excitement and almost childlike enthusiasm make the character's newfound appreciation for life completely infectious. Sim takes the top position because no other actor combines these qualities quite so successfully. His Scrooge is a genuinely unpleasant miser, a deeply unhappy man and an utterly joyful convert to Christmas. He is so quintessential that even seven decades later, he is the standard against which every subsequent Scrooge in A Christmas Carol adaptations is measured.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is a sleek, budget-friendly entry-level smartwatch with effective workout tracking and almost two weeks of battery life. However, initial step counts can be inaccurate, sleep tracking is unreliable, the bulky design won't suit everyone, and there's no third-party app support.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When it comes to finding the best cheap smartwatch, you want something that will suit everything about your lifestyle. Whether it’s sport or running errands, I know I don’t want my watch to get in my way — I need it to support me in my tasks.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is a good choice since it’s affordable and has a sleek design. Fitness tracking is effective, and the battery life is good too. But will it be for everyone? Not by a long shot.

I found the watch face very bulky on my small wrists, and the sleep tracking is inaccurate. The lack of third-party app support may also put off some users. To find out more, keep reading my full CMF Watch 3 Pro review.

Light Green, Orange, Light Grey, Dark Grey

Accelerometer, Gyroscope, Ambient light, Heart rate and SPO2 Blood Oxygen Saturation sensor

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is available to purchase on Amazon for $79 in the U.S. and £99 in the U.K. The watch comes in a range of colors, including Light Green, Orange, Light Grey and Dark Grey, which I tested.

This is a pretty cheap watch and is the same price as the Amazfit Bip 6. Sleep tracking in particular is far more accurate on the Bip 6 in comparison to the CMF, and the Bip 6 can also track more types of workouts.

A cheaper option is the Xiaomi Smart Band 10 for $51, which is much slimmer and will suit people with narrower wrists, as the CMF watch is very chunky.

If you don’t mind being without a screen and want some of the best fitness tracking out there, I’d recommend the Fitbit Air for $99. At just $20 more, it offers incredibly valuable fitness insights. For under $50, you can pick up the Amazfit Band 7, which has a very informative companion app to help improve training where needed.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

CMF is a sub-brand of Nothing, and as such, I expected some seriously stunning design work. Whether it’s headphones or milk carton-shaped speakers (CMF Speaker M), Nothing and CMF tech always stands out from the crowd. The CMF Watch 3 Pro is no different.

I tested the Dark Grey version, and I like how this looks for day-to-day wear. However, I felt that the watch face was far too large for my wrist. The circular AMOLED display has a 1.4-inch diameter, so it felt quite bulky. Unfortunately, the Watch 3 Pro doesn’t come in different sizes like the Apple Watch Series 12 or the SE 3 — these are available in multiple case sizes, making them more accessible.

With that said, the strap was secure thanks to the buckle closure. This strap can be removed with a small latch and swapped out for different colors, making customization easy. This was very easy to do when attaching the strap to the watch, but also very secure so it won’t come undone on its own.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro isn’t the brightest out there. The Amazfit Bip 6 can achieve 2,000 nits of brightness, but the CMF only reaches a maximum of 670 nits. It’s bright enough, but if you know you’ll be using the torch feature on the watch face frequently, definitely look at a brighter option like the Bip 6. It will also be hard to see the screen in bright lighting conditions, like running in direct sunshine.

The watch has a durability rating of IP68, meaning it is completely dust-tight and protected against water submersion beyond one meter. That means you can wear it anytime, whether you're working out or at the beach. However, most smartwatches have a durability rating of 5ATM, meaning they can withstand pressure underwater, so you can swim in them, but the CMF watch doesn’t have this level of protection.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro has 131 sport modes and uses built-in dual-band GPS to help you track your routes. It’s easiest to control this through the watch itself, as the app interface is very clunky, and I didn’t feel like I was getting a whole lot of detail, information, or control

I’ve been using the CMF Watch 3 Pro to track hikes, runs, and pilates sessions, and while I feel it’s been tracking my heart rate accurately throughout, I’m not entirely sold. Compared to my phone or Oura Ring 5, step counts, heart rate during workouts and sleep tracking weren’t accurate. This could also be because the watch face was so bulky on my wrist, and this meant that the sensors weren’t always in contact with my skin.

The watch tracks many metrics such as calories burned, step count, distance and of course heart rate, but the information is limited. I didn’t feel like I was getting feedback on my data as I do with other devices like the Amazfit Bip 6. Of course, this is a budget watch, but you get better workout analysis with Garmin, Apple, Amazfit, and even Xiaomi. This was missing from the CMF.

After using the watch for about a week, I started to notice that my movement tracking was improving, and my step counts were becoming more accurate. This likely happened as the watch used information like my height and GPS tracking for distance to affirm the count. It seems like the more it learns about my body, the more accurate it becomes. However, this has never been an issue for my Oura Ring, Apple Watch, or Xiaomi Smart Band, so there’s certainly some improvements to be made here.

The thing I get most excited about when I’m testing out a new fitness tracker is the health and sleep tracking. I track readiness and sleep almost to a fault, so it’s great to see how different devices can inform my health… I just don't think the CMF Watch 3 Pro is the one for the job.

The watch is a decent option for tracking heart health concerns, but shouldn’t be used as a diagnostic tool. It has automatic heart rate measurement that can run for 24 hours a day. It also tracks your resting heart rate throughout the day, and these readings were always about the same as I see with my Oura Ring 5.

You can set up heart rate reminders in the app settings. This means that if your heart rate goes above or below a specified number of beats, it will trigger an alarm. This is a great feature for anyone who may have a health condition. You can also set reminders for drinking water and standing up throughout the day.

I was disappointed by the sleep tracking on this watch. At first, I genuinely thought I was doing something wrong, but a quick look on Reddit and the Nothing community page showed me that this is a pretty common issue. I checked the firmware, battery, my wear position, and restarted the watch, but I was still having trouble logging sleep.

On my first night, the watch only detected three hours of sleep. My Oura Ring and Hatch Sleep clock both told me I was asleep for over eight hours. As I looked further into the data, I saw that the watch had also detected a nap at around eight o’clock in the evening. This was strange since I was cooking dinner, meaning I was moving around and my heart rate would have been slightly elevated.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro does not support any third-party apps; however, you can sync your data with your phone’s health app and directly sync with sports apps such as Strava. The watch also receives your phone's notifications, but you can’t reply to messages directly from the watch.

The dual-band GPS tracking is accurate, and I could see my route after my run. The watch also offers a custom running coach, and this is a great feature for those training towards shorter distances like a 5K or a 10K, but for longer distances I would recommend investing in a running programme that can be entirely tailored to you.

While the watch has some workout analysis, it’s not as in-depth as what you get from brands like Garmin, so if you’re seriously training towards a goal, I’d look into the Garmin Forerunner 70.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro has 13 days of battery life. This is pretty impressive, and about what I’ve come to expect with budget fitness trackers and smartwatches.

The Amazfit Bip 6 lasts for 14 days, and I got 15 days from the Xiaomi Smart Band 10. The CMF watch takes 99 minutes to charge.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is an affordable option for those new to smartwatches and who need something basic to track workouts. The design is sleek, and it’s effective in tracking most workouts, although step counting isn’t accurate at first. The battery life is good, giving almost two weeks of use with a single charge.

Although decent for tracking general health, it can’t track sleep as well as similarly priced rivals like the Xiaomi Smart Band 10. So if you’re someone who likes to make sure they’re getting enough rest, note that sleep tracking is wildly inaccurate. The bulky watch face was far too big for me and got in the way a lot, and unfortunately there isn’t support for third-party apps.

#3409. Google DeepMind analysis proves Signal and WhatsApp encryption is secure

The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol.

In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” …

“Formal verification” is the term given to mathematically proving or disproving that a cryptographic algorithm or protocol satisfies its security claims under all conditions. It guarantees that there is no situation in which the protocol will fail. This is a far higher standard than traditional testing methods which seek to find vulnerabilities but cannot promise that others do not exist.

Using agentic AI to carry out formal verification is a huge breakthrough for cryptography and AI alike. It is, however, extremely computationally demanding, so Google told Wired it’s unclear as yet how practical it will be to use it more broadly.

DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

It’s important to note that the validation is for the protocol itself rather than the Signal app as a whole. However, encouragement can be taken from the fact that when tested against older versions of Signal that contained known vulnerabilities, it identified those and flagged them as failing formal verification.

Also worth stating is that Google was able to build on some past formal verification work already completed without the use of AI. This analysis took four weeks, and the scale of resources required has not yet been disclosed, so we shouldn’t expect a whole array of other protocols to be validated overnight. All the same, this is a very big deal.

#3408. The 10 Greatest TV Serial Killers of All Time, Ranked

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Television has always had a complicated relationship with its monsters. A movie gets two hours with a killer before the lights come up, but a TV series asks viewers to spend entire seasons with them. Over that time, audiences get to see how they operate, and why they are the people they are. That extra time is exactly why the small screen has produced some of the most unsettling yet still fascinating killers in fiction.

Ranking them comes down to far more than body count, because the names on this list are defined by the great performances behind them that practically dare the audience to understand them a little too well. Here are the greatest TV serial killers of all time.

When Victoria Pedretti first shows up in You Season 2, Love Quinn seems like the exact opposite of Joe Goldberg's (Penn Badgley) darkness. Love is a grieving chef working at her family's upscale Los Angeles grocery store, Anavrin, warm and open in a way none of Joe's previous obsessions ever were. Then the Season 2 finale pulls the rug from under Joe and the audience and reveals that Love has known exactly who Joe is all along. Not only that, but the viewers learn that she is not very different from him and has a body count of her own, including Joe’s neighbor Delilah (Carmela Zumbado) and his ex, Candace (Ambyr Childers).

By Season 3, Love transforms into a full-blown antagonist alongside Joe as her killing streak continues. What makes Love so compelling as a character, though, is that she's the only “You” who ever turns Joe's logic back on him to show him the mirror. Pedretti nails the sudden switches. Love can be a devoted mother and a woman quietly measuring out a paralyzing dose of aconite in the same breath. Pedretti’s run on the show lasted for just two seasons but turned her into one of the most talked-about characters in the entire series. Fans still debate whether any of Joe’s other love interests ever matched up to Love because her absence was felt in every season that followed.

Noah Hawley's Fargo has introduced plenty of strange criminals across its anthology seasons, but none have lived up to Lorne Malvo’s (Billy Bob Thornton) legacy. The antagonist is a drifter-for-hire who rolls into Bemidji, Minnesota, and meets insurance salesman Lester Nygaard (Martin Freeman) in a hospital waiting room. Then, almost on a whim, Malvo offers to kill the bully who has tormented Lester since high school. That one conversation sets off a chain of murders that pulls in Deputy Molly Solverson (Allison Tolman) and Duluth cop Gus Grimly (Colin Hanks), while Malvo glides through Season 1 and leaves a trail of bodies and terrified witnesses behind him.

Malvo isn't a serial killer in the textbook sense. There's no ritual or compulsion behind his murders, and that's exactly what makes him so frightening. He kills simply because he can, and treats every encounter as a way to instigate the people around him. Malvo is a force of nature in the show because the audience never truly learns who he is. They only know what he does, and the mystery around the villain turns into his greatest strength.

Killing Eve turned the cat-and-mouse thriller into a flirtation, and Villanelle (Jodie Comer) is the reason the approach worked. Villanelle is a Russian-born assassin who works for a shadowy organization called The Twelve. She travels across Europe to carry out elaborate hits in increasingly outrageous outfits, and in the very first episode, she kills a man at a Tuscan villa with a hairpin to the eye. Her handler, Konstantin (Kim Bodnia), does his best to keep her under control, but that becomes nearly impossible once Villanelle fixates on MI5 officer Eve Polastri (Sandra Oh), the woman assigned to track her down.

What’s more fascinating is that Eve becomes just as obsessed with Villanelle in return. Comer, who won an Emmy for the role in 2019, delivers one of the most playful performances of her career as Villanelle. She kills with a carefreeness that makes murder feel like a cure for her boredom. However, as the seasons go on, the audience also understands her vulnerability and the need to be seen. Villanelle proved a villain could be charming and terrifying in the very same scene and has set the benchmark for female antagonists for years to come.

Turning Psycho into a modern-day prequel sounded like a terrible idea on paper, but Bates Motel became one of A&E's best dramas, and Freddie Highmore’s brilliant take on the iconic Norman Bates has a lot to do with that. Highmore plays the teenage version of the character from Hitchcock’s film, who moves with his mother, Norma (Vera Farmiga), to the coastal town of White Pine Bay, Oregon, after the sudden death of his father. There, Norma buys the motel that would become infamous, and over five seasons, the series traces Norman's slow transformation from an awkward, sweet kid into the messy antagonist that he was always destined to be.

As the story progresses, "Mother" takes up more and more space in his head. The show essentially makes the audience watch Norman fight a losing battle. They already know what is going to happen when Marion Crane (Rihanna) finally enters the picture, but the build-up to that point is what makes the show such an engaging watch. Highmore never plays Norman as a monster, but as a boy who desperately wants to be good, in spite of his dark side. The final season's reworking of Psycho's infamous shower scene and Norman’s fate is a bold swing, but Bates Motel manages to pull it off thanks to how carefully it shaped Norman’s character instead of just portraying him as a horror icon.

The Fall makes an unusual choice by telling the audience who the killer is in the very first episode. The series follows bereavement counselor and married father of two, Paul Spector (Jamie Dornan), who maintains the facade of being a family man while he stalks young professional women by night. The story picks up when Detective Superintendent Stella Gibson (Gillian Anderson) is brought in from London to review the unsolved murder of a young woman in Belfast, and she soon realizes that she is hunting a serial killer who just so happens to be Paul. Soon enough, her hunt for Spector becomes a game of cat and mouse, with the audience always knowing what both sides are planning.

The real thrill lies in watching the two of them inch closer to each other and watching Paul’s carefully crafted lies slowly fall apart. The Fall removes the whodunit element from the thriller genre and forces the audience to face how easy it is for Paul to fool everyone around him. He is a chilling villain because of how ordinary he seems, since there is no tragic backstory or supernatural force behind all his violence. Dornan plays the character with remarkable restraint, which makes him all the more disturbing and reminds the audience that the most dangerous killers are often the ones nobody would suspect.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

Mindhunter is built around conversations, and none of them are as chilling as the ones with Edmund Kemper (Cameron Britton). The villain, based on the real-life Co-Ed Killer, is serving life in a California prison when FBI agents Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holt McCallany) visit him as part of their early research into what would become modern criminal profiling. Kemper stands at six-foot-nine and is far sharper than either agent expects. He is also a little too happy to talk, and he walks them through his crimes in calm, matter-of-fact detail.

Britton earned an Emmy nomination for the role, and it's easy to see why. In the game-changing Mindhunter, he plays Kemper as polite and articulate, ready to help Holden and Bill in a way that almost makes him feel normal. Then, in that same easygoing way, he randomly describes the horrific ways in which he has killed people, and the audience is brought back to reality. Kemper only appears in a handful of episodes in the brilliant show, but it’s remarkable how Britton’s performances did so much with so little screen time.

Joe Goldberg (Penn Badgley) had to be on this list, because no other antagonist has come close to his level of creepiness. The character is a New York bookstore manager who falls for aspiring writer Guinevere Beck (Elizabeth Lail) the moment he sets eyes on her. That’s not the beginning of a romantic story, though, because it doesn’t take long for the audience to realize how obsessive and manipulative Joe really is. Over five seasons, his obsessions take him from New York to Los Angeles and eventually London. Anyone he believes stands between him and the woman of the moment ends up dead, and this completely reckless way of taking people’s lives is what makes Joe so scary.

On the surface, he appears to be the perfect lover boy who is willing to do anything for the woman he loves, but what he really wants is control. What makes the show work is Joe’s voiceover, which lets the audience hear every self-serving justification he tells himself. He genuinely believes he is the hero of every story, and the show is clever enough to make viewers almost agree with him before reminding them exactly who he is. This uncomfortable closeness to his thoughts is what keeps Joe more unsettling than nearly any other killer on TV.

The question of who killed Laura Palmer (Sheryl Lee) turned Twin Peaks into a cultural event in 1990, and the answer remains one of the most devastating reveals in TV history. Midway through Season 2, the show confirms that Laura's killer is her own father, Leland Palmer (Ray Wise), possessed by the demonic entity known as BOB (Frank Silva). In the episode "Lonely Souls," Leland's reflection reveals BOB's face as he attacks Laura's cousin, Maddy Ferguson, also played by Lee, while Agent Dale Cooper (Kyle MacLachlan) is still piecing the case together across town. Ray Wise is unforgettable in the role, especially since the show never fully explains whether Leland was BOB’s victim or something worse, and that mystery is a big part of why he still haunts viewers today.

David Lynch and Mark Frost used BOB to tell a story about abuse that TV in the '90s wasn’t ready to talk about openly. Leland is more than a typical antagonist because Twin Peaks lets viewers grieve with him first. He is the father sobbing at Laura’s funeral and singing show tunes in the hotel lobby, so the reveal feels like a betrayal of the audience as much as of his family. Even his final scene, where a freed Leland breaks down in Cooper’s arms as he remembers what he did, refuses to let viewers fully hate him. His impact also goes far beyond the show itself, since countless TV mysteries since then have tried to recreate the same sense of dread and shock that came with finally learning who killed Laura Palmer.

Plenty of actors have played Hannibal Lecter, but Mads Mikkelsen made the character entirely his own in Bryan Fuller's Hannibal. The titular character, who holds the reputation of a brilliant psychiatrist, is brought in by FBI Agent Jack Crawford (Laurence Fishburne) to keep watch over criminal profiler Will Graham (Hugh Dancy), whose ability to empathize with killers is slowly ruining him. Of course, no one knows that Hannibal is the very killer the FBI is chasing. Over three seasons, the psychiatrist organizes lavish dinner parties for the agents as he toys with Will's mind and, eventually, his heart.

No show on this list looks like Hannibal. Food stylist Janice Poon made every dish gorgeous, and knowing what's actually on the plate turns every dinner scene into an absurd comedy. Mikkelsen plays Hannibal with an unusual finesse and rarely raises his voice, but his fascination with Will is the emotional anchor of the show. It’s a shame that NBC canceled the series after three seasons, just as it hit its peak, because Mikkelsen’s Hannibal was pure nightmare fuel.

Before Dexter, a serial killer as the hero of a TV series seemed like an impossible sell. Then Michael C. Hall arrived on Showtime in 2006 as Dexter Morgan, a blood spatter analyst for Miami Metro Police by day and a killer by night. Dexter follows the Code of Harry, a set of rules his adoptive father, Harry (James Remar), taught him to aim his "Dark Passenger" at murderers who slipped through the system. Over eight seasons, he balances that double life with his family and his foul-mouthed detective sister, Debra (Jennifer Carpenter). He also faces a string of formidable rivals, including John Lithgow's Trinity Killer.

Hannibal may be the better-crafted show, but no TV serial killer has shaped the genre the way Dexter has. He allowed the audience to root for a murderer, and that alone changed what TV antiheroes could be. His Code gave viewers a way to justify cheering for him, since every victim seemed to deserve it, at least at first. Hall’s deadpan voiceover does the rest by turning Dexter’s emptiness into dark comedy. The longer the show runs, the clearer it becomes that the Code is just an excuse, and that tension between the monster and the man trying to pass as normal is what keeps Dexter so compelling. Nearly every killer on this list owes something to him, which is exactly why he takes the top spot.

#3407. Dungeons & Dragons Is Getting A Stunning New Release On November 24

Dungeons & Dragons has introduced generations of players to sprawling fantasy worlds, unforgettable adventures, and some truly terrifying villains. While the tabletop role-playing game offers countless opportunities to create original characters and stories, its established multiverse also contains an impressive collection of legendary antagonists. Fans will soon have a new way to explore these darker corners through an upcoming illustrated release.

Titled Dungeons & Dragons Fiends & Foes: Beasts, Villains, and Monstrosities from Across the Planes, the upcoming book arrives on November 24, 2026, through Ten Speed Press. Written by award-winning fantasy author Erin M. Evans, this officially licensed release takes an unconventional approach to exploring D&D lore, combining detailed character lore, original illustrations, and a story-driven journey through the franchise's most notorious figures.

Dungeons & Dragons Fiends & Foes: Beasts, Villains, and Monstrosities from Across the Planes is available to pre-order now through this link

Rather than presenting its subjects as a straightforward encyclopedia of monsters, Fiends & Foes frames its exploration around a mysterious delivery mission. The adventure begins with a request from Glasya, the Archduchess of Malbolge and ruler of the Sixth layer of the Nine Hells. She wants a letter delivered to an extraordinarily powerful individual who has deliberately made themselves difficult to find.

That assignment provides the narrative framework for a journey through the D&D multiverse, with Glasya guiding readers from one notorious figure to another. The identity of the letter's recipient remains an important mystery, giving the book an overarching story instead of simply moving between disconnected character profiles. The premise also allows its featured villains to become part of a larger adventure.

Along the way, readers encounter some of the most recognizable names in Dungeons & Dragons history, including Tiamat, Vecna, Strahd, Halaster Blackcloak, Lolth, Xanathar, and Demogorgon. The book explores more than just their reputations, offering information about different categories of supernatural threats alongside closer examinations of particularly significant characters. Antiheroes and morally complicated figures also receive attention.

One of the biggest attractions of Dungeons & Dragons Fiends & Foes is its emphasis on visual storytelling. The book features original, previously unpublished chapter-opening illustrations alongside artwork taken from official D&D adventures. This combination gives readers opportunities to appreciate the franchise's imaginative creature designs while revisiting the visual identity of its established fantasy settings.

The illustrated presentation also makes the release appealing beyond players searching for information to use during their campaigns. Its exploration of legendary enemies, frightening creatures, and complicated personalities offers a more immersive way to appreciate the mythology behind the tabletop game. For longtime fans, the combination of familiar characters and new artwork provides another reason to revisit the multiverse.

Astarion, Karlach, and other fan-favorite heroes are officially returning in 2027 with new adventures that expand the world of Baldur’s Gate 3.

Evans is particularly well suited to this project. She wrote the award-winning Brimstone Angels Saga, which takes place in the Forgotten Realms, and is also the author of the Books of the Usurper series, beginning with Empire of Exiles. Outside publishing, she co-hosts the Writing About Dragons and Shit podcast and participates in the actual-play series Dungeon Scrawlers. Her experience makes this a noteworthy addition to D&D's expanding collection of illustrated releases.

With its November 24, 2026, publication date, Fiends & Foes is also arriving at a convenient time for holiday shopping. Between its in-world narrative, extensive villain spotlights, and original illustrations, the book offers something for both dedicated tabletop players and readers interested in fantasy lore. Fans looking to explore the darker side of Dungeons & Dragons have a very intriguing and exciting release to anticipate.

#3406. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3405. Apple Maps could soon factor in how long it takes you to park

On some journeys in busy cities, it feels like it can take you longer to park than it does to drive there in the first place. Code spotted in iOS 27.3 suggests that Apple Maps may soon factor in parking time when it provides journey ETAs.

Separately, Waze has partnered with Garmin to help improve the safety of cyclists by using real-time location tracking to alert nearby drivers …

Currently, the estimated time of arrival shown in Apple Maps only measures how long it will take you to drive to your destination. The door-to-door time can be significantly longer if it’s going to take time to park and then walk from the parking spot to the final destination.

Code sleuth pdfu has spotted a strong indication that Apple is working on the problem.

Apple may be working on parking-aware ETAs.iOS 27.3 adds a TimeToPark flag. When enabled, CoreRoutine uses background location and motion data to measure how long you spent near your destination before parking, and how long you walked afterwards. It saves both metrics per trip,… pic.twitter.com/gwgwtHvbgy

Drivers may not be expecting to find cyclists on some roads, and where there are high speed differentials or limited forward vision that can take drivers by surprise and leave cyclists at risk. Garmin and Waze have announced a partnership intended to mitigate the problem.

When a cyclist using a Garmin bike computer or smartwatch chooses to opt in to sharing their live track location, it will show up for drivers using Waze.

The feature is available on the Garmin Edge and any Garmin smartwatch when used with a compatible smartphone and the Garmin Connect app.

#3404. Ring’s wheeled and flying robots will patrol your home

Some people use a whole bunch of fixed cameras to monitor their homes, but Amazon has just announced a more flexible solution through wheeled and flying robots.

Both the $250 Drone Cam and $1,000 Rover Cam can respond to alarms or door and window sensor alerts in order to go check out what’s happening and send live video …

Amazon says they are the first two Ring Robotics products, with more likely to follow. Both are autonomous.

Ring Drone and Ring Rover are both powered by AI Pilot, a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.

AI Pilot simplifies the customer experience, starting with setup. Simply carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan. It intelligently identifies rooms and suggests patrol points: spots worth extra attention. This could be a side door, windows, a register, or a long corridor, helping eliminate guesswork while also allowing you to add additional points customized to your space and security preferences.

When a patrol or flight is initiated, AI Pilot plans the most efficient route to get to a preset point based on the map it’s created. From there, it reacts in real time—autonomously navigating around furniture, shelving, and any obstacle it encounters.

You can set either device to patrol on a fixed schedule, as well as activate them manually, but they will also automatically respond to sensor alerts and alarms.

When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, [either device] automatically [moves] to previously set patrol points to investigate […] Continuous person motion detection means Ring Rover can alert you and start recording the moment it detects motion in its view—even when docked.

The Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping on December 16 for $999.99, but you can preorder it today. The Drone Cam starts shipping in late January for $249.99, but there’s no preorder yet.
