When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At just $229, the Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder is the cheapest bean-to-cup I’ve ever seen. It even has a PID controller, built-in timer, and a nice, weighty tamper. Surely this is too good to be true? Well, if you’re a coffee nerd, yes. The grinder is really inconsistent and the steam wand is quite weak — not to mention the pressurized-only portafilters. Could that sweet, sweet price of $229 be enough to convince you, though? I’m not sure it convinced me.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When I saw the price of the Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder, my eyes bulged out of my head like a cartoon rabbit being chased by a mountain lion. $229? For an espresso machine… and a grinder? What year is this, 2001?

It’s hard to explain just how cheap $229 is, but I’ll do my best. The entry-level Casabrews Tornado grinder is $139 — and that’s seriously budget. The De’Longhi Stilosa espresso machine is $149 — and, again, that’s seriously budget. So $229 for a grinder and an espresso machine is literally unheard of.

So, how does the Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder hold up? Well, it’s $229. That’s all I really have to say. While, yes, this is the cheapest bean-to-cup I’ve ever seen, it performs like it. But this might be enough to make it one of your best espresso machines if you’re on a budget best described as “as close to zero as possible”. Find out the full story in this Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder review.

2 x pressurized portafilters, scoop, tamper, tamping collar, brush

The Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder is $229 from Amazon U.S. and £239 from Amazon U.K. On Amzchef’s website, the Espresso Machine with Grinder is listed as “All-in-One” espresso machine and is $299 rather than $229. The “Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder” is a completely different product with a different screen style — albeit $229, not $299. I've raised this with Amzchef and have been informed it will correct this inconsistency.

They don’t make it easy for us, huh? Anyway, I would buy from Amazon due to the lower price. For ease of searching, the product code is CM1626 — but Amzchef doesn’t list this on its website (for any of its products… just a wonderful, transparent business strategy, I know). The links above are to the Amazon page, not Amzchef’s site.

Opaque pricing aside, the Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder is incredibly cheap. As I wrote in my “Pros” section above, it’s almost unbelievably cheap. A bean-to-cup espresso machine for $229? Seriously? Most electric grinders start at $150, like the Casabrews Tornado or Breville Dose Control Pro.

The only machines I’ve tested around the same price are the $350 Gevi Espresso Machine with Grinder and the $350 Casabrews Marenza. While this machine is a seriously budget option, the low, low pricing does raise questions about longevity — which I’ll get into later.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder is a cheap coffee machine, and it feels like it. The scoop is flimsy plastic, and the dosing collar isn’t wide enough to allow the tamper to pass through. The tamper itself is lovely and weighty, though.

There’s no milk jug, which isn’t unprecedented, but is still a kick in the teeth. Casabrews also ships its budget machines with no milk jug, but it sells one for $10. Amzchef doesn’t sell a milk jug at all, so you’ll have to buy a separate one from another brand.

On top of that, the steam wand is supposed to have a 360° swivel, but I’d describe it more as 200° grating. Every time I moved the steam wand, the metal grated against the ball joint.

There’s a bright screen with full-color pictures, which also houses the built-in timer and temperature adjustment screen. This screen is the best part of the machine’s design, although I’m not sure it’s enough of a unique selling point to recommend buying it.

Considering the Amzchef Espresso Machine has a built-in grinder, I was extremely concerned when I unboxed two pressurized portafilter baskets. If you don’t know the difference between pressurized and non-pressurized baskets, I’ll give you a quick rundown. Pressurized portafilter baskets use two walls to force the espresso through a little hole, which creates fluffier crema but destroys delicate flavors. You should use pressurized portafilter baskets if you have pre-ground coffee or an inferior grinder (subtle foreshadowing).

Non-pressurized portafilter baskets have a mesh-like bottom, which allows the espresso to extract naturally, with no extra pressure — that all comes from the fineness of the grind. These baskets are a little trickier to use for beginners, but brew delicate, nuanced espresso if you have a good grinder and good beans.

So I was immediately suspicious when I saw the pressurized baskets. If I’m using a machine with a built-in grinder — ergo, freshly ground coffee — surely I should be provided non-pressurized baskets? A dual-walled basket will over-pressurize my espresso and mask delicate flavors.

Anyway, I had to use what Amzchef provided, so I, of course, tested it with said pressurized baskets.

By default, the grinder grinds for 7 seconds. This resulted in 17.3g of coffee during my tests, but obviously this will change if you grind finer or coarser for different beans. I set the grinder to click 5, as this pulled the ideal 1:2 ratio in 25-28 seconds.

Then, the machine automatically doses water. It pulled 35g of coffee in 28 seconds, which is almost the perfect 1:2 ratio in 25-28 seconds.

Here’s a photo of said default shot. This is with zero customizations — straight from the machine’s brain.

The crema is a little flat, and there’s not a whole lot of depth to the shot. I usually love watching the black ‘body’ of the shot rise up after extraction, but that wasn’t the case with this espresso. It brewed this dark amber color and this dark amber color it remained. As for the taste, it was a little bitter, not particularly strong or weak, but it got the job done. If you’re a total beginner, this would be good enough, but coffee enthusiasts would be better off elsewhere.

However, coffee enthusiasts might be the intended target audience here. There are a few premium, coffee snob-certified features on the Amzchef. You’ve got a PID controller, which controls water temperature, and you can customize temps to your liking. It can go from 190°-201°F, more versatile than Breville’s set-at-200°F PID controller, which you’d find on the $299 Breville Bambino or the $499 Breville Bambino Plus.

All of these features are excellent — I wouldn’t buy an espresso machine without — and resulted in decent espresso. Pressurized portafilters aside, this coffee sits firmly in the “good enough” category. Especially for $229, which is crazy cheap.

I have never seen a bean-to-cup semi-automatic espresso machine cheaper than the Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder. I’ve tested $350 models — the aforementioned Casabrews Marenza and Gevi Espresso Machine with Grinder — but $229? That’s crazy cheap.

The grinder itself has 44 settings, so you can grind from superfine to cold-brew-coarse. As mentioned earlier, the grinder grinds for 7 seconds by default, which you can adjust. To test uniformity, I used my Kruve Coffee Sieves ($189). As espresso grounds should be 300-400 microns, I sift ground coffee through the 500-micron sieve. I’m looking for 100% pass-through. I used click 5 to test espresso, which extracted a 1:2 ratio in 28 seconds.

Here’s a photo to exemplify what I mean. The left is coffee bigger than 500 microns, and the right is coffee smaller than 500 microns (espresso size).

As you can see, this is a non-uniform, inconsistent grinder… and now I know why Amzchef only provides you dual-walled portafilters.

The steam wand is one of the biggest let-dows of the whole machine. It’s weak, spluttery, and takes over sixty seconds to steam a jug of milk (for one coffee).

To activate the steam wand itself, you have to press the steam graphic on the screen, not twist the knob on the side. After pressing the graphic, and the machine reading 107 (temperature), then you twist the knob. It needs a few seconds to switch to steam.

However, the steam wand is really disappointing. I still managed to get half-decent latte art, but the actual texture of the milk was undesirable. It had a layer of foam on top and then wet milk — no velvety aeration throughout.

As you can see, the latte art is still good. But this is after years of practice. I don’t think this is a good machine for beginners to learn on, because you have to know how to tease out “good” milk texture from a sub-par wand.

I don’t really have anything positive to say about the steam wand. If you aren’t fussed about milk drinks, this might be something you can overlook, but for me, I live for decadent, velvety milk, so it’d be a pass.

As it’s just 13 inches wide and 13 inches deep, the Amzchef Espresso Machine is relatively compact, especially for a bean-to-cup machine. If you’re seriously short on space (and budget), I might recommend the Amzchef, but that’s a might.

The machine has an “aluminum alloy” boiler, which means it’s more susceptible to corrosion than a stainless steel boiler, however, there’s no water filter slot in the water tank. Either the machine won’t last as long as a stainless steel boiler, or you’ll need to be seriously on top of descaling — even if you live in a soft water area. There are also no cleaning discs or a cleaning portafilter basket cover for backflushing, unlike Breville and De’Longhi’s machines.

Amzchef advertizes a 2-year warranty if you purchase from the Amzchef website, but the espresso machine is $70 more expensive on the Amzchef site (at time of writing — Amzchef has told me it will correct this). If you register it, the warranty increases to three years. However, you have to spend an extra $70 buying it directly from Amzchef. On the Amzchef warranty page, it reads, “Buy from Amazon, Walmart, or other online retailers? You may get an up-to-2-year limited warranty.” Schrödinger’s warranty!

Amzchef’s representative confirmed that you receive a 2-year warranty regardless of retailer, which is great news, but the language is still too opaque. What if you didn’t have a direct link to the company to find out this information (as I assume most of you won’t)? The language needs to be clearer.

Opaque business practices like this make me incredibly wary about recommending a product. It’s disingenuous. I wouldn’t spend my hard-earned money at a company with obfuscated warranty rules.

Everything about the Amzchef Espresso Machine feels too good to be true. A PID controller, customizable brew temperature, built-in grinder, cold brew, and 360° swivel steam wand for $229? There’s something not quite right here — and you can feel it in the build quality. The water tank is flimsy, the grinder hopper is flimsy, the portafilter is flimsy, and the steam wand grates as it moves. Not only that, but the steam wand is relatively weak, and the low-quality grinder makes for mediocre espresso.

This is a tricky one, because $229 is incredibly cheap for an espresso machine with a grinder. Normally, you’d be expecting to pay $229 for the espresso machine alone and an extra $229 for the grinder — and that would be cheap.

However, I can’t recommend this machine due to its low-quality build, low-quality accessories, and low-quality grinder. I would recommend grabbing the $350 Casabrews Marenza instead (but that’s also incredibly flimsy), or save up more for the Breville Barista Express — often around $499 during sales events like Black Friday — or the De’Longhi Arte Evo — also around $450 during sales events.

#3368. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3367. iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, details here

iOS 27.2 recently launched with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s new.

One of my favorite additions to Messages this year, Suggested Actions, debuts in iOS 27.2.

Suggested Actions appear underneath messages in a conversation when relevant. They can suggest creating a calendar event or reminder, adding to a note, and more based on the context of the message.

The feature was originally part of the iOS 27 beta this summer, but didn’t make the public build. Now it’s back in iOS 27.2, new and improved. There’s also an option to fine-tune which types of suggestions you’ll see.

Read more: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite

Every major streaming service has its own profiles feature, letting users on the same account keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. Apple TV has long offered such a feature in tvOS, but now with iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 it’s coming to iPhone and iPad too.

When you launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll be greeted by a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it if you don’t want to see if again. But if you ever share your iPhone with kids, the new profiles feature should come in handy.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

Dual Capture is one of FaceTime’s best new features in years. Added in iOS 27, on compatible iPhones it lets you keep your front and rear cameras both active at the same time while on a FaceTime call.

iOS 27.2 brings a key upgrade to Dual Capture: it’s now available for Group FaceTime calls.

To use the feature, just hit the flip camera button like usual, and by default on iPhone 17 and newer you’ll stream both camera feeds simultaneously.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Timed with its new Home products push, Apple adds a pair of new Home app features in iOS 27.2 for compatible smart locks.

‘Lock After Closing’ is a new automation setting that lets you choose how long after a door is closed that it should lock automatically. Previously you could only set a duration based on the time since a door was unlocked, not closed.

‘Door Left Open’ tackles a related, but distinct problem: a door being left open too long. With compatible locks, you can configure the Home app to automatically notify you if a door has been left open for a certain period of time.

Read more: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week

Apple Podcasts keeps getting better, with AI-powered automatic chapters and transcripts some of my favorite features. And in iOS 27.2, Apple has a welcome change to the Up Next queue on the Home tab.

Up Next is now split into two separate queues: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

Without the redesigned Health app, none of the new features appeal to me all that much. But performance improvements, bug fixes, and security fixes are always welcomed. What most of really wants is faster and more reliable Siri AI, along with support for a wider range of personal data, such as PDF documents on the iCloud Drive.

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.

Apple’s Games app introduces some small updates in iOS 27.2 as well.

The Home tab now shows you recently downloaded games that you haven’t yet played. Previously, you would only see games with some play activity. And Apple says achievement progress and leaderboard scores have been updated in the Home tab to be easier to track. Finally, the Friends tab “provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages” per Apple.

Which new iOS 27.2 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

#3366. ‘The Rings of Power’ Made the Right Call Saying Goodbye to This Storyline in Season 3

Editor's note: The below contains spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3.

Truth be told, The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has been pretty hit-or-miss over the past few years. Distinct departures from character and lore, poorly written dialogue, and odd pacing were struggles during the first season and carried over into the second as well. Fortunately, Season 3 has stuck more closely to J.R.R. Tolkien's works than ever, and part of that has to do with the consolidation and even eradication of certain storylines and characters. With four episodes premiering this week to kick off the third season, one thing has become abundantly clear: cutting out the Harfoots was absolutely the right move for the show.

We all love spending time in the Shire in The Lord of the Rings, and The Hobbit would not exist without Bilbo Baggins, but, without a doubt, the worst storyline in The Rings of Power's first two seasons was the traveling Harfoots. Nori (Markella Kavenagh) and Poppy (Megan Richards) were likable enough, but the whole thing felt like a discount Frodo and Sam story. While Hobbits are essential to the end of the Third Age of Middle-earth, their ancestors, the Harfoots, are nothing more than a blip in Tolkien's writings, and certainly not of grave importance in the Second Age. This is, in effect, why Bilbo, Frodo, Sam, and the others are so notable in The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings. For centuries, halflings were overlooked and undervalued, but Gandalf (played by Daniel Weyman here) sees something in them that Sauron (Charlie Vickers) would never expect.

The cast and creators break down the show's most personal storyline yet for Tolkien's most iconic wizard.

On The Rings of Power, the Harfoots always felt like an afterthought, like a good idea meant to echo what folks loved about The Lord of the Rings but without the traits that made them so endearing. In many respects, they felt out of place considering the events occurring around them, and unlike Tolkien's two seminal works where halflings were the main characters, the show had far too many threads to follow in order to do them justice. Any time they were on-screen, the entire tone of the program was altered — and not always in a fun, Tom Bombadil (Rory Kinnear) kind of way. Without them, The Rings of Power not only flows more smoothly, but also has the chance to finally expand on plotlines that were largely ignored or underdeveloped in previous seasons.

The truth is that The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit will always be the best Hobbit stories. Part of that is because Tolkien invented Hobbits in the first place and knows them unlike any other, and part of that is that their most heroic stories were always meant to be about Frodo and Bilbo. Beyond that, Hobbit culture as we know it is more refined and cozy by the Third Age, which means that The Rings of Power never really had the chance to nostalgically take fans to the very place that most associate with the Hobbits. As a result, the Harfoots always felt shoehorned in rather than a natural part of the larger story the Prime Video series has been telling. It's one thing for The Rings of Power to create new characters to supplement the adventures of Second Age staples like Galadriel, Elendil (Lloyd Owen), and Durin IV (Owain Arthur), but it's another entirely to insert Gandalf and then pair him with halflings like a page out of The Fellowship of the Ring.

If you want more Hobbits, Harfoots, or other halflings (and don't forget the Stoors, too), the best thing you can do is read Tolkien's "Concerning Hobbits" chapter of The Lord of the Rings. The next best thing is to revisit the rest of the books or even the Peter Jackson films themselves. As for The Rings of Power, Season 3 has finally hit its stride with a more focused plot, more well-rounded characters, and every storyline building toward something meaningful as Sauron threatens to rule over Middle-earth.

New episodes of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 are available for streaming Wednesdays on Prime Video.

#3358. Nicolas Cage Officially Confirms Why He’s Happy His Marvel Series Was Cancelled

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Nicolas Cage had already played a Spider-Man who sounded like he’d walked out of an old detective movie in the genre-defining Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Giving that idea eight hours of live action was a different proposition. In Spider-Noir, Cage plays Ben Reilly as a down-on-his-luck private investigator in Depression-era New York, with a past he’d rather leave alone. Prime Video even let viewers choose between color and black-and-white versions. The actor had plenty of room to see how far he could take the performance, and it turns out eight episodes was exactly as far as he wanted to go.

Prime Video canceled the series in September, a little over three months after it released. Spider-Noir drew 2.6 billion U.S. viewing minutes in its first six weeks, according to Nielsen, and earned 11 Emmy nominations. There were reasons for fans to expect another season. Cage, who’d already called one season enough in a statement after the cancellation, went a little further when he was asked about it on the Madden red carpet.

Cage told IGN in a recent interview that he was relieved Prime Video passed on Spider-Noir Season 2 because he worried that repeating his performance as Ben Reilly would wear out its welcome. He described the role as “pretty high-risk, tightrope stuff” and said the choices he made could lose their appeal over a second or third season. His reaction to the cancellation was simple: “Whew, thank you!”

Four powers, and four completely different kinds of person behind them. Here is what you would wake up with, what it would cost you, and why the MCU keeps handing it to somebody exactly like you.

You get the power that is really about taking the hit so that nobody else has to. Strength in the MCU always lands on people who were already carrying too much, which is exactly why it suits you.

You get the power that never switches off. Spider-sense is a gift and a nervous system on permanent alert, and the people who get it in these films are always the ones who were already worrying about everybody.

You get the quietest power in the building, and quietly the most useful. Invisibility comes with force fields for a reason, because the people who prefer not to be seen are usually the ones holding a shield around everybody else.

You get the biggest and least comfortable power on the list, the one that runs directly on feeling. Chaos magic is not really a superpower in the MCU so much as an emotional state with consequences attached.

Cage brought up True Detective in the same answer. He’s set to star alongside Antonio Banderas in the HBO anthology’s fifth season, where a single season is the deal going in. That gives him another detective to play and a defined stretch of time to figure out how he wants to play him. It also gives some context to what he meant by calling Spider-Noir a “perfect season.” He got to make the version of Ben Reilly he wanted to make, and he likes where he left him.

Cage has separately said he refused to sign an AI waiver for Spider-Noir and doubts he’ll work with Amazon again. In the IGN interview, his explanation for welcoming the end was about the performance itself. Plus, there’s something fitting about Cage getting a whole season to play a man who’s reluctant to put the suit back on and then deciding he’s happy to leave it hanging.

Season 1, which will be the only season Prime Video releases of Spider-Noir, is available to stream.

#3357. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

#3354. Apple to investigate accident that killed three workers at iPhone parts factory in India

Reuters reports that three contract workers died after inhaling gas during an inspection at a Tata Electronics factory that produces iPhone components in India. Here are the details.

As frequent 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple’s supply chain in India relies heavily on Tata, which manufactures iPhone components and accounts for a significant share of the country’s iPhone assembly operations.

Since Apple began diversifying its manufacturing operations away from China, India has emerged as a major production hub, with roughly a quarter of the world’s iPhones now manufactured in the country.

Earlier this year, Apple found itself linked to an environmental controversy in India, after the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board investigated allegations that wastewater from a Tata facility had contaminated nearby farmland water.

A few weeks later, however, Tata said the regulator had dropped further action against the facility after the company addressed the concerns raised.

At the time, Tata said it had ordered separate testing related to the facility and that the results supported its position that the plant was operating within the rules.

However, the matter was apparently not fully resolved, as just three days later, Reuters reported that local health officials were still investigating complaints from nearby farmers.

And while there had been no major developments reported about the wastewater investigation since then, Reuters reported today that three contract workers died in an accident at the same Tata facility.

The three contract workers died during maintenance work on an effluent treatment ​plant operated by Nalco Water at the Tata facility, which is located in Hosur in Tamil Nadu, ​district official Dinesh Kumar said, adding that the deaths occurred when the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank.

Reuters added that “Apple’s team is visiting ​the plant to assist in ​the ongoing investigation,” though the company did not respond when reached for comment.

The report added that Tata and Tamil Nadu authorities are also investigating the fatal accident, and noted that “production was not affected as the facility was closed for the Hindu festival of Deepavali this week.”

There are usually some invite-only deals that you can sign up for.

But if you only take one bit of advice for shopping on Amazon, let it be this one: Don't buy anything you weren't going to buy anyway. A good way to make sure you do this is by making a list of the products you do want, and only having eyes for those.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: Think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that you're less likely to see throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

I’ve been testing the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots for the last month on all of my hikes, and they’ve proved to be some of the best hiking boots for any season and any terrain. They look the part too, which helps me feel unstoppable on the trail.

The boots are comfortable out of the box and offer excellent traction as well as good cushioning and support on the trail. They are waterproof for all weather and are very durable with a tear-resistant upper.

Bear in mind that these boots have a narrow fit and don’t come in a wide size option, but that’s the only real downside to these excellent stompers. To find out more about my experience, you can keep reading this full La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX review.

Mocha/Redwood, Cypress/Azalea, Carbon/Redwood, Gravel/Cypress

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are available to purchase on the La Sportiva website for $249 in the U.S. and £220 in the U.K. The color selection differs between territories. In the U.S., there are only two choices — Carbon/Redwood or Mocha/Redwood — and in the U.K. you can choose from Cypress/Azalea, Carbon/Redwood or Gravel/Cypress. You can also purchase the shoes on Amazon for $310 in the U.S., but sizes and colors are limited.

When deciding on the boot size, you will need to convert from European sizing, since this is how the boots are sold on the site. The boots are available in women’s EUR sizes 36 to 42.5 with half sizes, and men’s EUR sizes 40 to 48.5 with half sizes. I’m usually a U.K. size 5 and needed to size up since the boots have a very snug fit. I ended up purchasing an EUR size 39, which is a U.K. size 6 and a U.S. women’s size 7.5.

These boots are certainly on the more expensive side, but it’s not hard to see why. They’re very well made and comfortable to walk in. Also very supportive are the Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid GTX. These boots cost $240, but this is the price to pay for a boot you’d happily spend your life walking in.

Another boot with excellent ankle support is the Keen Targhee IV, which costs $169. They’ve been my go-to boots for taking on the outdoors for over a year now, but I think the La Sportivas could end their reign.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

After speaking to friends and colleagues, it turns out the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots are a bit like cilantro — you either love it, or you hate it with a burning passion. But to me, they’re perfect. I like the look of the boots and the available colorways. They look like they mean business when you’re out on the trail.

The boots are perfect for narrow feet, and lace up for a snug, albeit supportive, fit. However, there’s no wide fit option, so those with wide feet need to look elsewhere, such as the Keen Targhee IV.

The upper is made from nubuck leather and a breathable Gore-Tex lining for a water-resistant finish. They coped well with heavy rain and deep puddles, and are also tear-resistant, so they can withstand even the rockiest terrain. The lacing system is very supportive, and cinched in all the right places to ensure a comfortable walk.

Although the laces get tight, my ankles moved freely. In other boots, I’ve been used to having a limited range of movement around my ankles like the Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid GTX, but these felt a lot more forgiving.

The La Sportiva boots have a footbed boost of 5mm, which is simply the insole height. This contributes to the cushioning of the boot and felt like it contoured to my feet. The drop value of 8mm (from heel to toe) also helped me get the best posture possible.

Usually, in other boots, I experience some strain on my lower back as a result of a smaller drop value, as there’s more pressure on my calves. Instead, I felt supported. The flex system with the CM EVE foam (a lightweight, rubber foam) also helps with rebound.

The outsole provided me with a lot of grip for every terrain I walked on. The lugs of the boot, which dig into the ground to provide traction, measure 4.5mm tall. This is a good height for grip and I find it to be the sweet spot, with most of my Keen boots also sitting in this range. The soles are made of Vibram rubber, so they absorb a lot of the impact of the ground, which helped reduce strain when walking over longer distances.

I have no complaints about the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots and their comfort level. I wore them right out of the box with no issues. My first walk in these boots took me through gravel, muddy fields, and shallow running water. The traction and flex felt great right off the bat.

The toe box of the boots is quite narrow, but this really wasn’t an issue for me. In fact, since my feet are very narrow, the ideal fit gave me more control, providing a more stable hiking experience.

My only very slight qualm is that my feet naturally swell from heat when walking, so the boots can start to feel a little tight. It’s obviously good that the lace-up system doesn’t slip, but sometimes, a little bit of give is a good thing, as you can move more freely. With that said, it didn’t cause me any major pain or blisters.

Cushioning in these boots is ideal. It took away some of the impact, especially when walking over bigger rocks and generally rough terrain, but I could still feel what was going on underfoot. The Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid boots also let you feel the ground beneath your feet through the soles, and this is a feature I’ve come to really appreciate.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are easily some of my favorite boots.. They’re comfortable, cushioned, and support me across any terrain. The cushioning helps support my knees by reducing impact.

The 4.5mm lugs on the outsole of the hiking boots made me feel stable across all terrain I walked on. Even on slippery surfaces like wet rocks, the Vibram soles provided a lot of grip, and I didn’t slip once despite my clumsy disposition.

The arch support is great, and this in turn improved my posture. Since the lace-up system is tight for narrow feet, I felt a lot of support from the side walls — these two things combined stopped my feet from turning inward as I walked and boosted protection for my ankles by increasing my overall stability.

The boots have a moderate amount of flex, but never bent too much. I had complete support where I needed it. The most flex is happening in the toe box, which worked perfectly for me, especially when navigating uneven, tricky terrain.

Waterproofing on the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots is very effective. I went out hiking in the pouring rain, and my socks stayed completely dry. My walk also took me through puddles and shallow running water, and luckily my feet stayed dry and warm. I know I’ll be able to rely on these boots for all seasons.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are easy to maintain, just like any other leather boot. If they get muddy on the trail, remove the laces and gently brush off any dry mud. Then, use a damp cloth to remove any stubborn stains. Let the boots air-dry naturally and avoid artificial heat, as it can compromise the boot's integrity.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are some of my favorite boots. They were comfortable and ready for a long walk right out of the box, and felt durable, even on trickier terrain. The boots provided excellent traction and stability across mud, gravel, and sand, and the waterproofing withstood stormy weather.

Although the cushioning and support are good, it’s worth noting that the boots fit narrowly. For people with wider feet, this boot simply won’t fit even if you size up, and unfortunately, La Sportiva doesn’t offer a wide fit option.

Nevertheless, this is still a great all-rounder boot to support you on the toughest adventures, and one I certainly recommend.

#3350. CleanupBuddy 2.0 expands beyond the keyboard with new display cleaning features

Developer Gui Rambo updated CleanupBuddy today, expanding its ability to prevent accidental inputs while cleaning your Mac from the keyboard to the touchscreen. Here are the details.

If you’re not familiar with CleanupBuddy, this is a nice little app that locks the keyboard to prevent accidental inputs while the user cleans it up.

Once they’re done cleaning, users can press and hold both Cmd keys to unlock the keyboard, then proceed to grease it up again.

The app also features a fun little animated character that reacts to your cleaning sessions with playful (and sometimes snarky) comments.

Today, CleanupBuddy was updated to version 2.0, with options to dim the display and ignore touch inputs, making it useful for users of both the new touchscreen MacBook Pro and Macs with traditional displays.

You can use the new “Lock Touch Screen” option to block touch input while cleaning a supported touch screen. On Macs without a touch screen, the “Dim Display” option can still be used to darken the display for easier cleaning.

Today’s update also tweaks the in-app character, which now uses on-device Apple Intelligence to generate personalized comments before and after cleaning sessions, based on stats such as time spent cleaning, key presses, and mouse clicks.

Rambo explains that these stats are collected only during cleaning sessions and stored locally on the Mac, and that users can independently turn off both cleanup stats and Apple Intelligence integration in the app’s settings.

Other tweaks in today’s update include temporarily disabling Sticky Keys and its Shift-key shortcut during cleaning sessions, as well as improving the readability of the “Start Cleanup” button when using Liquid Glass.

CleanupBuddy 2.0 is available for $2.99 and is compatible with macOS 14 and later, while the new personalized messages require macOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled and its models ready to use.

#3349. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3347. iFixit tears down touchscreen MacBook Pro, reveals light-up Apple logo details

iFixit published its teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display today, revealing interesting details about how Apple brought back its illuminated logo on the lid. Watch it below.

iFixit’s teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is now live, and it explores not only how the new illuminated Apple logo works, but also its tandem OLED and how Apple managed to trim its weight down to 3 pounds (1.38 kg) from 3.4 pounds (1.55 kg) on the standard 14-inch model.

The teardown opens with a close look at the tandem OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers to deliver higher brightness than conventional single-layer OLED displays.

Under a microscope, iFixit found that the blue subpixels are larger than the red and green ones, which they say should help reduce strain on the materials and potentially extend the display’s lifespan.

Most of the teardown process is quite familiar from past models, though iFixit noted that replacing the USB-C ports or fans still requires removing the entire logic board, despite both components being independently replaceable.

iFixit noted that the headphone jack also requires logic board removal, while the HDMI port, SDXC port, RAM, and storage remain soldered to the board.

As with past teardowns, iFixit also tested what happens when swapping logic boards between two MacBooks.

While last year’s M5 MacBook Pro failed to complete Touch ID calibration through Apple’s Repair Assistant, iFixit noted that the new model successfully recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor after a logic board swap, with True Tone, brightness controls, and the touchscreen all working as expected.

iFixit was also able to enroll a fingerprint with the donor board installed from another MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

As for the illuminated Apple logo, iFixit had a bit of a rough time getting to it, destroying the OLED panel in the process and even asking whether anyone had managed to remove it intact.

Once inside, iFixit found that the Apple logo is illuminated by a strip of four LEDs, which work in conjunction with a reflective layer and a diffuser to distribute the light evenly.

The Apple logo itself, in turn, has a two-way mirror coating that gives it a shiny, reflective appearance when the LEDs are off, while allowing light to pass through when they’re on.

When it comes to weight, Apple shaved 92 grams off the chassis and 101 grams off the display assembly, despite adding touch and an illuminated logo. The battery is just 2 grams lighter, while the slightly smaller trackpad saves another 8 grams.

Finally, iFixit gave the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display a repairability score of 5 out of 10. That was one point higher than last year’s M5 MacBook Pro, but one point below the cheaper MacBook Neo.

#3346. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.
